2011-01-26 · seizure. Days after the union's heads of state removed the BCEAO's governor, Laurent Gbagbo ordered the seizure of the Ivorian branches of the Central Bank of West African States, to keep control of state finances and his hold on power. The bank had said it would no longer honour his signature. Alassane Ouattara, the internationally recognised winner of the November 2010 election, responded by ordering the Ivorian branches closed and said anyone following Gbagbo's orders would be prosecuted; his parallel government, operating from a hotel in Abidjan under United Nations guard, said the closure was intended to secure the financial assets of the Ivorian state and of individuals. Guillaume Soro, Ouattara's prime minister, said that when Gbagbo goes to the BCEAO in Abidjan with tanks and Kalashnikovs he cannot but trigger bank closures and halt cash flow. Officials said the Gbagbo government had managed to pay pensioners through the bank the day before the seizure; diplomats said the amount of money held locally was small against his needs, which included a monthly wage bill of about 100 million dollars for the army and public sector. On 9 February 2011 the Gbagbo administration also seized the Bourse Regionale des Valeurs Mobilieres, the regional stock exchange, which then ceased operating in Abidjan. International banks left the country and the financial system largely stopped: money was paid into accounts that depositors could not withdraw from. Gbagbo was captured on 11 April 2011. Gbagbo seizes central bank branches (Al Jazeera)
2011-01-22 · forced resignation. The Central Bank of West African States is the central bank of eight countries, and in January 2011 its own member heads of state removed its governor. After the disputed Ivorian presidential election of November 2010, the bank recognised Alassane Ouattara as head of state and revoked Laurent Gbagbo's access to Ivorian state accounts in December, and the union's finance ministers decided on 23 December that only representatives of Ouattara's government would have signing authority. The Ouattara camp complained in mid-January that the bank was still channelling cash to Gbagbo, and the governor, Philippe-Henry Dacoury-Tabley, an Ivorian and a close confidant of Gbagbo, was accused of not cooperating. At an emergency summit of the heads of state of the West African Economic and Monetary Union in Bamako on 22 January 2011 he handed in his resignation. The bank's own statement, issued in Dakar that evening, said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders. He told reporters afterwards: "I agreed to hand in my resignation as that is what was asked of me", and defended his conduct by pointing to practical and technical reasons for not transferring control of the accounts. The union accepted the resignation and called on Ouattara to propose a successor; a deputy governor, Jean-Baptiste Compaore, took over in the interim. Gbagbo's administration, on state television it still controlled, rejected what it called the forced resignation of the governor and rejected the leaders' decision to let Ouattara name a replacement. The European Union listed Dacoury-Tabley, giving as its ground that as governor of the BCEAO he refused to recognise the authority of the democratically elected President and was helping to fund the illegitimate administration of Mr Laurent Gbagbo. This record is the removal of the governor by the member states; what he is alleged to have done with the bank's money is recorded separately as a corruption case. Keyed to the union, so it counts for all eight member countries. Pro-Gbagbo bank head quits (Al Jazeera)

The agreement provides that the currency will be renamed 'ECO'; the Banque de France page says the name 'is set to change' at member states' will, i.e. the CFA franc name remains in use.
ECOWAS Convergence Council (7 September 2026) kept 2027 as the target launch year for an ECOWAS single currency named the ECO.

Cameroon's money, the Central African CFA franc, is issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The franc is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, France guarantees its convertibility, and the BEAC must keep at least 50% of its foreign reserves at the French Treasury. CENTRAL BANK OF THE CONGO
DR Congo
The Central Bank of the Congo issues the country's money. In April 2021 a report by Congo's state finance inspectorate, the IGF, called a 43 million US dollar transfer from a central bank account at BGFI Bank to the food importer Egal an embezzlement of public funds, and said the bank kept false accounts to cover it: its 2013 accounts showed about 43.1 million dollars in that account when the real balance was about 119,000 dollars. The former governor Deogratias Mutombo, the bank and PricewaterhouseCoopers did not respond to the journalists who reported this from leaked BGFI documents. On 25 October 2023 the accounts of Mutombo and of Albert Yuma, former board chairman of the mining company Gecamines, were frozen over an alleged embezzlement of 25.521 million dollars, with both men required to remain available to the national audit court; that allegation is unproven and still under investigation. Belgium's federal prosecutor also opened a money laundering investigation into Mutombo and five others, with searches in September 2023; as of October 2024 the prosecutor said no suspect had been charged. The bank scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Giesecke+Devrient printed the 200-franc note issued on 31 July 2007. The bank's accounts are audited by Ernst & Young RDC of Kinshasa, which gave an unqualified opinion on the year ended 31 December 2024.

BANK OF CENTRAL AFRICAN STATES (BEAC)
Congo-Brazzaville
Congo-Brazzaville uses the XAF, issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The XAF is pegged, meaning held at a fixed rate, at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees to supply euros if the region cannot pay for imports. On a scale where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Congo-Brazzaville scores 45, more exposed than 92% of places with a figure, mainly from corruption in the country and money-laundering risk. One BEAC case is documented: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from its Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008, and on 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs. The bank's governor from July 2007, Philibert Andzembe, a Gabonese national, was fired in October 2009 by Gabon's president Ali Bongo in response to a scandal in which 28.3 million US dollars went missing from the bank's Paris branch; Gabon held the right to appoint the governor at the time, and Lucas Abaga Nchama of Equatorial Guinea took the post in 2010. A separate leaked US diplomatic cable, made public in December 2010, alleged that Gabonese officials working at the bank had taken about 36 million US dollars from the pooled reserves over roughly five years. The BEAC must deposit at least 50 per cent of the zone's foreign exchange reserves in an operations account (compte d'operations) opened in its name at the French Treasury, a share cut from 65 per cent in 2007. The required share earns interest at the European Central Bank's marginal lending facility rate, 0.25 per cent since 16 March 2016, and anything the BEAC chooses to deposit above that share earns the ECB's minimum rate on main refinancing operations, 0 per cent since 16 March 2016. KPMG Afrique Centrale and Mazars Cameroun audit the accounts jointly. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The BEAC's own site cannot be read by automated requests, so this does not rest on a BEAC document.

BANK OF THE REPUBLIC (COLOMBIA)
Colombia
The Bank of the Republic issues Colombia's peso and prints it at its own banknote works; it is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks themselves. One case is recorded: in 2011 two officials were investigated for allegedly passing reserved information about people and companies to the DAS security agency and were suspended for a month, but in January 2011 the bank reported that the Procuraduria's ruling on appeal revoked the suspension, finding they had broken no rule. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, each time to cut rates. On 31 July 2025, after the board voted 4 to 3 to hold the rate at 9.25 per cent, President Gustavo Petro accused the bank of wanting to “finish off the economy” and of having an electoral bet. Amundi won a mandate in 2023, as one of eight outside managers, over 1.7 billion US dollars of its assets, and its reserve gold sits in the custody of the Bank of England, which is storage rather than management. Leonardo Villar became general manager in January 2021 after serving as an executive director at the International Monetary Fund.

CENTRAL BANK OF THE COMOROS
Comoros
The Central Bank of the Comoros issues the Comorian franc, and France stands behind it. A monetary cooperation agreement signed at Moroni and Paris on 23 November 1979 rests on an unlimited French guarantee of the currency the bank issues. That agreement set the rate at 1 Comorian franc to 0.02 French francs; after a devaluation of 33 percent on 11 January 1994, the rate is now 1 euro to 491.968 Comorian francs. The bank must keep 65 percent of its foreign currency reserves on deposit with the French Treasury. Under statutes in force since March 2025, France names two of the six board members, two of the four members of the banking supervision committee and two of the four members of the committee that sets monetary policy and manages reserves. The notes are printed by the Banque de France, the French central bank; a new 10,000-franc note was reportedly introduced on 6 January 2026. Independence written into its law scores 0.439 of 1 on one index and 0.682 on another, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power. The Cayman Islands Monetary Authority acts as the central bank of the Cayman Islands, and the currency is the Cayman Islands dollar. A commemorative 70-dollar note for the Platinum Jubilee of Queen Elizabeth II, introduced on 12 October 2023, was printed by De La Rue and is not part of the circulating series. CZECH NATIONAL BANK
Czechia
The Czech National Bank issues the koruna and scores 20 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, leaving it less exposed than 95 percent of the places measured. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks themselves. Ales Michl was an economist and investment strategist at Raiffeisenbank from 2006 to 2015 and an external economic adviser to the finance ministry from 2014 to 2018 and later to Prime Minister Andrej Babis, joined the bank's board in December 2018 and was then appointed governor in succession to Jiri Rusnok. Czech Television reports that he founded Michl Fund Management in 2016, which co-founded the qualified-investor fund Robot Asset Management SICAV, that he later placed the company in a trust, and that some experts believe he may still have influence over it, which he denies; no ethics finding is recorded. In 2026 police arrested a long-serving employee accused of misappropriating tens of millions of koruna, after suspicious transactions on his account were flagged; the bank confirmed the theft was being investigated at its Brno branch, and the accusation is unproven. Government pressure was reported in 3 of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, all of it pressing for tighter policy, alongside three threats to replace leaders. The president of the Czech Republic appoints all seven members of the bank board alone, and on 18 February 2015 President Milos Zeman said he would appoint nobody who favoured devaluing the koruna and would name members who backed adopting the euro, at a time when the bank was holding the koruna weak against the euro; Andrej Babis, then finance minister, called that an unacceptable interference with the bank's independence. Zeman had five of the seven seats to fill before March 2018, and the bank kept the policy. State Street Global Advisors has held an equity mandate from the bank since 2007, since raised to 7.5 billion US dollars, and also advises it on alternatives to its reserve strategies; BNP Paribas Asset Management agreed a 500 million dollar mortgage-backed securities mandate in November 2019; and Ernst & Young Audit, s.r.o. audits the accounts. Some of the gold is kept in the bank's own high-security vault in Prague, mostly for making its gold coins, with most of the reserve stored in London under no named institution, which is storage rather than management. A commemorative banknote marking the establishment of the Czechoslovak currency, which entered circulation on 30 March 2022, carries the imprint of Statni tiskarna cenin; who prints the circulating notes is not stated.

2015-02-18 · public pressure. The president of the Czech Republic appoints every member of the seven-member Czech National Bank bank board alone, and in February 2015 President Milos Zeman said publicly what he would use that power for. Speaking on Wednesday 18 February 2015 he said he would not appoint anyone who favoured devaluing the Czech crown, and would name board members who backed adopting the euro - a direct condition on monetary policy views for a seat on the board. The bank was at the time holding the crown weak through a floor against the euro. On the same day, reported by bne IntelliNews on 20 February 2015, Zeman accused the bank of using non-standard policy tools and of deliberately impeding the country's progress towards the euro; Finance Minister Andrej Babis called those comments an unacceptable interference with the bank's independence. The Prague Monitor of 22 February 2015 described the remarks as among Zeman's most outspoken attacks on the bank to date and reported that he intended to fill it with nominees sharing his own economic views, which brought a standing debate about whether the Czech central bank is independent enough to the surface. Zeman was in a position to choose five of the seven board members before the end of his first term in March 2018. The bank did not change course and kept the weak-crown policy. Zeman says he will not appoint central bank board members who favour devaluation (Prague Monitor)

p:DEU:
DEUTSCHE BUNDESBANK
Germany
Germany uses the euro, and its central bank, the Deutsche Bundesbank, applies the interest rates the European Central Bank sets for the 21 countries using the currency. Bundesbank president Ernst Welteke resigned on 16 April 2004 after criticism for accepting a free New Year stay at Berlin's Hotel Adlon, paid two years earlier by the commercial bank Dresdner Bank, which the Bundesbank supervises; prosecutors and the Bundesbank both opened inquiries. Two further matters concern the European Central Bank. The European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum including private bankers; the ECB declined and he did not. And on 18 May 2015 board member Cœuré told a private London event the ECB would bring forward asset purchases, in a speech published only the next morning, which the ECB called an internal procedure error. Leaders have moved into private finance: Axel Weber to the chairmanship of UBS, Jens Weidmann to chairman of Commerzbank's supervisory board in May 2023. Most of the gold is stored abroad rather than managed by others: of 3,381 tonnes at the end of 2015, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York held 1,347.4 tonnes, the Bank of England 434.7 and the Banque de France 196.4. In May 1997 the finance minister proposed changing the Bundesbank law to revalue the bank's gold and hand part of the paper profit to the federal government that year, which would have helped Germany meet the deficit criterion for joining the euro. The Bundesbank's council rejected it in public, saying the plan could be construed as an attack on the bank's independence, and the bank had to break its usual silence to deny that its president was resigning. The chancellor and the coalition said at first that they would change the law regardless. They backed down in early June: the gold could be revalued, but not counted towards that year's figures. Germany scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

1997-05 · attempted law change. In May 1997 the German finance minister, Theo Waigel, proposed changing the Bundesbank law to revalue the bank's 95 million ounces of gold and channel part of the resulting paper profit to the federal government in that year, which would have helped Germany meet the Maastricht deficit criterion for joining the euro. After an unusually long meeting, the Bundesbank's central council rejected the plan in a public statement saying it could be construed as an attack on the bank's independence and did not fit the planned rules of the future European Central Bank. President Hans Tietmeyer had warned a closed Bundestag budget committee against revaluation on 19 March and said publicly on 17 April that the question belonged to the ECB's governing council once appointed. Chancellor Helmut Kohl and the coalition leaders initially said they would change the law anyway and that the bank's independence would not be diminished. The Bundesbank had to break its news blackout to deny rumours that Tietmeyer was resigning. The government backed down in early June: the gold could be revalued, but the proceeds could not count towards the 1997 criteria. Waigel survived a parliamentary motion against him on 4 June 1997 by 328 votes to 311, and imposed the strictest budget freeze in the country's history that November instead. Bundesbank says no to Bonn over gold revaluation (The Irish Times)

CENTRAL BANK OF DJIBOUTI
Djibouti
The Central Bank of Djibouti, created in 1977, runs what is called a currency board: the Djibouti franc is held at a fixed rate of 1 US dollar to 177.721 francs and is backed entirely by US dollars, so the bank cannot issue francs without dollars behind them. The franc itself was created in March 1949, outside the franc zone. The independence written into its law scores 0.698 of 1, where 1 means the bank holds the power rather than the government, and four reforms since 1970 have all raised that score. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. It scores 56 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, the second highest of the 194 places with a figure, with money-laundering risk in its banks rated 6.93 of 10, the thirteenth riskiest of 177. The country has had one systemic banking crisis since 1970. Its 2021 accounts were audited by Deloitte Côte d'Ivoire.

p:DMA:
EASTERN CARIBBEAN CENTRAL BANK
Dominica
Dominica's money is the East Caribbean dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, which sets monetary policy for eight members: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. The rate has been fixed at EC$2.70 to one US dollar since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling, and the founding agreement of 5 July 1983 requires reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation and other demand liabilities. One case is recorded, and it was dismissed. After the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it had fraudulently misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors. On 17 August 2018 a United States federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions. Gonsalves wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable, and that the spending invites disciplinary action; he proposed that the Monetary Council, which is made up of the member states' finance ministers, sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis, and said he had supported Antoine's appointment but wanted suitable and comfortable accommodation for him instead. On 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are made of and, by one report on the updated family announced on 9 July 2026, prints them; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. Dominica scores 26 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, less than 83 per cent of the 194 places scored. The World Bank has a hand in running the reserves: the bank's 2020/2021 annual report says it continued its engagement with the World Bank's Reserves Advisory Management Partnership (RAMP), and that a second engagement was judged appropriate to go on building up its newly formed Risk and Analytics Unit, the unit that reports on the reserves portfolio. The same report says the investment guidelines for the bank's external managers were reviewed and updated, and that the foreign reserve portfolio had grown to about EC$4.6 billion. The engagement is not repeated in the later annual report for 2024/2025 or in the audited accounts to 31 March 2025, so it stands as a 2020/2021 fact.

DANMARKS NATIONALBANK
Denmark
Danmarks Nationalbank issues the Danish krone and holds it at a rate against the euro that is announced in advance. At the end of 2025 it held assets of 109.8 billion US dollars. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks, and PwC signed the auditor's report on its 2025 accounts. Oberthur Fiduciaire was chosen as banknote supplier under a four-year framework, with the first notes in circulation in 2020, and the bank has since agreed with De La Rue to produce a new Danish series at De La Rue's plant outside London, due for launch in 2028 under a contract running at least six years. It can borrow foreign currency under two swap lines: up to 30 billion US dollars from the United States, agreed on 19 March 2020 as a temporary pandemic facility and expired on 31 December 2021, and a standing 24,000 million euros from the European Central Bank. Since 2002 about 97 per cent of its roughly 66.5 tonnes of gold has been kept at the Bank of England in London and about 0.5 per cent at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, with about 2.5 per cent in Copenhagen; those are storage arrangements, not management. Lars Rohde, who chaired the Board of Governors from 2013 to 2023, had worked at the mortgage bank Realkredit Danmark until 1998 and then ran the statutory pension body ATP; he joined the board of the bank Nordea in 2024, and no ethics finding is recorded. Denmark scores 16 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

p:ECU:
CENTRAL BANK OF ECUADOR
Ecuador
Ecuador uses the US dollar as its only legal tender, adopted in January 2000 at 25,000 sucres to the dollar, so the Central Bank of Ecuador issues no money of its own. Nor does it decide policy. The 1998 constitution had given the bank independence; the constitution that replaced it, published on 20 October 2008 and sponsored by Rafael Correa's government, took it away. Article 303 makes the drafting of monetary, credit, foreign exchange and financial policy the exclusive power of the Executive, to be implemented through the Central Bank, and the bank's own website describes its role in exactly those terms. The monetary board was replaced by a board of five members appointed by the president and confirmed by Congress. The academic monetary and fiscal history of Ecuador prepared for the University of Chicago lists 2008 as the suppression of central bank independence, and states that the constitution made the bank dependent on the executive branch, which became responsible for designing fiscal and monetary policy. Article 303 is still in force, so this is the standing arrangement rather than an episode with an end. It scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weak points being corruption in the country and the risk of money laundering in its banks. One case is recorded and it ended in conviction: on 8 January 2019 the National Court of Justice sentenced Pedro Delgado, a former president of the bank, to five years in prison, restitution of 788,855.94 dollars, forfeiture of assets and public apologies. Prosecutors described the crime as unlawful association while the court's own post called it illicit enrichment; the same source reports an earlier embezzlement conviction in 2015 carrying eight years, and says he allegedly allowed large loans without proper documents or guarantees while leading the bank, which is unproven. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, pressing the bank to loosen policy, change the law and print money. The bank joined the World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, described as giving it advice, executive training and asset-management expertise rather than a mandate to run Ecuador's reserves. Its 2021 accounts were audited by Kreston Audit Services Ecuador, and it holds 26.3 tonnes of gold, 27.7 percent of its reserves.

2008-10-20 · law change. Ecuador's 1998 constitution had granted the Banco Central del Ecuador independence. The constitution that replaced it, sponsored by Rafael Correa's government and published in the Registro Oficial on 20 October 2008, removed it. Article 303 states that the drafting of monetary, credit, foreign exchange and financial policy is the exclusive power of the Executive, to be implemented through the Central Bank, and that the Central Bank is a public-law entity whose organisation and operation are set by law. The bank was left as the body that carries out policy rather than the body that makes it: its own website describes its role as implementing the policies formulated by the Executive under article 303. The monetary board was replaced by a central bank board of five members appointed by the president and confirmed by Congress. The academic monetary and fiscal history of Ecuador prepared for the University of Chicago's series lists 2008 as the suppression of central bank independence, alongside the suppression of the fiscal stabilisation funds, and states that the constitution removed the bank's autonomy and made it dependent on the executive branch, which became responsible for designing fiscal and monetary policy. The change was structural rather than an episode with an end: Ecuador has been dollarised since 2000, so the bank had no currency of its own to run, and article 303 remains in force. p:ESP:
BANK OF SPAIN
Spain
Spain uses the euro, so the Bank of Spain follows interest rates set by the European Central Bank for 21 countries. It owns four fifths of Imprenta de Billetes S.A., or IMBISA, which prints the euro notes allotted to Spain. In 2002 a Madrid court sentenced De la Concha to six years in prison for falsifying public documents linked to a securities account of former governor Mariano Rubio; a wound-up company, NALVI, had hidden Rubio as the investor from at least 1986, and the ruling could be appealed. On 15 September 2017 the National Court decided not to prosecute the former governor over the 2012 failure of the commercial bank Bankia, and the case was dismissed, a decision described as final. Two further cases sit at the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints watchdog, found maladministration and recommended in January 2018 that Mario Draghi give up his membership of the Group of Thirty, which the bank declined and he did not; and a speech by Benoit Coeure to a private London event on 18 May 2015 was published only the next morning. Miguel Angel Fernandez Ordonez left the bank early under political fire: on 29 May 2012 he told the prime minister he would go on 10 June, a month before his term ended, four days after the BFA-Bankia group said it would need record public support and after figures in the governing party had blamed him publicly for the banking crisis. The day after announcing it he told the Senate he would not give the bank's account of the Bankia collapse because the government wanted him to stay silent, the governing majority having declined to approve his appearance before the Congress. Spain scores 25 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

BANK OF ESTONIA (EESTI PANK)
Estonia
Estonia uses the euro, so interest rates are set not by the Bank of Estonia but by the European Central Bank, for the 21 European Union countries that use the currency. The one Estonian case ended in acquittal: on 5 March 1999 the Tallinn City Court found Siim Kallas, a former head of the bank, and Kaju not guilty of abuse of power and of submitting false information over the loss of 10 million US dollars from the North Estonian Bank, a charge of preparing to embezzle having been dropped two weeks earlier; the prosecutor, Jaan Naaber, appealed ten days later. Two findings concern the European Central Bank. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and recommended that President Mario Draghi give up his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives; the bank declined and he kept it. And on 18 May 2015 board member Benoît Cœuré told a private London event that the bank would front-load its asset purchases, the speech appearing only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error. Six career moves between that bank and private finance are recorded, among them Jorg Asmussen going to the bank Lazard; a job move is not an accusation. The Estonian bank's other ties are to the auditors Ernst & Young Baltic AS and Forvis Mazars and the fund manager BlackRock. NATIONAL BANK OF ETHIOPIA
Ethiopia
The National Bank of Ethiopia issues the birr. It scores 32 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 56% of the 194 places scored. Its legal independence is low: 0.495 of 1 on one index of 42 rules and 0.291 of 1 on another, rank 176 of 191. In March 2008 Ethiopian anti-corruption officials arrested 26 people after 90 kilos of fake gold were found in the bank's vaults: 7 from the bank, 4 from the Ethiopian Geological Survey and 15 businessmen and collaborators. What is known covers the arrests only, not charges or court outcomes. Some of the notes are made abroad: the bank awarded Francois-Charles Oberthur Fiduciaire of France a 19.6 million birr share of a 206 million birr banknote printing deal, covering the 50 birr note. BANK OF FRANCE
France
France uses the euro, so the Bank of France does not set rates on its own; the European Central Bank does that for the 21 countries using the currency. France scores 20 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Jean-Claude Trichet, while governor, was charged with spreading false information and publishing inexact accounts of the state-owned bank Crédit Lyonnais for 1991 to mid-1993, and prosecutors asked for a ten-month suspended sentence; in June 2003 judges cleared him, writing that he had only imprecise or incorrect information about the losses. Jacques de Larosière, a Banque de France governor at the time, was accused alongside him, and the verdict for him is not stated. Two findings stand against the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, which the bank declined and he did not do; and on 18 May 2015 Benoît Cœuré told a private London event that the bank would front-load asset purchases, the speech appearing only the next morning, which the bank called an internal procedure error and which Draghi said revealed nothing market-sensitive. François Villeroy de Galhau was chief operating officer of the BNP Paribas group until 1 May 2015 and took office as governor on 1 November 2015, a career move and not an accusation. The bank prints more than 2.5 billion notes a year at its own works at Chamalières, and stores its gold, 2,436.8 tonnes at the end of May 2023, mainly in its own vault 27 metres underground.

p:GAB:
BANK OF CENTRAL AFRICAN STATES (BEAC)
Gabon
Gabon uses the XAF, issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The XAF is pegged, meaning held at a fixed rate, at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees to supply euros if the region cannot pay for imports. On a scale where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Gabon scores 44, more exposed than 90% of places with a figure, mainly from money-laundering risk and corruption in the country. One BEAC case is documented: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from its Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008, and on 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs. Gabon's president Ali Bongo fired the bank's governor, Philibert Andzembe, a Gabonese national who had held the post since July 2007, in October 2009, in response to a scandal in which 28.3 million US dollars went missing from the bank's Paris branch; Gabon held the right to appoint the governor at the time, and Lucas Abaga Nchama of Equatorial Guinea took the post in 2010. A leaked US diplomatic cable, made public in December 2010, alleged separately that Gabonese officials working at the bank had taken about 36 million US dollars from the pooled reserves over roughly five years. The BEAC must deposit at least 50 per cent of the zone's foreign exchange reserves in an operations account (compte d'operations) opened in its name at the French Treasury, a share cut from 65 per cent in 2007. The required share earns interest at the European Central Bank's marginal lending facility rate, 0.25 per cent since 16 March 2016, and anything the BEAC chooses to deposit above that share earns the ECB's minimum rate on main refinancing operations, 0 per cent since 16 March 2016. KPMG Afrique Centrale and Mazars Cameroun audit the accounts jointly. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The BEAC's own site cannot be read by automated requests, so this does not rest on a BEAC document.

Central African CFA franc (CEMAC/UMAC) – France cooperation (external guarantee)

The currency (XAF) is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs; the euro replaced the French franc as anchor on 1 January 1999 with no change in parity.
France provides an unlimited convertibility guarantee, committing euro funds if the sub-region cannot pay for imports in foreign currency.
The BEAC must deposit at least 50% of its foreign exchange reserves in its operations account at the French Treasury (lowered from 65% in 2007).
Mandatory deposits earn the ECB marginal lending facility rate (stated as 0.25% since 16 March 2016); amounts above earn the ECB main refinancing rate; holdings are protected against euro depreciation against the SDR.
France designates two BEAC administrators and two Monetary Policy Committee members, the same number as each of the six CEMAC states.
A France–CEMAC ministers and governors meeting on 17 March 2026 discussed reserves, public finances and integration; the French Treasury's account records no decision changing the operations account, reserve deposit, French representation or currency name. The next meeting in this format is planned for 2027.
The CFA franc was devalued 50% on 11 January 1994.

p:GBR:
BANK OF ENGLAND
United Kingdom
The Bank of England is the central bank of the United Kingdom and issues the pound sterling. It scores 23 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, 169th of the 194 places with a figure, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. In the 2022 Conservative leadership contest Liz Truss said she would review the bank's mandate if she became prime minister, her campaign saying she would be more directive in setting it, and an ally said the review would consider the bank's independence. Governor Andrew Bailey defended independence publicly while saying he was open to a review of the mandate. Truss dropped the proposal once in office. A group of 44 Conservative MPs later called for a Treasury-led review of the bank's mandate and independence over its handling of inflation and of the unwinding of its bond holdings. Two cases are recorded. Deputy governor Charlotte Hogg resigned on 14 March 2017 after the House of Commons Treasury Committee called it a very serious breach that she had repeatedly failed, since joining the Bank in 2013, to declare that her brother was director of group strategy at the bank Barclays; she said she had also unintentionally misled the committee. The Bank itself passed material on its 2007 and 2008 liquidity auctions to the Serious Fraud Office, which investigated from 2015 and closed the matter in June 2017, finding no evidence of criminality. Eighteen career moves between the Bank and private finance are on file. Mervyn King joined Citigroup as a senior adviser after retiring as governor in 2013, and Katharine Braddick moves from Barclays to deputy governor for prudential regulation on 1 July 2026, barred for six months from decisions on Barclays.

2022-08-03 · public pressure. During the Conservative leadership contest, Liz Truss said she would review the Bank of England's mandate if she became prime minister, first raising it at a campaign event in Cardiff on 3 August 2022. Her campaign said that after 25 years she believed it was right to ensure the mandate was fit for purpose, and that she would be more directive in setting it; Suella Braverman, who was backing her, said the review would consider the bank's independence. Truss and her allies repeatedly criticised governor Andrew Bailey's handling of inflation. Bailey publicly defended independence as one of the great virtues of the system and said he would not be drawn into the leadership contest, while indicating he was open to a review of the mandate. The shadow chancellor called the proposal deeply irresponsible, and Truss's rival Rishi Sunak said the discussion could spook international investors. Once in office Truss backed the bank's authority to set interest rates and dropped mention of a review. The argument returned later: a group of 44 Conservative MPs, among them Jacob Rees-Mogg, Iain Duncan Smith, Braverman and Robert Jenrick, published a report attacking the bank's handling of inflation and quantitative tightening and calling for a Treasury-led review of its mandate and its independence, with Rees-Mogg accusing it of miserable incompetence. NATIONAL BANK OF GEORGIA
Georgia
The National Bank of Georgia issues the lari. Its law scores 0.847 of 1 for independence from government, and it scores 26 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. On 17 July 2015 parliament voted 80 to 19 to move banking supervision out of the bank to a new agency, after Bidzina Ivanishvili blamed the bank and its chairman Giorgi Kadagidze for the lari's fall. In September 2023 the bank unfroze assets tied to Otar Partskhaladze, a former Prosecutor General sanctioned by the US Treasury, arguing that Georgian citizens cannot be sanctioned without a conviction in a Georgian court; acting president Natia Turnava confirmed on 20 September that she had changed the procedure single-handedly, three of the four vice presidents and an adviser resigned, and no court verdict or official finding followed. In 2026 the Prosecutor's Office began investigating Council member Nana Keinishvili over possible unlawful involvement in business, after complaints from the crypto firm Bitexchange LLC, which the bank had fined; it was still open in October 2026 and nothing is proven. The World Bank's Reserves Advisory and Management Partnership advises the bank on its reserves investment strategy and gold policy rather than managing the money. KPMG Georgia LLC audited the bank's accounts for 2020, signing at Tbilisi on 23 April 2021. Koba Gvenetadze was picked as president by the bank's board on 16 March 2016 and approved by the President of Georgia the next day, replacing Giorgi Kadagidze; he had joined the International Monetary Fund in 2002 and was its resident representative in Azerbaijan from early 2008 to late 2009 and in Kyrgyzstan from 2010 to 2014, and he was Georgia's Deputy Finance Minister in 2000 and 2001.

BANK OF GHANA
Ghana
The Bank of Ghana issues the cedi, and Ghana scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Governors keep being pushed out. In March 2016 the MP Kwasi Ameyaw-Cheremeh said the government had forced out Henry Kofi Wampah; Wampah said he had agreed with President Mahama to leave early, and no government response is reported. Abdul Nashiru Issahaku resigned with effect after 1 April 2017 citing personal reasons, under an agreement with the government that month, after the New Patriotic Party won the 2016 election and the party's Anthony Akoto Osei said he should step down; a governor's four-year term is protected by the 1992 constitution. In December 2017 the government pushed for second deputy governor Johnson Asiama to go; he said he had not resigned, and nothing further was reported. In November 2022 Isaac Adongo, for the Minority in Parliament, called governor Ernest Addison incompetent over the cedi's fall and said he should resign or be sacked, with no answer reported. The bank said in February 2023 that its claims on the government at the end of 2022 included a 37.9 billion cedi overdraft covering auction shortfalls and maturing bonds, 7.2 billion cedis of treasury bonds bought from banks and 8.9 billion cedis of International Monetary Fund money passed on, after government, bank and Fund had adopted zero deficit financing. In February 2020 the Attorney-General charged Kwabena Duffuor, a former finance minister and governor, and seven others with 68 counts over uniBank's collapse: Duffuor with dishonestly receiving 663.28 million cedis and money laundering, Asiama with approving a 300 million cedi unsecured facility from the distressed uniBank to Universal Merchant Bank. Asiama's charges were withdrawn around 30 January 2025 and the case against Duffuor and the others was ended on 22 July 2025 after more than 60 per cent of the funds allegedly lost had been recovered; none of it was proven. Duffuor had gone from governor between 1997 and 2001 to founder and president of HODA Holdings, whose largest holding was uniBank. De La Rue, a security printer in the United Kingdom, prints the notes and charges in British pounds, and KPMG audits the accounts. On the 2020 accounts, gold held with the Bank of England and the US Federal Reserve came to 2.05 billion cedis between them, with 907 million cedis with the Swiss firm UBS Gold Investment and 111.7 million in its own vault: storage of gold, not management of its money.

Guinea
Guinea's money, the Guinean franc, is issued by the Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea. The country scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and the weakest part is corruption and secrecy around the bank. CENTRAL BANK OF THE GAMBIA
Gambia
The Central Bank of The Gambia issues the dalasi and scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. The Janneh Commission, a public inquiry into the finances of former president Yahya Jammeh, found that governor Amadou Colley had let Jammeh and General Sulayman Badjie take money out without proper authorisation, including millions of dollars by Badjie. Appearing before that commission on 19 September 2017, Colley said accounts controlled by the Office of the President had been opened at the bank, that an account for sand mining was opened at that office's request, which he called irregular, and that withdrawals followed instructions from someone in the office without the account signatory's approval. The government's White Paper on the inquiry accepted that between September 2015 and January 2017 Badjie, purportedly acting for Jammeh, instructed the governor or his deputies to release US dollars, and that cash was handed over by the governor to soldiers and loaded into vehicles. It held Badjie accountable for $15,785,601, 300,000 euros and 9,606,000 dalasi and ordered the money recovered by forfeiting and selling his properties, and it also records $28.5 million illegally granted in one bank account in 2000 and 2001 and $268,000 stolen from the bank and used to buy the Observer newspaper. Colley was banned from holding public office for life and held jointly liable for the money taken in breach of the bank's procedures. Colley was also sacked, a month before that commission was set up. On Tuesday 9 May 2017 President Adama Barrow dismissed him along with his deputies Basiru Njai and Oumie Savage-Samba and the bank's director of finance, Ousainou Corr. No reason was given; Colley said they received their letters that day stating only that their services had been terminated with immediate effect. Barrow had taken office in January, after Jammeh lost the December 2016 election and left the country under diplomatic pressure, and had been replacing officials in key positions across a state still largely staffed by Jammeh's allies. The bank's own research economist, Bakary Jammeh, was named governor. The dismissals came while inflation was high and the dalasi was depreciating. De La Rue has printed notes for the bank, and PKF Gambia and PKF Nigeria audited the 2021 accounts.

2017-05-09 · dismissal. On Tuesday 9 May 2017 President Adama Barrow dismissed the governor of the Central Bank of The Gambia, Amadou Colley, together with his deputies Basiru Njai and Oumie Savage-Samba and the bank's director of finance, Ousainou Corr. No reason was given. Colley told Reuters that they received their letters that day without being given any reason for the sacking, the letters stating only that their services had been terminated with immediate effect. He had been governor since 2010, appointed under Yahya Jammeh, who lost the December 2016 election and left the country in January 2017 after weeks of diplomatic pressure. Barrow, who inherited a state whose institutions were still largely staffed by Jammeh's allies, had been progressively replacing officials in key positions to establish his authority. The bank's own research economist, Bakary Jammeh, was named governor. The dismissals came while inflation was high and the dalasi was depreciating. Colley said he was surprised at his unceremonious removal and was proud to have served the country for more than three decades. This is separate from what the Janneh Commission later found about his conduct as governor under Jammeh, which is recorded as a corruption case: the commission was only established in June 2017, a month after he was removed, so the dismissal was not a consequence of its findings. The Gambia: Jammeh-era central bank chief fired without reasons (Africanews, citing Reuters)

CENTRAL BANK OF WEST AFRICAN STATES (BCEAO)
Guinea-Bissau
Guinea-Bissau uses the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The franc is pegged — held at a fixed rate — at one euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France gives an unconditional, unlimited promise to advance euros if the bank's reserves run out. An agreement signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one: it ended the requirement that the bank keep at least half its reserves at the French Treasury, and France withdrew its representatives from the board, the Monetary Policy Committee and the banking commission, though one independent committee member is still appointed in consultation with the French government. Guinea-Bissau scores 45 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, mostly because of corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. One case is documented: in January 2011 a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution; the account says the bank paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date, and Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo after being dismissed, with no audit result given. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of the reserves is run by outside institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it has bought units in an investment fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and that it has joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program managed by the World Bank, worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two sets of fund units came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025, and the accounts group the BISIP K units with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The accounts are audited by firms appointed in pairs, one doing the work and one standing in: Mazars Senegal with Grant Thornton Senegal for Guinea-Bissau, and Deloitte Cote d'Ivoire with Mazars Senegal for the BCEAO itself.

2011-01-22 · forced resignation. The Central Bank of West African States is the central bank of eight countries, and in January 2011 its own member heads of state removed its governor. After the disputed Ivorian presidential election of November 2010, the bank recognised Alassane Ouattara as head of state and revoked Laurent Gbagbo's access to Ivorian state accounts in December, and the union's finance ministers decided on 23 December that only representatives of Ouattara's government would have signing authority. The Ouattara camp complained in mid-January that the bank was still channelling cash to Gbagbo, and the governor, Philippe-Henry Dacoury-Tabley, an Ivorian and a close confidant of Gbagbo, was accused of not cooperating. At an emergency summit of the heads of state of the West African Economic and Monetary Union in Bamako on 22 January 2011 he handed in his resignation. The bank's own statement, issued in Dakar that evening, said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders. He told reporters afterwards: "I agreed to hand in my resignation as that is what was asked of me", and defended his conduct by pointing to practical and technical reasons for not transferring control of the accounts. The union accepted the resignation and called on Ouattara to propose a successor; a deputy governor, Jean-Baptiste Compaore, took over in the interim. Gbagbo's administration, on state television it still controlled, rejected what it called the forced resignation of the governor and rejected the leaders' decision to let Ouattara name a replacement. The European Union listed Dacoury-Tabley, giving as its ground that as governor of the BCEAO he refused to recognise the authority of the democratically elected President and was helping to fund the illegitimate administration of Mr Laurent Gbagbo. This record is the removal of the governor by the member states; what he is alleged to have done with the bank's money is recorded separately as a corruption case. Keyed to the union, so it counts for all eight member countries. Pro-Gbagbo bank head quits (Al Jazeera)

Equatorial Guinea uses the Central African CFA franc (XAF), issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The franc is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs. France guarantees convertibility without limit, and the BEAC must deposit at least 50% of its foreign exchange reserves at the French Treasury (lowered from 65% in 2007). Exposure score is 48 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The BEAC scores 0.5 of 15 on transparency, last of 112, and government pressure to cut rates or ease was reported in 3 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from the Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008. On 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs. A governor lost his job over the same affair: Philibert Andzembe, a Gabonese national, had led the bank since July 2007, and in October 2009 Gabon's president Ali Bongo fired him in response to a scandal in which 28.3 million US dollars went missing from the bank's Paris branch; Gabon held the right to appoint the governor at the time, and Lucas Abaga Nchama of Equatorial Guinea took the post in 2010. KPMG Afrique Centrale and Mazars Cameroun audit the accounts jointly. Its money is printed in France. BANK OF GREECE
Greece
Greece uses the euro, so its interest rates are set by the European Central Bank. The Bank of Greece is unusual in being a listed company: 19,864,886 of its shares trade in Athens. The Greek State holds 1,774,088 of them, 8.93 percent, after taking over 1,309,210 shares from DEKA S.A. when that body was dissolved under a law of 2011. A social security fund, e-EFKA, is listed at 12.4402 percent as of 7 August 2020, but that figure comes from Wikipedia and is not confirmed in a filing by the bank. From the spring of 2015 the SYRIZA government and the party press attacked the governor, Yannis Stournaras, who had been finance minister in the previous conservative-led government. The party's parliamentary spokesman, Nikos Filis, said on party radio that Stournaras was undermining the negotiations with creditors; the party-affiliated newspaper Avgi called the bank an organ working against the government; and the government issued a non-paper telling the bank to investigate a leak to a journalist. Handelsblatt reported that Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras wanted to replace him with someone he trusted, and Bloomberg reported on 13 May 2015 that the European Central Bank was concerned about the pressure and publicly backed him. The Speaker of Parliament, Zoi Konstantopoulou, returned his June 2015 monetary policy report as unacceptable. In September 2016 corruption prosecutors raided his home over his wife's alleged role in an advertising case, and in February 2019 a deputy health minister, Pavlos Polakis, leaked a recording of a telephone call in which he had raised his own bank loan with the governor; Stournaras called that a preposterous attempt to interfere and asked Tsipras to protect the bank's independence. The bribery case against him collapsed: on 29 August 2019 prosecutors dropped charges that he had taken bribes from the drug company Novartis while he was finance minister, along with charges against six other former senior officials; the allegations reached back to 2001 and predated his central bank post. Two findings concern the European Central Bank, where the European Ombudsman found maladministration and recommended in January 2018 that President Mario Draghi give up his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives, which the bank declined to do, and where a speech of 18 May 2015 told a private London audience about front-loaded asset purchases before it was published. Georgios Provopoulos, governor from June 2008 to 2014, came straight from Greek private banking, having advised Alpha Bank from 1993, held a management role at Emporiki Bank from 2004 and been vice president and chief executive of Piraeus Bank from 2006 to 2008. Grenada
Grenada's money is the EC dollar, issued not by a national bank but by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank for eight members, among them Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada and Saint Lucia. The agreement was signed on 5 July 1983. The currency has been fixed at EC$2.70 to US$1.00 since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling to the US dollar, and the law requires reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation. For Grenada the bank scores 28 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, and its legal independence is 0.549 of 1 on Romelli's rules; no government pressure was reported in 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded and it was dismissed: after the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it had fraudulently taken assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors; on 17 August 2018 a United States federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. A head of government has since pressed the bank's governor to think about going. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions, wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable and that the spending invites disciplinary action, and proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis; on 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are printed on and printed the 2027 family; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. The bank's 2020/2021 annual report says it continued its engagement with the World Bank's Reserves Advisory Management Partnership (RAMP), and that a second engagement was judged appropriate to go on building up its newly formed Risk and Analytics Unit, the unit that reports on the reserves portfolio; the same report says the investment guidelines for its external managers were reviewed and updated and that the foreign reserve portfolio had grown to about EC$4.6 billion. The annual report for 2024/2025 and the audited accounts to 31 March 2025 do not repeat the RAMP engagement, so it stands as a 2020/2021 fact.

Eastern Caribbean Currency Union (monetary union)

The ECCB is the monetary authority for Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.
The ECCB agreement was signed on 5 July 1983 and the Bank was commissioned on 1 October 1983.
The EC dollar has been fixed at EC$2.70 = US$1.00 since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling to the US dollar.
Section 24(2) of the ECCB Agreement Act requires an external reserve of not less than 60% of currency in circulation and other demand liabilities.

p:GTM:
BANK OF GUATEMALA
Guatemala
The Bank of Guatemala issues the quetzal and in practice holds it close to a fixed rate against the US dollar. One case is recorded. In May 2015 the bank's president, Julio Suarez, was arrested along with other members of the board of the social security institute, the IGSS. Prosecutors said the group took part in the irregular award of a 116 million quetzal IGSS contract, about 14.5 million US dollars, to the drug company Pisa de Guatemala, on charges of unlawful association, influence peddling, illegal commissions and active bribery. He was acquitted on appeal in June 2019, and the Supreme Court's Criminal Chamber upheld that acquittal, as reported in October 2021. An earlier president of the bank was prosecuted and sentenced: Guatemala's Public Ministry and the UN-backed International Commission Against Impunity in Guatemala, CICIG, charged Edgar Barquin, a former president of the bank and a 2015 vice-presidential candidate, with influence trafficking, after investigators found he had warned Francisco Edgar Morales Guerra, known as Chico Dolar, of a coming investigation and later helped him evade scrutiny for monetary gain. On 16 September 2016 Barquin was sentenced to 30 months in prison, which the judge suspended on the attorney general's recommendation as part of a plea bargain in which Barquin admitted guilt and agreed to cooperate; he was barred for five years from public office and from exercising his political rights, and the report says he admitted involvement in laundering 30 million US dollars. One career move is documented: Alvaro Gonzalez Ricci was Guatemala's Minister of Public Finance from January 2020 and then became president of the Bank of Guatemala for a four-year term reported on 1 October 2022 and running to 20 September 2026. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. The bank keeps coined gold worth about 315.5 million US dollars at the end of 2024 in its own vaults, and gold worth about 263.1 million dollars in storage at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which holds it while Guatemala still owns it. Its smaller notes are printed abroad: on 20 August 2018 the bank agreed with the Polish printer Polska Wytwornia Papierow Wartosciowych to produce 5- and 10-quetzal notes on a material containing synthetic fibres. It is also a member of the World Bank Treasury's RAMP network, which offers advice, training and asset management, without saying which of those Guatemala gets. Guatemala scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

HONG KONG MONETARY AUTHORITY
Hong Kong
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority runs the Hong Kong dollar as a currency board, meaning it is tied to another currency: the monetary base is fully backed by US dollar assets in the Exchange Fund. The link began on 17 October 1983 at 7.80 Hong Kong dollars per US dollar, and since May 2005 the authority sells Hong Kong dollars at 7.75 and buys at 7.85. It scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case is recorded: in 2012 a Legislative Council subcommittee found that former chief Joseph Yam Chi-kwong should bear “ultimate responsibility” for investors' losses on Lehman's minibonds. The authority replied that the report had not fully taken into account the information it submitted, and some members prepared a minority report. One career move is recorded, and it is his: Joseph Yam headed the Office of the Exchange Fund from 1991 to 1993 and ran the authority from 1 April 1993 to 30 September 2009, and after leaving he was an independent non-executive director of China Construction Bank from 2010 until 23 October 2013, was elected in April 2011 to the board of the Swiss bank UBS AG, where he sat on its risk committee and its corporate culture and responsibility committee from 2011, and sat on the UBS Group AG board from November 2014 to May 2017. Banknotes are printed in Hong Kong by Hong Kong Note Printing Limited, in which the government keeps management control and a majority stake.

Croatia uses the euro, so the European Central Bank sets its monetary policy, for 21 countries in all; the ECB is also one of 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. The Magyar Nemzeti Bank issues Hungary's forint and owns outright the company that prints the notes. Hungary scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. In July 2010 the cabinet went ahead with a bill cutting governor Andras Simor's monthly pay by 75 percent, from about 8 million to 2 million forints, under a cap on all public pay; the European Central Bank said such changes should apply only to future appointments. In December 2011 parliament's constitutional committee tabled an amendment merging the bank with the financial regulator under a head appointed by President Pal Schmitt on Prime Minister Viktor Orban's nomination, cutting Simor to deputy, and Simor said he refused what he called bullying. On 12 March 2024 the bank said a proposed law widening its supervisory board's control could erode its independence. The Constitutional Court ruled on 31 March 2016 that the foundations the bank endowed in 2014 with over 267 billion forints were managing public money, and the Public Procurement Board fined six of them 200,000 forints each. In March 2025 the State Audit Office found mismanagement and losses of hundreds of billions of forints there and filed a criminal complaint. On 21 October 2026 former governor Gyorgy Matolcsy was detained on suspicion of economic fraud and use of a forged private document, which is unproven.

Indonesia
Bank Indonesia is the central bank of Indonesia and issues the rupiah, printed by Perum Peruri, the state banknote printing firm, at Karawang in West Java. The country scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In October 2011 Securency and Note Printing Australia, both subsidiaries of the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to provide benefits to foreign public officials to win the banknote business of Indonesia's note-issuing authority between 1999 and 2001; the officials are not named. Governor Syahril was released in December 2000 after six months in detention, while the administration was pushing to remove him and install its own candidates; he was sentenced to three years in 2002 over the 546 billion rupiah Bank Bali scandal, and in 2004 the Supreme Court acquitted him on all charges. In October 2008 the Corruption Court sentenced former governor Burhanuddin Abdullah to five years for approving 100 billion rupiah of the bank's funds in 2003 to pay officials' legal fees and bribe legislators over an amendment to the bank's law. In July 2014 the anti-corruption court sentenced Budi Mulya to 10 years over a 689.39 billion rupiah loan to Bank Century. In August 2025 the anti-corruption commission named two members of the House as suspects over alleged misuse of the bank's money for social projects; that is unproven.

RESERVE BANK OF INDIA
India
India's money is the rupee and its central bank is the Reserve Bank of India, which scores 29 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case is recorded and unproven: in December 2016, while 500 and 1,000 rupee notes were being withdrawn from circulation, the Central Bureau of Investigation arrested bank official K. Michael in Bangalore and charged him with converting 15 million rupees of withdrawn notes into 100 rupee notes without legal documentation, with a state bank employee. On 10 December 2018 governor Urjit Patel resigned, giving only personal reasons; media reports said he was annoyed by repeated government efforts to influence policy after a public spat. In September 2010 banknote paper supplier De La Rue said some employees had deliberately falsified paper test certificates, which was reportedly followed by suspension of supply to the bank. Three leaders came from elsewhere: Duvvuri Subbarao, governor from 2008 to 2013, had been a lead economist at the World Bank; Raghuram Rajan was the International Monetary Fund's chief economist from 2003 to 2006 before his appointment in 2013; and Patel arrived as deputy governor in January 2013 from the Fund, Reliance Industries and Boston Consulting Group. Part of India's gold is kept in safe custody with the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements, which is storage, not management of the money.

p:IRL:
CENTRAL BANK OF IRELAND
Ireland
Ireland uses the euro, so its interest rates are set not by the Central Bank of Ireland but by the European Central Bank, for the 21 European Union states that use the currency. The Irish bank's books are checked from outside by Grant Thornton Ireland, under a term covering 2023 to 2027, and its gold bars are held at the Bank of England, which stores them rather than manages them; the remaining coin stocks stay at the Central Bank of Ireland. In 2008 and 2009 the financial regulator, Neary, said he would retire early over the regulator's handling of 87 million euros in secret directors' loans at Anglo Irish Bank; an internal committee found the matter, discovered in January 2008, was not pursued, partly because a letter from Anglo went missing, and Neary said he was not told until the finance minister raised it in December 2008. Two further findings sit at the European Central Bank. The European Ombudsman found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a club of central bankers and private bankers; the bank declined and he kept it. And a speech of 18 May 2015, in which Coeure told a private London event that the bank would front-load asset purchases, was published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error; Draghi said no market-sensitive information was revealed. Seven career moves run between these banks and private finance, among them Matthew Elderfield, the Irish deputy governor and financial regulator, hired by Lloyds Banking Group as director for conduct and compliance from October 2013. The sharpest pressure on Ireland's central bank came from outside the country. Emergency lending to banks is paid out by the Central Bank of Ireland but has to be allowed by the European Central Bank's governing council, and on 19 November 2010 the ECB's president wrote to the finance minister, in a letter marked secret, saying that further emergency lending would be authorised only if Ireland committed in writing to apply for an international rescue programme, along with commitments on austerity and bank recapitalisation. Support to Irish banks had passed 50 billion euros by then. Ireland applied two days later. The ECB refused to publish the letter for four years and released it on 6 November 2014, after the European Ombudsman and an Irish member of the European Parliament pressed for it and after a newspaper had obtained and printed it. Ireland scores 23 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

2010-11-19 · foreign pressure. On 19 November 2010 the president of the European Central Bank, Jean-Claude Trichet, wrote a letter marked secret to Ireland's finance minister, Brian Lenihan, saying the ECB's governing council would authorise further Emergency Liquidity Assistance to Irish banks only if it received in writing a commitment that Ireland would apply for an international rescue programme, together with commitments on austerity, bank recapitalisation and a guarantee to repay the liquidity. Emergency lending is provided by the Central Bank of Ireland but has to be allowed by the ECB's governing council, which is what gave Trichet the leverage; ECB support to Irish banks had passed 50 billion euros and dominated emergency liquidity for the whole euro area. An earlier letter of 15 October had warned that the scale of the lending should not be taken for granted. Lenihan, who had insisted publicly the week before that Ireland needed no bailout, wrote back that Sunday accepting. Ireland applied on 21 November. The ECB refused for four years to publish the letter and released it on 6 November 2014, after approaches from the European Ombudsman and an Irish MEP and after The Irish Times had obtained and printed it; the ECB's own statement with the release said documentation showed domestic factors pushed Ireland towards the programme. Iran
The Central Bank of the Islamic Republic of Iran issues the rial, which is in free fall. Its law leaves most power with government, 0.448 of 1 where 1 means the bank holds it. Its notes and coins come from the Security Printing and Minting Organization, a state printing works owned by the bank since 1962; before 1982 the notes were printed abroad. The government replaced governor Valiollah Seif on 25 July 2018 without reason, and dismissed his successor Abdolnasser Hemmati on 30 May 2021 for standing for president. In October 2021 a Tehran court sentenced Seif to ten years, his deputy Araghchi to eight and the intermediary Aghakhani to thirteen over an illegal foreign-currency scheme; the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts in 2023, and the prosecution of Seif and Araghchi was dropped in March 2025. Abroad, Bahrain's High Criminal Court in November 2020 fined the bank and other Iran-owned banks one million Bahraini dinars each; prosecutors said it planned to launder billions of dollars through Future Bank. Bahrain's top court upheld the conviction in 2021, with confiscation of remittances put at 184 million US dollars, 967 million euros, 53 million dirhams and 235 billion riyals. CENTRAL BANK OF ICELAND
Iceland
The Central Bank of Iceland issues the króna and keeps it within 2 per cent or less of the euro. It scores 18 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, lower than 97 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, and it ranks 9th of 112 for what it tells the public. No government pressure on it was reported in any of the 37 quarters covered between 2010 and 2018. One case is on its record, an official finding: in April 2010, after the 2008 collapse of Iceland's three largest banks, parliament's Special Investigation Commission found that seven officials, among them central bank head Oddsson and officials Gudnason and Fridriksson, had acted with gross negligence by failing to act on information about the banks' condition. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank for central banks. The bank's leadership was changed by statute after the collapse. The incoming prime minister wrote to the three governors on 2 February 2009 asking them to resign so the bank could be restructured; Davíð Oddsson, a former prime minister who chaired the board, refused in public and called the demand interference with the bank's independence. Parliament then passed a bill on 26 February, by 33 votes to 18, replacing the three-person board with a single governor and a deputy, which removed him. A Norwegian economist was named interim governor the next day. Asgeir Jonsson was named governor by Prime Minister Katrin Jakobsdottir for a five-year term starting 20 August 2019, succeeding Mar Gudmundsson; he had been chief economist and head of the research department at Kaupthing Bank, later Arion Bank, from 2004 to 2011, worked as an economic consultant for the finance companies Virding and Gamma, and has taught at the University of Iceland since 2004.
