2025-09-04 · public pressure. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich ran a sustained public campaign against Bank of Israel governor Amir Yaron over the level of interest rates. Speaking to business leaders on 4 September 2025, Smotrich said Yaron "should have lowered interest rates six months ago" and told them: "If the governor doesn't lower interest rates, I will lower taxes" - that is, he would offset the bank's monetary policy with fiscal policy of his own. The same campaign ran through earlier decisions: after the committee held the rate at 4 percent in February 2025 he called the decision wrong, said no inflationary risk justified such restrictive policy and publicly called on the governor to reverse it; after the January 2025 cut he said it should have come six months earlier and should have been deeper. The Bank of Israel answered that the governor and the Monetary Committee decide on professional grounds alone, that high inflation hurts weaker households most, and that keeping it in check is essential. Smotrich also said in the same remarks that the independence of Yaron and of the bank was critical, that he had no intention of interfering, and that monetary policy was the governor's responsibility while fiscal policy was his - so this is open ministerial pressure on rate decisions, not an attempt to change the bank's powers. BANK OF ITALY
Italy
The Bank of Italy is Italy's central bank, and because Italy uses the euro its interest rates are set by the European Central Bank. It has shareholders: capital of 7.5 billion euro in 300,000 quotas of 25,000 euro each, held by Italian banks, insurers, social security bodies, pension funds and banking foundations, 173 holders on 30 April 2026, with no holder allowed above 5 per cent since 1 January 2022, up from 3 per cent under Law 5/2014. UniCredit sits at that cap with 15,000 quotas, the pension bodies INARCASSA, ENPAM and Cassa Forense hold 14,800 each, Intesa Sanpaolo 14,736, CNPADC 11,000 and BPER Banca 9,765. On 28 May 2011 a Milan court sentenced former governor Antonio Fazio to four years and a 1.5 million euro fine for market rigging in the 2005 attempt by Banca Popolare di Lodi to take over Antonveneta, prosecutors arguing he had favoured Gianpiero Fiorani's bank over ABN Amro; the appeal court cut that to two years and six months on 28 May 2012, and the Court of Cassation made the conviction final on 28 November 2012. Over Unipol's attempted takeover of BNL he was sentenced to three and a half years in October 2011 and then acquitted, with twelve other defendants, on 30 May 2012. Two findings concern the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman found maladministration and in January 2018 asked Mario Draghi to suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives, and the ECB declined, so he kept it; and Coeure's remark to a private London event on 18 May 2015 that the ECB would front-load asset purchases was published only the next morning, which the ECB put down to an internal procedure error. Draghi was vice chairman and managing director of Goldman Sachs International from 2002 to 2005 before becoming governor in 2006. Of its 2,452 tonnes of gold, 1,100 tonnes are stored in the bank's own security rooms at Via Nazionale. Deloitte audits the accounts. Antonio Fazio's departure from the bank in 2005 was itself a case of a government forcing out a governor it could not dismiss. Under the law as it then stood he held office for life, and the government said it had no power to remove him, so he refused for months to go despite calls from across the political spectrum, including from the prime minister. The economy minister resigned in protest in September 2005 at the government's failure to act; his successor said on the day Fazio finally quit, 19 December 2005, that he wanted parliament to change the laws governing the bank so the governor could be replaced, and legislation to that effect was being prepared when the resignation came. The reform that followed ended the open-ended tenure and put a fixed term in its place. Italy scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

On 28 May 2011 a Milan court sentenced former governor Fazio to four years in prison and a €1.5 million fine for market rigging (aggiotaggio) in the 2005 attempted takeover of Antonveneta by Banca Popolare di Lodi; prosecutors argued he repeatedly favoured Fiorani's bank over ABN Amro by speeding some authorisations and slowing others. 2005-12-19 · resignation under pressure. Antonio Fazio resigned as governor of the Bank of Italy on 19 December 2005, after months of pressure over his handling of the contest for Banca Antonveneta, in which wiretaps suggested he had favoured a domestic bidder over the Dutch bank ABN AMRO. Under the law as it then stood the governor held office for life and the government said it had no power to remove him; Fazio refused for months to go, despite calls from across the political spectrum including Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi. Economy Minister Domenico Siniscalco resigned in protest on 21 September 2005 at the government's failure to act. His successor Giulio Tremonti said on the day Fazio quit that he wanted parliament to change the laws governing the Bank of Italy so that the governor could be replaced, and the government was preparing that legislation when Fazio resigned. The reform that followed ended the governor's open-ended tenure and replaced it with a fixed term, and moved competition oversight of bank mergers to the antitrust authority. Fazio had been placed under investigation for insider trading in Milan three days before he quit, and in May 2011 a court sentenced him to four years for market-rigging. Bank of Italy governor steps down (BBC News, 19 December 2005)

BANK OF JAMAICA
Jamaica
The Bank of Jamaica issues the Jamaican dollar and moves its rate against the US dollar in small announced steps. It scores 27 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters to 2018. One case is recorded and unproven: governor Derick Latibeaudiere borrowed 51 million dollars from the bank for a house, furnishings and landscaping. At a Public Accounts Committee hearing on 26 May 2009, Auditor General Pamela Monroe Ellis said she had no documents showing the loans were secured and that 25 million of it was still unsecured; the bank's lawyer said 30 million was fully secured against the governor's house, and the committee told both sides to resolve their differences and report back. That contract is also why he lost the job. On Friday 30 October 2009 the Minister of Finance terminated his services, after thirteen years as governor. Prime Minister Bruce Golding told the House of Representatives that the government found the terms unacceptable, embarrassing and repugnant: a basic salary starting at 11,226,271 dollars, rising each year by whatever increase public sector employees were granted and by further incremental and performance adjustments, which had carried it to 14,545,000 dollars by the day of his dismissal, inside a package reported at about 38 million dollars a year - more, Golding said, than the Chairman of the United States Federal Reserve was paid, and set against a government that had not met nurses' demand for reclassification. Latibeaudiere had held that the bank's obligations to him must be met, writing to the minister on the day itself that if the principle governing the sanctity of contracts was to mean anything, the contract he had signed with the minister under statute had to be honoured. He was at that moment Jamaica's lead negotiator for a standby agreement with the International Monetary Fund and said he was in those talks until two hours before he was dismissed. Standard and Poor's downgraded Jamaica's sovereign bonds the next day, which Golding called a knee-jerk reaction. The National Workers Union questioned the legality of the decision and said the government should have consulted him first; the Economist reported talk in Kingston of a policy disagreement with the finance minister. Brian Wynter took over on 1 December 2009. Richard Byles became governor on 19 August 2019, after running Pan Caribbean Merchant Bank from 1988, the Pan Jam group from 1991 for thirteen years and Sagicor Jamaica from 2004 until he retired in 2017. Crown Agents Investment Management manages the bank's investments of special drawing rights, which began at 250 million US dollars and have since doubled, with the bank leaving the investment decisions to the firm. De La Rue prints the banknotes. The Independent Auditor's Report in the bank's Annual Report 2025 is issued by Ernst & Young Chartered Accountants of Kingston and signed on 4 March 2026.

2009-10-30 · dismissal. On Friday 30 October 2009 the Minister of Finance terminated the services of the Governor of the Bank of Jamaica, Derick Latibeaudiere, who had held the post since 1 April 1996. Prime Minister Bruce Golding told the House of Representatives that the government found the terms of his contract unacceptable, embarrassing and repugnant: it provided a basic salary at commencement of 11,226,271 Jamaican dollars, rising annually by whatever increase was granted to public sector employees and by further incremental and performance adjustments, which had taken the basic salary to 14,545,000 dollars by the date of dismissal, within a total remuneration package reported at about 38 million dollars a year - more, Golding said, than the Chairman of the United States Federal Reserve was paid. Golding set that against a government that had not been able to meet nurses' demand for reclassification. Apart from a concession on rent, the governor had held that the bank's contractual obligations to him must be met, writing to the minister on the day of his dismissal that if the principle governing the sanctity of contracts was to have any meaning, the contract he had signed with the minister under statute had to be honoured. Latibeaudiere was at the time Jamaica's lead negotiator for a standby agreement with the International Monetary Fund and said he was in those discussions up to two hours before he was dismissed. Standard and Poor's downgraded Jamaica's sovereign bonds the following day, which Golding called a knee-jerk reaction to the dismissal. The president of the National Workers Union questioned the legality of the decision and said the government should have consulted the governor before terminating a legitimate contract. Latibeaudiere declined to speculate on the reasons; the Economist reported talk in Kingston of a policy disagreement with the finance minister. Brian Wynter took over as governor on 1 December 2009. Statement by the Prime Minister on the dismissal of the Governor of the Bank of Jamaica, Minutes of the House of Representatives (Parliament of Jamaica)

p:JOR:
CENTRAL BANK OF JORDAN
Jordan
The Central Bank of Jordan issues the Jordanian dinar and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar, an arrangement called a peg. One case is documented, and it grew out of the collapse of a bank the central bank supervised. Governor Mohammed Said Nabulsi issued a decree requiring banks to hold 30 per cent of their foreign holdings as reserves at the central bank; Petra Bank was the only Jordanian bank unable to comply, which triggered an investigation and accusations of embezzlement and false accounting. Petra Bank collapsed on 2 August 1989 and was placed under government supervision with an audit of its books, the central bank announced a 350 million dollar bail-out of depositors, and Jordan's losses came to about 200 million dollars. A Jordanian military tribunal convicted Chalabi in absentia on 31 charges, including embezzlement, theft, misuse of depositor funds and currency speculation, and sentenced him to 22 years; he had fled the country about two weeks after the collapse, never served the sentence, and maintained that the prosecution was a politically motivated effort to discredit him. No government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed between 2010 and 2018. Parliament pushed once: in September 2003 members signed a petition urging Prime Minister Ali Abulragheb to remove governor Umayya Touqan, after Touqan froze all the bank accounts of six leaders of Hamas; whether the government acted on it is not known. One leader later crossed into private banking. Mohammed Said Mohammed Shahin, a former Governor and Chairman of the bank and earlier a deputy governor, became chairman of the Islamic International Arab Bank, a commercial bank, on 31 March 2017. Jordan scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side corruption and secrecy around the bank.

p:JPN:
BANK OF JAPAN
Japan
The Bank of Japan issues the yen and has capital of 100 million yen, of which the government holds 55 percent and private investors 45 percent through subscription certificates traded on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. Those holders have no say in running it, and the bank does not name them. One case is on file: in June 2006 governor Fukui apologised and took a 30 percent pay cut for six months after disclosing that he had kept a 10 million yen investment, made in 1999, in a fund run by Yoshiaki Murakami, who was arrested for insider trading; by then the stake was worth 22 million yen. The bank said he broke no law or internal rule, and he did not resign. Nine people have moved between its Policy Board and private finance, among them Atsushi Mizuno, who joined Credit Suisse the month after his term. Japan scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. The sharpest pressure on the bank was legal rather than personal. From December 2012 Prime Minister Shinzo Abe repeatedly said his government would revise the 1998 law that guarantees the bank's independence unless it adopted a 2 percent inflation target, and his coalition held enough seats to pass such a bill. The bank adopted the target and an open-ended asset purchase commitment on 22 January 2013, in a joint statement with the government, and the government then said there was less need to change the law. Officials inside the bank described the outcome as fending off the most serious threat to its independence in fifteen years.

2012-12-23 · public pressure. Before and after taking office in December 2012, Prime Minister Shinzo Abe repeatedly threatened to revise the 1998 Bank of Japan Law, which guarantees the bank's independence in monetary policy, unless the bank adopted a 2 percent inflation target. On 23 December 2012 he said his government would consider revising the Act if the bank did not adopt the target at its January meeting, and that if it refused, "we have to amend the BoJ law, reach an accord and we will have the policy". His party and its coalition partner held a two-thirds majority in the lower house, enough to overrule the upper house on such a bill, so the threat was credible; reporting at the time noted a revision could have given the government power to impose a binding target on the bank or to remove its governor. Lawmakers had already summoned governor Masaaki Shirakawa to the Diet several times in February 2012 to criticise his caution. The bank adopted the 2 percent target and an open-ended asset purchase commitment on 22 January 2013, in a joint statement with the government. Officials inside the bank described the outcome as fending off the most serious threat to its independence in fifteen years, and the government's chief spokesman then said there was less need to revise the law. In February 2013 Abe told parliament that if the bank could not responsibly deliver results, "we would have to consider revising the BoJ law". Japan's Abe heaps pressure on BOJ to set 2 percent inflation target (Reuters, via Fox Business)

NATIONAL BANK OF KAZAKHSTAN
Kazakhstan
The National Bank of Kazakhstan issues the tenge, which floats within a de facto band of about 5 per cent against the US dollar, and gold makes up 77 per cent of its reserves, 368.4 tonnes. On 2 November 2015 President Nursultan Nazarbayev replaced chairman Kayrat Kelimbetov with presidential adviser Daniyar Akishev, telling parliament that confidence in the bank and the tenge had fallen and that tenge liquidity was short; Kelimbetov is not quoted. It prints its own money through the Banknote Factory of the National Bank, one of its subsidiaries, which also makes passports, identity and payment cards and has released three series of tenge notes. Landqart AG says the bank's 20,000 tenge note, issued for the 30th anniversary of independence, is printed on its Durasafe material, the second such note the bank has issued. PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP audited the accounts for the year ended 31 December 2025. It has five swap lines, arrangements to borrow another central bank's currency: Turkiye for 28.0 billion Turkish lira in 2025, Russia for 35 billion roubles on 28 May 2026 and China for 7 billion yuan on 14 December 2014. Kazakhstan scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Grigory Marchenko chaired the bank from October 1999 until 2004, then chaired Halyk Bank, the country's third-biggest financial institution, from January 2005, and was appointed chairman of the National Bank a second time, replacing Anvar Saidenov, as reported on 30 January 2009.

2025-2026 · staff bonuses paid from reserve-management funds; failure to comply with an audit order · fined or settled. After a state audit of the National Bank of Kazakhstan in late 2025, the Supreme Audit Chamber issued a binding order requiring the bank to return to the state budget bonuses that had been paid to staff whose work was unrelated to managing the country's gold and foreign-exchange reserves. The deadline for compliance was 1 April 2026 and the money was not returned. A court then found deputy chair Aliya Moldabekova guilty under Part 3 of Article 462 of the Administrative Code, which covers failing to comply with a lawful order, and fined her 64,875 tenge. She said the bonuses had been paid lawfully under the bank's own decisions and could only be recovered through court, which takes time. The National Bank said the ruling had not yet taken effect and asked the Audit Chamber to extend part of the deadline to 31 August 2026. The report is dated 24 July 2026. CENTRAL BANK OF KENYA
Kenya
The Central Bank of Kenya is the country's central bank and issues its money. Three cases are on file. In the Goldenberg scandal, the government paid cash subsidies for fictitious gold and diamond exports under President Daniel arap Moi. In March 2006 prosecutors indicted five people, including former governor Kotut and former deputy governor Riungu. They are charged, which is unproven. On 23 March 2006 governor Andrew Mullei was charged with four counts of abuse of office, including hiring his son as a consultant. He denied awarding Sh9 million in contracts irregularly, and no court outcome was found. From 2015 to 2018, Kenya's anti-corruption commission investigated current and former officials over the collapse of Imperial Bank, whose directors said bank officers helped embezzle Sh34 billion. That is under investigation and unproven. Kenya scores 37 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

NATIONAL BANK OF THE KYRGYZ REPUBLIC
Kyrgyzstan
The National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic issues the som and holds it within 2 per cent of the US dollar. One case is recorded. In September 2005 prosecutors placed the governor, Ulan Sarbanov, under house arrest, accusing him of abuse of power for handing more than 400,000 US dollars to the deposed president Askar Akayev in 1999. Sarbanov denied wrongdoing, and Euromoney reported that his position had been insecure since Akayev was ousted in March 2005. On 26 April 2006 Judge Esenjan Abylkasymov acquitted him and four other former finance officials, ruling that there was no crime because they had acted in the interests of the state; the prosecutor's office said it would appeal, and no appeal outcome was found. Two heads have left since: parliament approved the early resignation of Kubanychbek Bokontaev on 26 June 2024, and Melis Turgunbaev, chairman from that same day, resigned on 18 March 2026, which the report calls voluntary. Neither article gives a reason. Crane Currency printed the 5,000-som note introduced on 10 May 2024; Central Asian Secure Printing Typography began printing at home in September 2026, with 20- and 50-som notes entering circulation on 27 October, while an earlier attempt by Uchkun in March 2025 produced 10-som notes that never circulated. Kyrgyzstan scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

p:KHM:
NATIONAL BANK OF CAMBODIA
Cambodia
The National Bank of Cambodia is the country's central bank. It scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and neither matter on record was ever confirmed. The Phnom Penh Post reported that governor Thor Peng Leath lent three million US dollars of central bank money on 31 May 1994 so Credit Bank of Cambodia could meet its minimum capital, which bank officials admitted was highly irregular, and that on 8 May 1995 the bank released 145,000 dollars from former commerce minister Var Huot's frozen account. Preferential treatment was claimed, but Var Huot said there was none, and no charges or findings followed. In November 2013 Chea Serey, daughter of governor Chea Chanto, was promoted to director-general; former deputy governor Tioulong Saumura said being the governor's daughter should exclude her, Nguon Sokha called her a skilled technocrat, and no investigation followed. The bank belongs to the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which central banks join for help with their reserves. BNY Mellon supplies it with reporting systems and staff training.

p:KNA:
EASTERN CARIBBEAN CENTRAL BANK
St. Kitts & Nevis
St Kitts and Nevis does not issue its own money. The East Caribbean dollar is issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, set up under an agreement signed on 5 July 1983, for eight member places, and the rate has been held at 2.70 East Caribbean dollars to one US dollar since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling. The country scores 30 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it, and no government pressure on the bank was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case concerns the bank: after it seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it had fraudulently taken assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors; on 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, called the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions, wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable and that the spending invites disciplinary action, and proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis; on 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. Trevor Brathwaite, an accountant who earlier worked for KPMG Peat Marwick, was deputy governor from April 2006 to September 2021 and sat on the board of East Caribbean Financial Holding Co. Ltd, a financial holding company; no dates are given for that seat, and the move is not an accusation. De La Rue prints the notes and PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. The bank's 2020/2021 annual report says it continued its engagement with the World Bank's Reserves Advisory Management Partnership (RAMP), and that a second engagement was judged appropriate to go on building up its newly formed Risk and Analytics Unit, the unit that reports on the reserves portfolio; the same report says the investment guidelines for its external managers were reviewed and updated and that the foreign reserve portfolio had grown to about EC$4.6 billion. The annual report for 2024/2025 and the audited accounts to 31 March 2025 do not repeat the RAMP engagement, so it stands as a 2020/2021 fact.

2025-02-17 · public pressure. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Eastern Caribbean Central Bank Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions. Gonsalves wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable, and that the spending invites disciplinary action. He proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis, and said he had supported Antoine's appointment but wanted suitable and comfortable accommodation for him instead. On 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. The Monetary Council is made up of the member states' finance ministers, so this is pressure from heads of government on the union's own central bank. PM Gonsalves wants ECCB governor to consider resigning amid controversy over his official residence (Caribbean Times)
OWNERSHIP AND OUTSIDE CONTROL

Eastern Caribbean Currency Union (monetary union)

The ECCB is the monetary authority for Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.
The ECCB agreement was signed on 5 July 1983 and the Bank was commissioned on 1 October 1983.
The EC dollar has been fixed at EC$2.70 = US$1.00 since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling to the US dollar.
Section 24(2) of the ECCB Agreement Act requires an external reserve of not less than 60% of currency in circulation and other demand liabilities.
The IMF AREAER 2023 classification lists the ECCU members as a currency board.

BANK OF KOREA
South Korea
South Korea's money is the won, issued by the Bank of Korea, which scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One episode of government pressure is recorded. Choi Kyung-hwan became deputy prime minister for the economy and finance minister in July 2014 and pressed publicly for lower interest rates, launching a stimulus package and warning that the economy stood between a leap forward and a recession; he said in public that he had not mentioned the base rate and that the central bank should get the hint. On 14 August 2014 the bank cut its base rate by a quarter point to 2.25 percent, the first move in fifteen months, and cut again to 2.0 percent on 15 October. Reporting at the time described both cuts as made under government pressure rather than as the start of a policy cycle, and a Reuters survey ahead of the August meeting recorded a sharp reversal in market expectations that raised questions about the bank's independence. Governor Lee Ju-yeol said the decision was his committee's and that its independence was guaranteed. Independence is written into the Bank of Korea Act, but the same reporting noted a long record of governments pressing the bank to cooperate: the May 2013 cut under a previous governor was read the same way, and in October 2010 a vice finance minister attended a rate-setting meeting to deliver the government's view of the economy. Two cases are recorded, both ending in conviction. Between 2022 and 2023 a currency-exchange employee at the bank's Daejeon Sejong-Chungnam headquarters broke the rule that older coins leave the vault first, at a coin collector's request, letting 240,000 one-hundred-won coins from 2018 and 2019 go out ahead of 2017 coins; the collector made about 180 million won selling them and gave the employee about 55 million, and the Daejeon District Court imposed two years and six months in prison, a fine and confiscation. Between 2013 and 2015 an employee handling receipts from the bank's publication sales diverted about 56 million won to a personal account and spent about 12 million won on commemorative banknote sheets with a company card; the Seoul Central District Court gave eight months suspended for two years, the money having been repaid. Two officials came from international lenders: Hwang Geon-il of the World Bank was nominated to the rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee, and Rhee Chang-yong of the International Monetary Fund was nominated governor on 23 March 2022. Three audits cover the bank: the Board of Audit and Inspection once a year, an auditor appointed by the President on the finance minister's recommendation who serves three years and reports to the Monetary Policy Committee, and an outside accounting firm the law requires but does not name. The notes and coins are made by the state-run mint, the Korea Minting and Security Printing Corporation, the country's only maker of banknotes and coins and a close partner of the bank, and the Bank of Korea is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, whose capital has been held by central banks alone since private shares were bought back in 2001. Its officials also sit on the Financial Stability Board, which lists the Bank of Korea and the Financial Services Commission as its member institutions for the country and is chaired by Andrew Bailey, governor of the Bank of England. A newspaper report of 12 February 2025 says all 104.4 tonnes of South Korea's gold, bought between 2011 and 2013, is stored at the Bank of England. That is the paper's own wording, not attributed to the Bank of Korea, so it is a claim rather than a confirmed fact.

CENTRAL BANK OF KUWAIT
Kuwait
The Central Bank of Kuwait issues the Kuwaiti dinar and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar announced in advance. Its assets were 36.4 billion US dollars at the end of 2025, and it is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Two accounting firms check its books, Al-Aiban, Al-Osaimi & Partners of Ernst & Young and KPMG, Safi Al-Mutawa & Partners, which signed off the accounts for the fiscal year ended 31 March 2013, and Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank. One case is recorded and it is unproven: the Kuwaiti newspaper Al Jarida, citing unnamed sources, reported that the securities regulator had decided to refer Governor Mohammad Al Hashel to prosecutors over a suspected breach of investment rules involving shares in a local bank. He denied it, saying he had never traded shares in a listed company while in senior posts; the regulator did not answer Reuters' calls. Governor Basel Al-Haroon, in post since April 2022, worked at the bank from 1989 to 2006 and from late 2006 to 2012, and in between and afterwards led a Kuwaiti investment company and was vice chairman of a Kuwaiti bank from 2016 to 2018. No ethics finding is recorded. Kuwait scores 32 of 100, and 3 of 15 on how much it tells the public.

BANK OF THE LAO P.D.R.
Laos
The Bank of the Lao P.D.R. is the central bank of Laos, which uses the kip; its top-denomination 100,000-kip note is printed by Goznak, the Russian state currency works. One case is recorded and it ended in convictions. On 8 September 2026 the Vientiane People's Court sentenced two former directors general to life imprisonment for abusing their positions to withdraw foreign currency from the bank's reserves and exchange unlimited amounts; one of them, Aod, was sentenced in his absence because he died during the proceedings. In a related case nine bank employees were convicted of corruption and money laundering, including trading currency at special rates. Losses across the cases exceeded 2.29 trillion kip, about 102.6 million US dollars. Government pressure was reported in 1 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, and that instance was a demand to print money. The bank has two swap lines with China, arrangements to borrow each other's currency: one of 6 billion yuan, and one from January 2020 with no amount stated. p:LBN:
BANQUE DU LIBAN
Lebanon
Banque du Liban issues Lebanon's currency, the Lebanese pound. Riad Salameh ran it for three decades until 2023, arriving from Merrill Lynch, where he worked from 1973 to 1993 and managed the personal portfolio of Rafic Hariri, the prime minister who then appointed him governor. A 2023 forensic audit by Alvarez & Marsal found the bank's foreign-currency position swung from a 7.2 billion US dollar surplus at the end of 2015 to a 50.7 billion dollar deficit at the end of 2020 with no loss shown on the balance sheet, and that Salameh set the accounting standards that concealed the losses and decided which banks benefited from financial engineering, unchallenged by the Central Council. The 2018 accounts, signed off with qualifications by EY and Deloitte, carried a 6.82 billion dollar asset called seigniorage on financial stability while the bank helped fund a widening government deficit. On 18 May 2020 the prosecutor Ali Ibrahim charged Mazen Hamdan, the bank's director of cash operations, with illegally manipulating the exchange rate; that charge is unproven. In May 2023 French prosecutors issued an arrest warrant for Salameh over illicit enrichment and alleged laundering of 330 million dollars, and Germany issued a second a week later; he called the French warrant a violation of the law. Arrested in Beirut in September 2024, held about thirteen months and released in September 2025 on bail of more than 14 million dollars, he was indicted with two lawyers in January 2026 over 44.8 million dollars allegedly taken from a consultancy account. He is also under investigation over allegations that more than 300 million dollars was siphoned off between 2002 and 2015 through Forry Associates, a company controlled by his brother Raja. All of it is unproven, and both brothers deny wrongdoing. The bank holds 286.8 tonnes of gold, 74.5 percent of its reserves, and scores 44 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Press reporting says KPMG was appointed in 2020 to audit the bank's accounts and that its findings have not been made public; this rests on a news report rather than a Banque du Liban document.

p:LBR:
CENTRAL BANK OF LIBERIA
Liberia
Liberia's money is the Liberian dollar, issued by the Central Bank of Liberia, which scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In March 2019 a Monrovia court ordered former deputy governor Sirleaf, former governor Weeks and official Hagba held for trial on charges of economic sabotage, theft or misuse of public money and criminal conspiracy, over banknotes printed in 2016 to 2018 that could not be accounted for. The Justice Minister later dropped the charges against Sirleaf and three others, while Weeks remained under indictment, so nothing was proven against him. Crane Currency printed those notes under two contracts totalling 15 billion Liberian dollars, and a Presidential Investigation Team alleged it conspired with bank officials to print 18,151,000,000, beyond what was contracted; Crane denied wrongdoing and kickbacks and said it had not been charged, and the allegation is not a court finding. In July 2024 Liberia suspended governor Tarlue indefinitely after the General Auditing Commission reported on 2018 to 2023 and found irregularities in lending to the government, including more than 80 million US dollars in apparently unauthorised financing for salary payments, irregular contract awards and spending beyond approved limits; that stands as an official finding. His own career before the bank is documented in the bank's published profile of him: J. Aloysius Tarlue, Jr. was a compliance analyst at HSBC Bank NA from 2001 to 2004, a compliance officer at Merrill Lynch from 2004 to 2007, a senior risk officer at Deutsche Bank NA from 2007 to 2008, a compliance officer at BNY Mellon NA from 2008 to 2013 and a compliance officer at J.P. Morgan Chase from 2013 to 2018, then executive chairman of the board of commissioners of the Liberia Electricity Regulatory Commission from 2018 to 2020, and has been Executive Governor and chairman of the board of governors since 2020. A governor also left at the president's request. In May 2019 President George Weah announced that Executive Governor Nathaniel Patray was stepping down because of his age, which surprised the public and the banking sector, and Patray resigned that October. CENTRAL BANK OF LIBYA
Libya
The Central Bank of Libya issues the dinar, and Britain's De La Rue prints the notes. The bank has signed a cooperation agreement under the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership; it describes an exchange of expertise and capacity building, not handing its reserves over to be managed. The Misrata Criminal Court convicted two people over a scheme to seize 128 million US dollars and 5 million euros from the Sirte branch in 2013, with sentences of 15 and 13 years. In November 2022 the bank accused its deputy governor, Ali al-Hibri, of signing forged 50-dinar notes printed in Russia, and Governor Saddek Elkaber asked the Attorney-General to pursue a complaint; that allegation is unproven. Global Witness reported on 19 February 2021 that senior officials hold paid directorships abroad and that Elkaber chairs a London bank the central bank indirectly owns, calling this a conflict of interest while alleging no lawbreaking. On 18 August 2024 the Presidential Council decreed that the governor be replaced; a delegation from the Dbeibah government then took over his office, al-Kabir said he had fled over militia threats, and banking operations were suspended. Libya scores 50 of 100 for exposure to outside influence. Libya's central bank publishes no annual auditor's report, but Deloitte audited both of the branches it split into in 2014, covering September 2014 to June 2020. The Presidency Council commissioned that review with United Nations support, and the final reports were handed over in Tripoli on 8 July 2021.

EASTERN CARIBBEAN CENTRAL BANK
St. Lucia
St. Lucia has no central bank of its own: it uses the EC dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank for eight members, among them Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada and Saint Lucia. The currency has been fixed at EC$2.70 to one US dollar since July 1976, and the law requires reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation; the agreement was signed on 5 July 1983. One case is recorded. After the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it fraudulently misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors. On 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions; he wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable and that the spending invites disciplinary action, and proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis. On 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. For St. Lucia the arrangement scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are made of, and a report on the updated 2027 banknote family says the notes are printed on Safeguard polymer by De La Rue; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. The bank's 2020/2021 annual report says it continued its engagement with the World Bank's Reserves Advisory Management Partnership (RAMP), and that a second engagement was judged appropriate to go on building up its newly formed Risk and Analytics Unit, the unit that reports on the reserves portfolio; the same report says the investment guidelines for its external managers were reviewed and updated and that the foreign reserve portfolio had grown to about EC$4.6 billion. The annual report for 2024/2025 and the audited accounts to 31 March 2025 do not repeat the RAMP engagement, so it stands as a 2020/2021 fact.

2025-02-17 · public pressure. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Eastern Caribbean Central Bank Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions. Gonsalves wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable, and that the spending invites disciplinary action. He proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis, and said he had supported Antoine's appointment but wanted suitable and comfortable accommodation for him instead. On 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. The Monetary Council is made up of the member states' finance ministers, so this is pressure from heads of government on the union's own central bank. PM Gonsalves wants ECCB governor to consider resigning amid controversy over his official residence (Caribbean Times)

Eastern Caribbean Currency Union (monetary union)

The ECCB is the monetary authority for Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

The EC dollar has been fixed at EC$2.70 = US$1.00 since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling to the US dollar.
Section 24(2) of the ECCB Agreement Act requires an external reserve of not less than 60% of currency in circulation and other demand liabilities.
The IMF AREAER 2023 classification lists the ECCU members as a currency board.

Sri Lanka
The Central Bank of Sri Lanka issues the rupee. It scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it, at 63. On 14 November 2023 a majority of a five-judge Supreme Court bench ruled that the three Rajapaksa brothers, former governors Cabraal and Lakshman and members of the bank's Monetary Board violated the public trust in their handling of the economy, leading to the 2022 crisis. In June 2019 the Attorney General filed a 23-count indictment against former governor Arjuna Mahendran and nine others over a February 2015 treasury bond auction; these are charges, not findings. Mahendran's term ended on 30 June, and he told the Monetary Board he would not seek reappointment until the parliamentary committee COPE finished its bond inquiry. President Maithripala Sirisena, who had said in June 2015 that he should resign, tweeted that he would name a new governor within hours; Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe said Mahendran could not be removed because the charges had never been proved, and nobody was named that day. Sirisena said in 2017 that he personally removed him, and the Auditor General found a loss of 1.6 billion rupees. CENTRAL BANK OF LESOTHO
Lesotho
Lesotho issues the loti, and the South African rand circulates alongside it. Under the Common Monetary Area, which replaced a Rand Monetary Area agreement signed in December 1974 and was followed by a Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992 when Namibia joined, member currencies are pegged to the rand one for one and are legal tender only in the country that issues them; Lesotho must back what it issues fully with rand assets, and South Africa pays it an imputed return on rand circulating there. All five of its current notes, introduced on 23 December 2021, are printed by De La Rue. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand said to have been stolen from the Central Bank of Lesotho. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa, and that some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are unproven. Its 2023 accounts were audited by Moteane, Quashie & Associates with SizweNtsalubaGobodo Grant Thornton. Lesotho scores 30 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and corruption and secrecy around the bank is its weakest side, at 60.

Common Monetary Area (common monetary area)

The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho; it was replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and by the Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined.
Member currencies have been pegged to the rand at par since their introduction; they are legal tender only in the issuing country.
Lesotho and Namibia must fully back their currency issues with rand assets; Eswatini does not face this requirement.
The rand has not been de jure legal tender in Eswatini since 1986.
South Africa makes compensatory payments representing an imputed return on rand circulating as legal tender in Lesotho and Namibia; Eswatini has received none since 1986.

BANK OF LITHUANIA
Lithuania
Lithuania uses the euro, so the Bank of Lithuania does not set interest rates itself: the European Central Bank sets them for the 21 countries that share the currency, a group Bulgaria joined on 1 January 2026. Lithuania's own case ended in acquittal. An official who monitored the commercial bank Snoras was sacked in November 2011 and charged with letting Snoras keep information from the bank's leadership, including on assets in Swiss banks; a guilty verdict in March 2014 was annulled by a Vilnius court, which found that no crime had been committed, and that ruling can still be appealed to the Supreme Court. Two further cases sit at the European Central Bank. In case 1697/2016/ANA the European Ombudsman found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum where central bankers sit alongside private financiers such as Citi's chief executive Jane Fraser, saying it was not in keeping with the bank's independence; the bank declined, and Draghi did not suspend it. On 18 May 2015 one of its officials, Cœuré, told a private evening event in London that the bank would bring forward its asset purchases, and the speech was published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error; Draghi said no market-sensitive information had been revealed. Six of that bank's officials have moved to or from private finance, among them Otmar Issing, its former chief economist, who in 2006 took what he called a loose advisory position with Goldman Sachs, and Luis de Guindos, who headed Lehman Brothers and Nomura Securities in Iberia from 2006 to 2008 and became vice-president in 2018. Lithuania's 5.8 tonnes of gold, 466 bars, are all stored at the Bank of England as custodian, none of it at home. UAB Ernst & Young Baltic audited its accounts for 2018 to 2021, UAB ROSK Consulting for 2022 to 2024. It scores 20 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

BANK OF LATVIA (LATVIJAS BANKA)
Latvia
Latvia uses the euro, so policy is set by the European Central Bank for the 21 countries on the currency, and the Bank of Latvia takes part in it; the Latvian bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank central banks use among themselves. Former governor Ilmars Rimsevics was convicted of taking a bribe and other material inducements by the Riga District Court on 20 December 2023, sentenced to six years in prison with a five-year ban on public office, and lost about 25,000 euro and several properties to confiscation; he was tried alongside the businessman Maris Martinsons. Parliament had moved on the bank's rules while he was still in post: on 22 February 2018 the Saeima sent draft amendments to the Law on the Bank of Latvia to its committees, proposed by lawmakers of the Unity faction, which would limit the governor to two successive terms and would allow the bank's top officials to be suspended if they become suspects or defendants in criminal proceedings. The proposal came days after the Corruption Prevention and Combating Bureau detained Rimsevics, who denied the allegations and refused to resign. Two further matters concern the European Central Bank. From 2016 to 2018 the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives; the bank declined and he did not. On 18 May 2015 Cœuré told a private London event the bank would front-load asset purchases, and the speech appeared only the next morning, which the bank called an internal procedure error; Draghi said no market-sensitive information was revealed. Six officials have moved between that bank and private finance, among them Otmar Issing, who became an international adviser to Goldman Sachs in 2006, with no ethics finding attached. Latvia's gold is stored at the Bank of England, which is custody of a reserve asset rather than management of money, and the bank manages its yen share of euro reserves jointly with the Oesterreichische Nationalbank. KPMG Baltics SIA audits its accounts for 2025 to 2029; Forvis Mazars audits the European Central Bank for 2025 to 2029, where BlackRock was also hired to help design asset-backed securities purchases. Latvia scores 23 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed.

MONETARY AUTHORITY OF MACAO
Macao
Macao's money, the pataca, is issued by the Monetary Authority of Macao, and in December 2025 it was held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. The top note of the Bank of China Macau series, the 1,000-pataca note, is printed by Hong Kong Note Printing Limited; Macao's other note-issuing bank is BNU. One case is documented, and it is an administrative finding by a foreign regulator rather than a criminal conviction: on 15 September 2005 the US Treasury named Banco Delta Asia, a bank licensed and supervised in Macao, a primary money laundering concern under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, and FinCEN proposed a rule cutting it off from US correspondent accounts. Treasury said the bank had served North Korean government agencies and front companies for more than 20 years, handled the bulk of North Korea's precious metal sales, and alleged that senior bank officials accepted large cash deposits, including counterfeit US currency, and agreed to put the notes into circulation; Under Secretary Stuart Levey said Macao needs significant improvement in its money laundering controls, and the bank denied wrongdoing. Its law leaves it little independence from government: 0.271 of 1 on one index, the lowest of 155 places, with its power to refuse lending to the government scored at zero. It has two borrowing lines with China's central bank, one signed on 5 December 2025 that runs both ways for 50 billion yuan, or 57 billion patacas, with no end date, and an earlier line of 30 billion renminbi from December 2019 whose standing is not known. It scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

2005 · money laundering at a supervised bank; foreign regulator finding on weak local controls · official finding. On 15 September 2005 the US Treasury named Banco Delta Asia, a bank licensed and supervised in Macao, a primary money laundering concern under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, and FinCEN proposed a rule cutting it off from US correspondent accounts. Treasury said the bank had served North Korean government agencies and front companies for more than 20 years, handled the bulk of North Korea's precious metal sales, and helped agents make multi-million dollar cash deposits and withdrawals. It alleged that senior bank officials accepted large cash deposits, including counterfeit US currency, and agreed to put the notes into circulation, and that the bank serviced an account for a known international drug trafficker. Treasury said the bank tailored its services to North Korea with little oversight or control, and Under Secretary Stuart Levey said Macao needs significant improvement in its money laundering controls. Morocco
Bank Al-Maghrib issues Morocco's dirham, held to a pre-announced peg, meaning a fixed rate, against the euro. It prints the notes and mints the coins at its own unit, Dar As-Sikkah, founded in 1987, and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Morocco scores 26 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported between 2010 and 2018. Two cases are on record, both under investigation and unproven. In 2022 the bank complained to the prosecutor's office about one of its own staff and a service provider over suspected corruption in awarding contracts, with no amounts, charges or ruling given. On 4 July 2019 it said 1.2 million dirhams, about 125,000 US dollars, had been stolen while cash was moved from the Dar As-Sikkah mint to northern cities, and opened an investigation, with no findings reported. Abdellatif Jouahri was named wali, or governor, in 2003, coming from the presidency of the CIMR, a private-sector employers' pension body.

Abdellatif Jouahri (Wali, i.e. Governor, of Bank Al-Maghrib from 2003; previously president of BMCE until 1995 and then president of the CIMR): from president of the CIMR, a private-sector employers' pension body per the ACAPS regulator, directly into the governorship of Bank Al-Maghrib in 2003. Le Matin's report of 23 April 2003 on King Mohammed VI naming Abdellatif Jouahri wali of Bank Al-Maghrib sets out his career. It states he was president of BMCE, the Banque Marocaine du Commerce Exterieur, until 1995, the year the bank was privatised and taken over by Othman Benjelloun, after which he stepped back from business affairs; he was then appointed president of the CIMR, the Caisse Interprofessionnelle Marocaine de Retraites, and reworked it after a major reform; and he was then named wali of the central bank. Bank of Africa's own investor-relations page on its board of directors independently states that Banque Marocaine du Commerce Exterieur was privatised in 1995 and that the sale attracted a consortium of Moroccan and foreign institutional and financial investors led by Royale Marocaine d'Assurance. Neither source states that BMCE was privately owned during Jouahri's presidency, and both place the privatisation at the end of it, so on this evidence the BMCE side of his career was not private. The CIMR side is different. The official summary sheet published by Morocco's insurance and social-welfare regulator ACAPS, at https://acapsd10new.fornetmaroc.com/sites/default/files/fiche_synthetique_cimr.pdf, states that the CIMR was founded by a group of private-sector employers, was managed as an employers' association governed by the dahir of 15 November 1958 on associations, has governing bodies made up only of employer representatives, operates a voluntary scheme supplementary to the state social security system run by the CNSS, and converted into a societe mutuelle de retraite only in 2017 under Law 64-12. So the regulator's own text establishes that the CIMR was a private-sector employers' pension body, not a statutory public pension fund, at the time Jouahri led it immediately before taking the governorship. Le Matin gives no start or end dates for the CIMR presidency, so the commonly cited 2002 to 2003 span is not confirmed by these sources. S.M. le Roi nomme M. NATIONAL BANK OF MOLDOVA
Moldova
The National Bank of Moldova issues the leu, which is held within 2 percent of the euro. Its law scores 0.861 of 1 for independence, where 1 means the bank holds the power, and it scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence. Dorin Dragutanu resigned as governor on 21 September 2015 after criticism for failing to prevent about 1 billion dollars disappearing from three Moldovan banks; he blamed pressure from politicians and denied responsibility, and President Nicolae Timofti and Prime Minister Valeriu Strelet had both said he should go. On 5 March 2020 prosecutors searched the bank's headquarters and detained deputy governor Cincilei, former deputy governor Tabirta and a division head on suspicion of fraud and money laundering tied to that theft, which surfaced in 2014 and 2015 after the bank made a 13 billion leu emergency loan later turned into public debt; they also moved to arrest Dragutanu. None of it is proven. On the evening of 21 December parliament dismissed governor Octavian Armasu by 81 votes, citing insufficient and defective work on the fraud case. KPMG Moldova SRL checks the bank's accounts from outside. Armasu had come to the bank from the government: he became Governor on 30 November 2018, appointed for a seven-year term, having served before that as Moldova's Minister of Finance.

p:MDV:
MALDIVES MONETARY AUTHORITY
Maldives
The Maldives Monetary Authority issues the Maldivian rufiyaa, and its record turns on one scandal: the embezzlement of 1.3 billion rufiyaa from the Maldives Marketing and Public Relations Corporation. An Anti-Corruption Commission report made public in February 2019 found the authority negligent. Its Financial Intelligence Unit, the office that watches for suspicious money, was told in 2014 of a 59 million US dollar cheque from that company to a firm called SOF but did not look into it properly, did not examine SOF's large transactions through the Bank of Maldives and the Bank of Ceylon, and did not pass suspected money-laundering cases on. The unit's former head, Ibrahim Athif Shakoor, said governor Azeema Adam objected to filing a police report, citing too few staff and resources; Azeema said she had told him to investigate SOF's transactions and gave no specific instructions because the unit decided its own actions. In March 2019 police summoned governor Ahmed Naseer and confirmed he was being investigated for obstruction of justice, with no charge or court outcome named. He resigned in July 2019 amid allegations that he had got around the authority's rules and interfered in the unit's inquiries, one of them into a 22.5 million rufiyaa deposit to then-President Abdulla Yameen's account shortly before the 2018 election; Naseer denied influencing the unit and made counter-allegations, and no charges or findings followed. In February 2020 the Prosecutor General's Office charged Shakoor with negligence and failing to act appropriately on the case; he denied the allegations, and on 14 October 2025 that office withdrew the charge, citing how long it had been in court, with no conviction reported. One career move is documented: Ali Hashim, who was finance minister under former president Mohamed Nasheed from November 2008 to December 2010 and who also chaired the Addu International Airport Company during the previous MDP government, with no years given for that, was nominated by President Ibrahim Mohamed Solih for the vacant post of governor of the authority, as reported on 29 August 2019. Deloitte Partners in Male' audited the 2024 accounts. On 7 October 2024 India agreed a currency-borrowing line of 400 million US dollars and 30 billion Indian rupees. p:MEX:
BANK OF MEXICO
Mexico
Mexico's money is the Mexican peso, and its central bank is the Bank of Mexico, known as Banxico, one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Mexico scores 29 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. On 9 December 2020 the Senate approved a bill from Morena's Senate leader Ricardo Monreal obliging the bank to buy foreign banknotes and coins that commercial banks collect and cannot send back to the country they came from. The bank said the same day that this would violate the autonomy the Constitution gives it, because the law itself would fix the active operations it must carry out, and that those operations are high risk and could compromise its holdings of international reserves. It answered the premise with figures: foreign cash is less than 1 per cent of remittances sent to Mexico, and of the foreign cash that entered the country in the first nine months of 2020 the banks placed or repatriated 98 per cent themselves. Governor Alejandro Diaz de Leon said the bank could challenge the law in the Supreme Court, and that foreign authorities could bar it from transacting with counterparts abroad or freeze and confiscate reserves. Monreal said it was no attack on the bank's autonomy. The lower house never carried it. On 23 March 2022 President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador announced the bank's unanimous rate rise, from 6 to 6.5 per cent, before the bank published it; on 25 March he said finance minister Rogelio Ramirez de la O, who sits in on board meetings, had told him the evening before, and he apologised to the governor and accepted that the Bank of Mexico law had been violated. Deputy governor Gerardo Esquivel called it an error rather than a leak. People also move between the bank and private finance: Agustin Carstens came from deputy managing director of the International Monetary Fund to be governor from 1 January 2010 to 31 December 2015, and former governor Guillermo Ortiz became chairman of BTG Pactual's Mexico business from 1 January 2016. The bank makes its own notes in every denomination, at two factories of its own in Mexico City and El Salto, Jalisco; the notes it first circulated in 1925 were made by the American Bank Note Company of New York, and printing moved in-house in 1969. Note Printing Australia also says it has supplied the bank with polymer banknotes.

2020-12-09 · attempted law change. On 9 December 2020 the Senate approved a bill, brought by Morena's Senate leader Ricardo Monreal, amending the Bank of Mexico Law to oblige the central bank to buy foreign banknotes and coins that commercial banks collect and cannot return to the country they came from. Banco de Mexico issued a statement the same day saying the draft decree would violate the autonomy the Constitution gives it, because the law itself would determine active operations the central bank is obliged to carry out, and those operations are high risk and could compromise its holdings of international reserves and its constitutional mandate to preserve the purchasing power of the currency. The bank set out the facts it said the Senate had ignored: foreign cash is less than 1 percent of remittances sent to Mexico, and of the 4.7 billion dollars in foreign cash that entered the country between January and September 2020, commercial banks placed or repatriated 98 percent through correspondent arrangements. It said foreign banknotes are treated as high risk under anti-money-laundering standards, that the decree would weaken those standards and spread the risk to the central bank itself, and that foreign authorities could respond by restricting the correspondents that process Mexican banks' foreign currency, or by restricting Banco de Mexico's own operations and agreements abroad. Governor Alejandro Diaz de Leon said in a radio interview that the bank could challenge the law in the Supreme Court and warned that the central bank could be sanctioned by foreign authorities, which could include being barred from transacting with counterparts abroad and the freezing or confiscation of international reserves. Monreal said it was no attack on the bank's autonomy and that Banco de Mexico had to be less conservative. The bill still needed the lower house, where the vote was put off to February 2021 and never carried; the obligation did not take effect. NATIONAL BANK OF THE REPUBLIC OF NORTH MACEDONIA
North Macedonia
North Macedonia's money is the denar, issued by the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia and held in practice at a fixed rate to the euro. It scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. Its notes are printed abroad, by three firms in turn. The bank contracted the French firm Oberthur Fiduciaire to print 100-denar notes, reported on 8 May 2026, for 59,800,000 denars, about 972,358 euros. It had contracted the Russian state company Goznak for the 100-denar notes in 2021, for about 400,000 euros, as part of a 2.2 million euro reissue carrying the state's changed constitutional name. Three separate contracts with De La Rue International cover the 10, 500 and 1,000 denar notes, 45 million notes for 3.775 million euros in total, 20 million of them polymer. One case is recorded, running from 2017 to 2020, and it is unproven: an association of depositors of Eurostandard Bank said in a press release that the governor tipped off the finance minister and other large depositors so they could take their money out before the bank was put under administration, and that financial police reports were kept secret so it could keep operating. The association said Finance Minister Nina Angelovska withdrew more than 200,000 euros months before the central bank acted, and that over 60 million euros were lost; no charges and no official finding are reported. The European Central Bank gave the bank a temporary line to borrow euros against collateral from 15 December 2022 to 15 January 2024, which has expired.

p:MLI:
CENTRAL BANK OF WEST AFRICAN STATES (BCEAO)
Mali
Mali's money is the CFA franc, issued not by a national central bank but by the Central Bank of West African States, known as the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The rate is fixed at 1 euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France gives an unconditional, unlimited guarantee that the currency can be exchanged, advancing money to the bank if its foreign currency reserves run out. A cooperation agreement signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one and ended the requirement that the bank keep at least half its reserves at the French Treasury; the bank's account there was closed in April 2021 according to a French Senate report, while the Treasury's own page says there has been no such account since January 2020. France approved the agreement by a law of 3 February 2021 and withdrew its representatives from the bank's board, its Monetary Policy Committee and the regional banking commission, though one independent member of that committee is still appointed in consultation with the French government. The agreement provides for the currency to be renamed the eco, and a West African meeting on 7 September 2026 kept 2027 as the target year for launching a single currency of that name. Mali scores 42 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, mainly because of corruption in the country and the risk of money laundering. One case is recorded at the bank: a summit of heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011 after he was criticised for ignoring a decision of 23 December by the union's finance ministers that handed control of the institution to Alassane Ouattara, and the report says the bank paid out 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade called for an audit and alleged that the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo after being dismissed; another figure given is 300 billion, and no audit result is reported. Its accounts are checked by firms appointed in pairs, one the titulaire that does the audit and the other the suppléant that stands in: Grant Thornton Senegal with a grouping of PKF BAGE and Crowe TG ICAAF behind it, and Deloitte Côte d'Ivoire with Mazars Senegal behind it for 2024 to 2029. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of its reserves sits in two funds run by other institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it bought units in a fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and grouped with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The same accounts say the bank joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program, managed by the World Bank, whose units were worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025.

2011-01-22 · forced resignation. The Central Bank of West African States is the central bank of eight countries, and in January 2011 its own member heads of state removed its governor. After the disputed Ivorian presidential election of November 2010, the bank recognised Alassane Ouattara as head of state and revoked Laurent Gbagbo's access to Ivorian state accounts in December, and the union's finance ministers decided on 23 December that only representatives of Ouattara's government would have signing authority. The Ouattara camp complained in mid-January that the bank was still channelling cash to Gbagbo, and the governor, Philippe-Henry Dacoury-Tabley, an Ivorian and a close confidant of Gbagbo, was accused of not cooperating. At an emergency summit of the heads of state of the West African Economic and Monetary Union in Bamako on 22 January 2011 he handed in his resignation. The bank's own statement, issued in Dakar that evening, said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders. He told reporters afterwards: "I agreed to hand in my resignation as that is what was asked of me", and defended his conduct by pointing to practical and technical reasons for not transferring control of the accounts. The union accepted the resignation and called on Ouattara to propose a successor; a deputy governor, Jean-Baptiste Compaore, took over in the interim. Gbagbo's administration, on state television it still controlled, rejected what it called the forced resignation of the governor and rejected the leaders' decision to let Ouattara name a replacement. The European Union listed Dacoury-Tabley, giving as its ground that as governor of the BCEAO he refused to recognise the authority of the democratically elected President and was helping to fund the illegitimate administration of Mr Laurent Gbagbo. This record is the removal of the governor by the member states; what he is alleged to have done with the bank's money is recorded separately as a corruption case. Keyed to the union, so it counts for all eight member countries. Pro-Gbagbo bank head quits (Al Jazeera)

West African CFA franc (WAEMU/UMOA) – France cooperation (external guarantee)

The currency (XOF) is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs.
France gives an unconditional and unlimited convertibility guarantee through advances to the central bank if its foreign exchange reserves run out.
A new cooperation agreement was signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019, replacing the 1973 agreement; France stated the reform would enter into force in 2020.
The 2019 agreement ended the centralisation of BCEAO reserves at the French Treasury, ending the requirement that the BCEAO hold at least 50% of its reserves there.
The BCEAO's operations account at the French Treasury was closed in April 2021 (French Senate report); the Treasury page states it has had no operations account since January 2020.
France approved the agreement by Law no. 2021-108 of 3 February 2021.
France withdrew its representatives from the BCEAO board, the Monetary Policy Committee and the UMOA Banking Commission; one independent member of the Monetary Policy Committee is appointed in consultation with the French government.
The agreement provides that the currency will be renamed 'ECO'; the Banque de France page says the name 'is set to change' at member states' will, i.e. the CFA franc name remains in use.
ECOWAS Convergence Council (7 September 2026) kept 2027 as the target launch year for an ECOWAS single currency named the ECO.

CENTRAL BANK OF MALTA
Malta
Malta uses the euro, so its interest rates are set by the European Central Bank, in which the Central Bank of Malta takes part. Its books have been checked from outside by two firms: KPMG under an approved term covering the financial years 2019 to 2025, and Deloitte Audit Ltd under a term covering 2023 to 2027. Its own case concerns governor Scicluna, a former finance minister: on 29 May 2024 he pleaded not guilty to fraud over the government's handling of a private hospital contract, the Vitals concession, while he was minister. He stepped aside in July 2024 and was reinstated in July 2025 after the European Central Bank was consulted and raised no objections; the charges remain unproven. Two findings sit at the European Central Bank: the European Union's complaints office found maladministration over president Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a club of central bankers and private bankers, and recommended in January 2018 that he suspend it, which the bank declined and he did not; and a speech of 18 May 2015 to a private London event was published only the next day. Malta's own share of the European Central Bank's US dollar pooled reserves is not run from Malta: the Central Bank of Ireland has managed it since 1 January 2008, at Malta's own request. Each euro-area country transferred foreign reserves to the ECB in proportion to its shareholding, and the ECB's page says those reserves are managed in a decentralised way by the national central banks, which act for the ECB on a disclosed agency basis; Malta is the one that handed the job to another country's central bank. The combined value of Ireland's and Malta's share of the ECB's US dollar pooled reserves is USD 1.5 billion, and Ireland's own portion of the ECB reserves amounted to EUR 0.4 billion. CENTRAL BANK OF MYANMAR
Myanmar
The Central Bank of Myanmar issues the kyat, and the military has taken hold of its leadership. Three days after the coup of 1 February 2021 the military's State Administration Council made Than Than Swe a deputy governor; she later became governor in place of Than Nyein. In August 2022 the junta replaced Than Nyein and a vice chairman with Than Than Swe and Major General Zaw Myint Naing, two months after installing six lieutenant colonels as deputy directors. The former deputy governor Bo Bo Nge, arrested on the morning of the coup, was sentenced by a junta court in December 2022 to 20 years in prison after a months-long secret trial, which sources said concerned mismanagement of banks trading foreign currency; the junta-backed Anti-Corruption Commission accused him of not collecting tax on a 5 million US dollar Open Society deposit and of placing a 350 million dollar loan in a lower-interest account. Those accusations are the commission's own, and the economist Sean Turnell called Bo Bo Nge someone fighting against corruption. Government pressure was reported in 18 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, mostly pressing the bank to ease and to print money. Giesecke+Devrient of Munich, which had supplied raw materials and system components for printing kyat notes, suspended all deliveries to the state-owned Security Print Works after the military crackdown. The bank's own printing works at Wazi printed a 20,000-kyat commemorative note introduced on 31 July 2023, which is not the circulating series. Myanmar scores 57 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, second of the 194 places scored.
