p:MNE:
CENTRAL BANK OF MONTENEGRO
Montenegro
The Central Bank of Montenegro does not issue money. Montenegro took the euro on its own: the Deutsche Mark became sole legal tender on 1 January 2001 and the euro replaced it in March 2002. The bank issues no euros and is not a member of the European System of Central Banks, but has a repo line, a short-term loan arrangement, of up to 250 million euros with the Eurosystem. It scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Three cases are documented, all alleged and unproven. In July 2018 the bank's Council reportedly found that deputy governor Irena Radovic put personal interest ahead of the public interest and disclosed business secrets, and the bank asked parliament to dismiss her; she called the decision illegal retaliation and said she would sue, and no court has ruled. The NGO MANS said five payments totalling 4,100 euros went to relatives of governor Radoje Zugic in 2017 and 2018; he reportedly said he did not act illegally. In July 2012 MANS alleged to a prosecutor that First Bank got a 44 million euro state loan in 2008 it could not repay; no charge has been brought. “Ernst&Young Montenegro” Ltd Podgorica audits the bank's accounts. Zugic has moved between the bank and the government several times: he was Deputy Director General for Payment System Operations at the bank from 2001 to 2004, director of Montenegro's Pension and Disability Insurance Fund from 2004 to 2010, Governor from 2010 to 2012, Minister of Finance from 2012 to 2016, Advisor to the Prime Minister from May to October 2016, and Governor again since October 2016; he also sat as a board member representing state capital at the commercial banks Podgoricka banka, before its privatisation, and Prva banka Crne Gore.

p:MNG:
BANK OF MONGOLIA
Mongolia
The Bank of Mongolia issues the tugrik. Two cases and two departures centre on N. Zoljargal, governor from 2012, who was replaced on 20 July 2016, two years before his term was due to end and with no reason given. The anti-corruption agency IAAC arrested him on 29 November 2017 over the Chinggis bond and a price-stabilising programme, part of a wider look at how the bank was run from 2012 to 2016; a court released him with a travel ban, prosecutors had not formally charged him and no later outcome was found, so nothing there is proven. In April 2020 he and three politicians were reported charged with abuse of power over illegally transferring 49 per cent of the Erdenet Mining Company; no outcome is recorded and those charges are unproven too. Lawmakers accepted the resignation of his successor, Nadmid Bayartsaikhan, on 21 November 2019, after the Financial Action Task Force, which sets international rules against money laundering, put Mongolia on its grey list over enforcement. The present governor, B. Lkhagvasuren, came from the World Bank in Washington to the bank as adviser to the governor in 2000, and the rest of his career is in Mongolian public bodies. Ernst & Young Mongolia Audit LLC audited the accounts for the 2020 financial year, and Giesecke & Devrient printed the new 5,000-togrog note. It holds two currency swap lines with China, arrangements to lend each other money, one renewed on 26 June 2026 at 15 billion yuan against 7.85 trillion tugrik, and scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

p:MOZ:
BANK OF MOZAMBIQUE
Mozambique
The Bank of Mozambique is the country's central bank, and it scores 43 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Four of its records come out of the 'hidden debts', more than two billion US dollars of loans from Credit Suisse and VTB of Russia. Letters from 2013 shown at a trial in the United States had the bank authorising the company Proindicus to seek 372 million dollars, later 622 million, and Ematum 850 million; board member Silvia de Abreu signed them after an instruction from governor Ernesto Gove, who in 2016 denied responsibility and said he had never heard of Proindicus. That strand is still under investigation, so nothing in it is proven. At the Maputo City Court on 23 November 2021 Gove testified that he had signed on grounds of sovereignty and national security and admitted irregularities, and judge Efigenio Baptista rejected his argument that the law barring such approvals did not apply; the same day the bank's administrator Silvina de Abreu testified that it should not have authorised the loans and that Gove told her to keep technical staff out. Both of those stand as official findings. In April 2023 the daily Noticias reported Gove and two other board members among four people accused in a second trial then being prepared, with no date set and no charges listed, which is unproven. President Filipe Nyusi fired deputy governor Antonio Pinto de Abreu on 26 January 2016 without giving a reason, and on 31 August 2016 replaced Gove with Rogerio Zandamela, an International Monetary Fund official, which is a career move and not an accusation. On 2 September 2026 President Daniel Chapo revoked Waldemar Fernando de Sousa's appointment as governor, citing circumstances he did not specify, and named Felisberto Dinis Navalha; the Attorney General's Office accuses De Sousa over the hidden debts, though he was not tried in the main case. 2023 · rescues or hidden losses · charged. In April 2023 the daily Noticias, citing judicial sources, reported that former governor Ernesto Gove and two other central bank board members were among four accused in a second hidden debts trial being prepared. No trial date had been set, and the report lists no specific charges. Follow-up to the earlier record on the same case; no later outcome was confirmed in this search. Hidden debts: second trial under preparation (Club of Mozambique)
2013-2021 · central bank authorisation of state-guaranteed loans · official finding. Testifying as a witness at the Maputo City Court on 23 November 2021 in the hidden debts trial of 19 people, former Bank of Mozambique governor Ernesto Gove said he signed authorisations for foreign loans to Proindicus, Ematum and MAM on grounds of sovereignty and national security, and admitted irregularities in how the central bank granted them, including that the requests were handed personally to senior bank officials by Eugenio Matlaba and Antonio Carlos do Rosario rather than submitted at a counter, and that the financing contracts with Credit Suisse had already been signed. Article 83 of the Foreign Exchange Law regulations bars the central bank from authorising foreign loans to private companies whose repayment depends on a state guarantee; Gove argued it applied only to guarantees obtained after loans were agreed, and judge Efigenio Baptista rejected that reading. The loans exceeded two billion US dollars, from Credit Suisse and VTB of Russia. Hidden debts trial: Illegal loans were in interests of 'sovereignty', claims ex-governor of Bank of Mozambique (Club of Mozambique / AIM)
2013-2021 · central bank approval of state-guaranteed loans (later development in the hidden-debts case) · official finding. On the 49th day of the trial, 23 November 2021, Banco de Mocambique administrator Silvina de Abreu testified that under normal conditions the central bank should not have authorised the ProIndicus, EMATUM and MAM loans, because the Foreign Exchange Law bars approving loans whose disbursement depends on a State guarantee. She said then governor Ernesto Gove told her to work only with the management group and not to involve technical staff, as the file concerned state security and sovereignty. The approvals she described were US$372 million for ProIndicus in March 2013, US$850 million for EMATUM in August 2013 and a further US$250 million sought for ProIndicus less than three months later. 49o dia do julgamento do escandalo das 'dividas ocultas': Banco de Mocambique nao deveria ter autorizado emprestimos da ProIndicus, EMATUM e MAM (CDD Mocambique trial-monitoring bulletin, Year 03 No. 255)
2013-2019 · rescues or hidden losses · under investigation. Letters from 2013 presented in a US trial showed the Bank of Mozambique authorized Proindicus to seek a $372 million Credit Suisse loan, later $622 million, and Ematum an $850 million loan, part of the 'hidden debts' of over $2 billion. The letters were signed by board member Silvia de Abreu after a dispatch from governor Ernesto Gove, who in 2016 denied responsibility and said he had never heard of Proindicus. The newssheet Carta de Moçambique reported Gove's suspect status was confirmed and that he may face charges of abuse of office and membership of a criminal organisation. Bank of Mozambique involved in hidden debts – AIM report (Club of Mozambique)

CENTRAL BANK OF MAURITANIA
Mauritania
The Central Bank of Mauritania issues Mauritania's money, the ouguiya, and scores 28 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. One case is recorded, from 2020 and 2021, and it is still an investigation. In July 2020 police working under the Nouakchott-Ouest prosecutor arrested six people, one of them a bank employee, over foreign currency taken from the central bank. Early reports put the amount at about 1 million US dollars and later reports at 2.4 million, plus 500,000 dollars in counterfeit notes. By March 2021 seven people were in pretrial detention, presumed to have taken about 1 million dollars, and supporters held a sit-in demanding a quick trial. No trial or verdict is reported. The governor also signed an agreement with the World Bank treasury for advice on managing reserves.

EASTERN CARIBBEAN CENTRAL BANK
Montserrat
Montserrat uses the East Caribbean dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, which sets monetary policy for eight members, among them Montserrat, Anguilla, Dominica and Saint Lucia. The rate has been fixed at EC$2.70 to one US dollar since July 1976, and the founding agreement of 5 July 1983 requires reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation and other demand liabilities. One case is recorded and it was dismissed: after the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it had fraudulently misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors, and on 17 August 2018 a United States federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018. One of the member governments has since pressed the bank in public: in a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, called the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions, wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable and that the spending invites disciplinary action, and proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis; on 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are made of and, by one report, prints them under what governor Timothy Antoine called a long-term service agreement, with no value given; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. Montserrat scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, pulled up by corruption and secrecy around it, at 71, mainly because local law hides who owns money. The bank's 2020/2021 annual report says it continued its engagement with the World Bank's Reserves Advisory Management Partnership (RAMP), and that a second engagement was judged appropriate to go on building up its newly formed Risk and Analytics Unit, the unit that reports on the reserves portfolio; the same report says the investment guidelines for its external managers were reviewed and updated and that the foreign reserve portfolio had grown to about EC$4.6 billion. The annual report for 2024/2025 and the audited accounts to 31 March 2025 do not repeat the RAMP engagement, so it stands as a 2020/2021 fact.

BANK OF MAURITIUS
Mauritius
The Bank of Mauritius issues the Mauritian rupee and holds it within about 2 per cent of the United States dollar. Mauritius scores 27 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and 0.733 of 1 on an index of independence in law, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power. On 9 and 10 April 2025 the country's Financial Crimes Commission arrested the former governor, Seegolam, for fraud by abuse of position; he was charged with fraud and released on bail. The investigation concerns the alleged taking of 300 million rupees, about 6.7 million United States dollars, from the Mauritius Investment Corporation, a vehicle owned by the central bank and set up during the COVID pandemic. Seegolam and Renganaden Padayachy deny wrongdoing, and the charge is unproven. Rama Krishna Sithanen became governor on 16 November 2024, the day after he stopped chairing the fund administration firm Apex Group (Mauritius); he had chaired Sanne Mauritius from 2017 to 2022 and International Financial Services from 2011 to 2016. That is a career move, not an accusation. An earlier governor was dismissed outright. Rundheersing Bheenick took the post in February 2007; his first term was not renewed when it expired in February 2010 while allegations of abuse of power were investigated, he was cleared and reinstated on 21 May 2010, and was given a further term in 2013. Days after the general election of December 2014 brought in a new government, he received a letter from the secretary of the President of the Republic terminating his contract with immediate effect, and said the next day that he would consult his lawyers about whether the newly elected government had the constitutional right to dismiss the central bank governor. No reason was made clear at the time. Under section 13 of the Bank of Mauritius Act 2004 the governor is appointed by the President on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, and the bank is accountable to the Minister of Finance. Ramesh Basant Roi took over on 30 December 2014. Bheenick later sued the bank for 270 million rupees after settlement talks failed, saying he had been paid a nominal 10 rupees a month across his 91 months in office; the bank's deputy secretary confirmed that about 51.6 million rupees remained owed to him. The bank holds 12.4 tonnes of gold, with bars in storage at the Bank of England.

RESERVE BANK OF MALAWI
Malawi
The Reserve Bank of Malawi issues the kwacha, and presidents have removed its leaders twice. President Joyce Banda removed governor Perks Ligoya, according to two unnamed sources, with Charles Chuka reportedly chosen to succeed him and no official reason given; the date is not stated. Newly elected president Lazarus Chakwera dismissed governor Dalitso Kabambe and appointed Wilson Banda on 8 July 2020. After a forensic audit of the bank's payments between January 2019 and June 2020, the state charged Kabambe and three others with abuse of office, negligence, money laundering and causing loss of public funds, alleging that 4.3 billion kwacha went to FDH Bank without board approval; pleas were not taken because the charges were subject to change, and nothing is proven. In December 2021 police arrested Kabambe and Joseph Mwanamvekha, saying the two procured and masterminded the falsification of gross liability and net reserve base returns to make the International Monetary Fund believe Malawi was meeting the conditions of its Extended Credit Facility loan; that too stands only as an accusation. In January 2026 President Peter Mutharika appointed Henry Mathanga deputy governor, although the bank had dismissed him after a disciplinary inquiry and he faces criminal charges, and critics say the appointment breaches section 16(2) of the Reserve Bank of Malawi Act. Its 2,000-kwacha note is printed by Giesecke & Devrient. Malawi scores 37 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. President Lazarus Chakwera dismissed the governor he had himself installed: having removed Dalitso Kabambe in July 2020 and appointed Wilson Banda, he dismissed Banda in early January 2025 and moved up the deputy governor, MacDonald Mafuta Mwale. One career move is documented, and it is Mafuta Mwale's: he served as Secretary to the Treasury, the senior civil service post in the finance ministry, with no years given for it, was redeployed back to the Reserve Bank in January of the previous year, two years after that post, and was its deputy governor until he was appointed Governor with immediate effect, as reported on 7 January 2025, subject to confirmation by Parliament's Public Appointments Committee. The government's statement thanked Banda and gave no reason; Nyasa Times reported that the President had been demanding monetary reforms since June of the previous year and that a source close to State House said the results were painfully slow. Banda had devalued the kwacha by about 25 percent in May 2022, calling it a necessary evil to align the supply of foreign exchange with the fundamentals, and by a further 44 percent in November 2023, and the gap with the parallel market widened after both. Malawian civil society organisations said in January 2026 that the dismissal of the whole board at the time breached the Reserve Bank of Malawi Act's requirement of continuity in leadership, and that one of those removed was targeted for perceived political associations; Nyasa Times reported instead that he had been removed after a formal disciplinary inquiry under the Act and faced criminal charges. The two accounts have not been reconciled.

BANK NEGARA MALAYSIA
Malaysia
Bank Negara Malaysia is the country's central bank and issues the ringgit. Malaysia scores 31 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Two bribery cases are recorded, both from banknote printing. In July 2011 the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission charged former official Mohamad Daud with taking two bribes of 50,000 ringgit in 2004 and 2005 over a 95 million ringgit contract for the five-ringgit polymer note, won by Note Printing Australia; the court acquitted him on 6 December 2015 and the Attorney-General withdrew the appeal in February 2016. In October 2011 Securency and Note Printing Australia, both belonging to the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to provide benefits to foreign public officials to win banknote business with Malaysia's note-issuing authority between October 2001 and December 2003; no Malaysian official was named, and they paid 19,809,772 and 1,856,710 Australian dollars. Zeti Akhtar Aziz, governor for 16 years until 2016, became group chairman of the fund manager Permodalan Nasional Bhd. The bank's leadership changed hands under political conflict once. In late August 1998, during the Asian financial crisis, governor Ahmad Mohd Don and his deputy Fong Weng Phak resigned in disagreement with the government's currency plans. He had favoured tight monetary policy and was backed by the finance minister, while the prime minister and his special functions minister wanted an expansionary course and had attacked the governor publicly over it. A row over how the new currency controls were to be carried out prompted both resignations. The finance minister was sacked days later; Zeti Akhtar Aziz was appointed acting governor on 31 August 1998, and capital controls and a ringgit peg to the dollar followed the next day.

1998-08 · resignation under pressure. Bank Negara Malaysia governor Ahmad Mohd Don and his deputy Fong Weng Phak resigned in late August 1998, during the Asian financial crisis, in disagreement with the government's currency plans. Ahmad Don had favoured tight monetary policy and was backed by Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim, while Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and Daim Zainuddin wanted an expansionary course; Mahathir and Daim had attacked the governor publicly over the tight policy. Reporting at the time said a row over the implementation of comprehensive and unorthodox currency controls prompted the two resignations, and that the central bank had sided with Anwar in the dispute. Anwar was sacked days later. Zeti Akhtar Aziz was appointed acting governor on 31 August 1998, and capital controls, a ringgit peg to the dollar and a freeze on repatriating foreign portfolio capital followed on 1 September. BANK OF NAMIBIA
Namibia
The Bank of Namibia is the country's central bank. Namibia belongs to the Common Monetary Area with South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, joining under the agreement of February 1992: the Namibian dollar is pegged to the South African rand one for one, and every Namibian dollar issued must be fully backed by rand assets. The bank scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and the law gives it middling independence, 0.637 of 1 and 103rd of 155 countries. In 2002 court papers in a suit by Nambib Resources against the Minister of Mines listed governor Tom Alweendo as a 10 per cent shareholder in Trade Line Namibia, which held an exclusive licence to prospect on the Skeleton Coast. Alweendo said he had been made a director without his knowledge, and no finding or outcome is reported, so the allegation is unproven. Johannes !Gawaxab came from a private-sector banking career to the governorship on 1 June 2020, succeeding Ipumbu Shiimi; the bank's board page now shows Ebson Uanguta as governor from 1 January 2026. Deloitte Namibia and Grand Namibia audit its accounts, and De La Rue printed its new 50-dollar note.

Common Monetary Area (common monetary area)

The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho; it was replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and by the Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined.
Member currencies have been pegged to the rand at par since their introduction; they are legal tender only in the issuing country.
Lesotho and Namibia must fully back their currency issues with rand assets; Eswatini does not face this requirement.
The rand has not been de jure legal tender in Eswatini since 1986.
South Africa makes compensatory payments representing an imputed return on rand circulating as legal tender in Lesotho and Namibia; Eswatini has received none since 1986.

CENTRAL BANK OF WEST AFRICAN STATES (BCEAO)
Niger
Niger uses the CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO), which sets monetary policy for 8 members. The currency is pegged, held at a fixed rate of 1 euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and the French Treasury guarantees, without condition or limit, to advance euros if the BCEAO's reserves run out. A cooperation agreement signed on 21 December 2019 ended the requirement that the BCEAO keep at least 50% of its reserves at the French Treasury. Niger scores 43 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, mainly from money-laundering risk and corruption in the country. The BCEAO has one documented case: a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by finance ministers giving Alassane Ouattara power over the institution; reports say the BCEAO paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. Senegal's President Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo; another figure given is 300 billion, and no audit result is reported. Mazars Niger was selected to audit the BCEAO's accounts for 2024 to 2029. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of its reserves sits in two funds run by other institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it bought units in a fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and grouped with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The same accounts say the bank joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program, managed by the World Bank, whose units were worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025.

2011-01-22 · forced resignation. The Central Bank of West African States is the central bank of eight countries, and in January 2011 its own member heads of state removed its governor. After the disputed Ivorian presidential election of November 2010, the bank recognised Alassane Ouattara as head of state and revoked Laurent Gbagbo's access to Ivorian state accounts in December, and the union's finance ministers decided on 23 December that only representatives of Ouattara's government would have signing authority. The Ouattara camp complained in mid-January that the bank was still channelling cash to Gbagbo, and the governor, Philippe-Henry Dacoury-Tabley, an Ivorian and a close confidant of Gbagbo, was accused of not cooperating. At an emergency summit of the heads of state of the West African Economic and Monetary Union in Bamako on 22 January 2011 he handed in his resignation. The bank's own statement, issued in Dakar that evening, said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders. He told reporters afterwards: "I agreed to hand in my resignation as that is what was asked of me", and defended his conduct by pointing to practical and technical reasons for not transferring control of the accounts. The union accepted the resignation and called on Ouattara to propose a successor; a deputy governor, Jean-Baptiste Compaore, took over in the interim. Gbagbo's administration, on state television it still controlled, rejected what it called the forced resignation of the governor and rejected the leaders' decision to let Ouattara name a replacement. The European Union listed Dacoury-Tabley, giving as its ground that as governor of the BCEAO he refused to recognise the authority of the democratically elected President and was helping to fund the illegitimate administration of Mr Laurent Gbagbo. This record is the removal of the governor by the member states; what he is alleged to have done with the bank's money is recorded separately as a corruption case. Keyed to the union, so it counts for all eight member countries. Pro-Gbagbo bank head quits (Al Jazeera)
OWNERSHIP AND OUTSIDE CONTROL

West African CFA franc (WAEMU/UMOA) – France cooperation (external guarantee)

The currency (XOF) is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs.
France gives an unconditional and unlimited convertibility guarantee through advances to the central bank if its foreign exchange reserves run out.
A new cooperation agreement was signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019, replacing the 1973 agreement; France stated the reform would enter into force in 2020.
The 2019 agreement ended the centralisation of BCEAO reserves at the French Treasury, ending the requirement that the BCEAO hold at least 50% of its reserves there.
The BCEAO's operations account at the French Treasury was closed in April 2021 (French Senate report); the Treasury page states it has had no operations account since January 2020.
France approved the agreement by Law no. 2021-108 of 3 February 2021.
France withdrew its representatives from the BCEAO board, the Monetary Policy Committee and the UMOA Banking Commission; one independent member of the Monetary Policy Committee is appointed in consultation with the French government.
The agreement provides that the currency will be renamed 'ECO'; the Banque de France page says the name 'is set to change' at member states' will, i.e. the CFA franc name remains in use.
ECOWAS Convergence Council (7 September 2026) kept 2027 as the target launch year for an ECOWAS single currency named the ECO.

The French economy ministry, answering a question from Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, said the rules for depositing the BCEAO's monetary gold with the Banque de France are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, including financially, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. Press reporting puts the Paris holding in the Banque de France's underground vault, La Souterraine, in the first arrondissement. The concentration is politically contested in West Africa: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence, and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the UEMOA states' operating-account deposits at the French Treasury were. CENTRAL BANK OF NICARAGUA
Nicaragua
Nicaragua's money is issued by the Central Bank of Nicaragua, which scores 31 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case runs from 2000 to 2008 and ended in an official finding. In 2007 the country's Comptroller General, the state auditor, concluded that the bank's board sold CENI certificates, paper issued to cover the collapse of banks, for less than they were worth and then raised interest rates to the benefit of the main buyer, Bancentro; the fraud is put at 500 million dollars. The Comptroller alleged criminal involvement by six men, among them former finance minister Eduardo Montealegre, who denied wrongdoing and called it a political witch hunt, and in July 2008 a special prosecutor filed charges against 39 people including him. No central bank officials are named among the accused and no court ruling is given, though former bank president Francisco Mayorga had already been found guilty in the banking scandal. At the end of 2024 the statute governing the bank was rewritten in a week. The presidency sent the National Assembly the Ley de Administracion del Sistema Monetario y Financiero on 19 December 2024; it went to committee on 23 December during the legislative recess, was approved on 26 December and published in La Gaceta on 30 December. It repealed the bank's own organic law and the law governing the Superintendency of Banks and Other Financial Institutions, and put the two institutions, until then independent of each other, under one statute and one common board chaired by the bank's president, Ovidio Reyes, abolishing the Superintendency's own board; Reyes was also given coordination of the Financial Analysis Unit and the deposit fund. The law's own text says the institutions keep organic, functional, administrative, financial and budgetary autonomy and their institutional specialisation. Divergentes read it the other way, writing that the law eliminates the autonomy of the monetary and financial institutions and gives plenipotentiary powers to Reyes and to the Executive, and that removing the cross-checks between supervisor and central bank removes a safeguard against political and economic bias. Article 24 obliges every person resident or domiciled in Nicaragua, national or foreign, to give the bank and the Superintendency whatever economic, financial, statistical and regulatory information they ask for. The bank did not object publicly and its president gained authority rather than losing it; what changed was that the law governing the bank was rewritten by the Executive, without consultation. Baker Tilly Nicaragua, S.A. audited the accounts for 2024, and on 27 March 2024 the printer Orell Fussli was reported to have been partly awarded a tender to print and supply the bank's banknotes, with no value or quantity given.

On 19 December 2024 the presidency sent the National Assembly a bill, the Ley de Administracion del Sistema Monetario y Financiero, which was sent to committee on 23 December during the legislative recess, approved on 26 December and published in La Gaceta on 30 December. p:NLD:
DE NEDERLANDSCHE BANK
Netherlands
The Netherlands uses the euro, whose rates the European Central Bank sets for the 21 countries on it, and De Nederlandsche Bank is the Dutch central bank inside that system; it scores 23 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In June 2010 the Scheltema committee, set up by finance minister Wouter Bos, found that the bank had fallen seriously short in supervising DSB bank, missing flaws when licensing DSB in 2005 and being too patient afterwards, though it thought a different approach probably would not have prevented DSB's collapse. Parliament pressed the bank hard after that report: members called for a major overhaul of how it operates, the Christian Democrats said it had seriously fallen short as a regulator and that president Nout Wellink should explain publicly how he would restore its credibility, the GroenLinks member Jolande Sap said it would be very difficult to keep him on, and Roland van Vliet of the Freedom Party asked finance minister Jan Kees de Jager to sack him with a year of his term still to run. On 1 July 2010 the lower house voted on a motion of no confidence in Wellink and he survived it. He accepted the report's conclusions, which several members said was enough for them, and left at the end of his term in 2011. Two further findings sit at the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration over president Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum of central bankers and private financiers, and in January 2018 recommended he suspend it, which the bank declined and he did not; and a board member's 18 May 2015 remarks in London that the bank would front-load asset purchases were published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error. Wim Duisenberg joined the Dutch bank in 1981 and became chairman in 1982, after three years at the International Monetary Fund and a seat on Rabobank's board. Most of its gold is stored for it rather than managed: 32 per cent at the Bank of England, 18.5 per cent at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and 18.5 per cent at the Royal Canadian Mint in Ottawa. p:NOR:
NORGES BANK
Norway
Norges Bank issues the Norwegian krone and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, whose capital has been held by central banks alone since private shares were bought back in 2001. Both recorded cases come out of one hiring. On 24 March 2020 the Executive Board appointed Nicolai Tangen, who had started the hedge fund AKO Capital in 2005, to run Norges Bank Investment Management, which manages the country's oil fund. The bank's Supervisory Council warned that the hire risked breaking laws, rules and guidelines, saying Tangen still appeared to be AKO Capital's main owner with voting control, although the bank said he had cut those ties. After the Storting's finance committee raised the same concern, the Executive Board revised his terms in August 2020: he would give up his holding in AKO Capital LLP and hand it and its dividend rights to the charitable AKO Foundation, and hold his personal fund assets as bank deposits. Supervisory Board chair Julie Brodtkorb said guidelines, regulations and laws had been breached; Executive Board chair Oystein Olsen said the board had thought the existing contract was enough but accepted that the Storting took a different view. Tangen could take office on 1 September. Ernst & Young audits the bank from the 2022 financial year for six years, and at the end of 2025 103 organisations ran outside mandates worth 1,062 billion kroner. Notes were printed by Oberthur Fiduciaire in France from 2016 to 2019 and, from 2020, by Crane NXT in Malta. A commission appointed by the Ministry of Finance and chaired by Svein Gjedrem, a former governor of the bank, proposed in late June 2017 that the oil fund be managed by a separate statutory entity outside Norges Bank, which would have taken away the largest thing the bank does. Its reasoning was that central banking and investment management differ in nature, that both had grown and now placed greater demands on the board, senior management and the organisation, and that separate bodies could tailor their skills to each task. The bank's own leadership and the fund's split in public: governor Oystein Olsen wanted the fund kept inside Norges Bank, while the fund's chief executive Yngve Slyngstad was reported as believing it should be taken out. The Ministry of Finance rejected the proposal and decided the management should stay in the central bank, on the reasoning that Norges Bank enjoyed a high level of trust in Norway and internationally and that its performance in both roles had been good over time; the Central Bank Act the Storting passed on 28 May 2019, in force from 1 January 2020, left the bank both responsibilities. Government pressure reported in 0 of 37 quarters, 2010–2018.

2017-06-30 · attempted law change. In late June 2017 the Central Bank Law Commission, appointed by the Ministry of Finance and chaired by Svein Gjedrem, a former governor of Norges Bank and former secretary general of the ministry, proposed in its report NOU 2017:13 that responsibility for managing the Government Pension Fund Global - the oil fund, then about 8.1 trillion kroner and Europe's largest sovereign wealth fund - be transferred out of Norges Bank to a separate statutory entity. The fund is managed inside the bank by Norges Bank Investment Management, and removing it would have taken away the largest thing the bank does. Gjedrem's reasoning was that central banking and investment management differ in nature, that both had grown and now placed greater demands on the board, senior management and the organisation, and that separate bodies could tailor their skills to each task; he said the separation would have to be carried out soundly and must not otherwise affect the framework for the fund. The bank's own leadership was split in public from the fund's: governor Oystein Olsen wanted the fund kept inside Norges Bank, while the fund's chief executive Yngve Slyngstad was reported as believing it should be taken out. Norges Bank itself later described the separation proposal as the one that had drawn the most public attention of anything in the Commission's work. The Ministry of Finance rejected it, deciding the management should stay within the central bank, on the reasoning that Norges Bank enjoyed a high level of trust in Norway and internationally and that its performance in both roles had been good over time. The Storting passed the new Central Bank Act on 28 May 2019 and it entered into force on 1 January 2020, leaving the bank both core responsibilities and creating a separate monetary policy and financial stability committee. The question was raised again in the mandate of a later committee and the government withdrew it, saying the placement of the fund had recently been examined thoroughly, that there had been broad consensus in the Storting in 2018 and 2019 that management should remain within Norges Bank, and that stability in the management of the fund mattered. Norway rejects idea of hiving off SWF management (IPE)

NEPAL RASTRA BANK
Nepal
Nepal Rastra Bank issues Nepal's rupee and holds it at a fixed rate against India's rupee, and scores 31 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In 2007 the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority charged sitting governor Bhattarai and executive director Pradhan with embezzlement over the hiring of American consultants; Bhattarai was suspended, and the Supreme Court later cleared both. In October 2011 Note Printing Australia, owned by the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to provide benefits to foreign public officials to obtain banknote business with Nepal's note-issuing authority between February 2000 and May 2002, and paid 1,856,710 Australian dollars. On 8 April 2022 the government suspended governor Adhikari over charges, still unproven, of leaking sensitive government decisions; the Supreme Court stayed the suspension on 19 April and he returned to work. Adhikari retired as the bank's deputy governor in December 2015 after three decades there, then became chief executive officer of the Nepal Investment Board, and was appointed the bank's 17th governor on 6 April 2020 for five years.

2022-04-08 · suspension. On 8 April 2022 the government of Nepal suspended the governor of the Nepal Rastra Bank, Maha Prasad Adhikari, and formed a three-member committee headed by a former Supreme Court judge to investigate him, on charges of leaking sensitive information about government decisions and of not fulfilling his responsibilities. This record is the executive's suspension of a sitting governor and the inquiry it set up; the allegations against him are recorded separately as a corruption case. Nepal's governors have been suspended before: a sitting governor was suspended in 2007 after the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority charged him over the hiring of consultants, and the Supreme Court later cleared him and allowed his reinstatement. p:NZL:
RESERVE BANK OF NEW ZEALAND
New Zealand
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand issues the New Zealand dollar. It scores 24 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, less exposed than 84% of the 194 places scored, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. On 10 March 2016 the decision on the Official Cash Rate, the interest rate the bank sets, leaked from its media lock-up before release. Deloitte, engaged on 11 March 2016 and reporting on 12 April 2016, traced it to a Mediaworks employee: one journalist emailed a draft story out of the lock-up, and another emailed the economics blogger Michael Reddell at 8.04am, before the 9am announcement. Mediaworks reported itself on 5 April 2016, and the bank ended embargoed lock-ups. Adrian Orr, governor from 27 March 2018, was chief economist at the bank Westpac in New Zealand from 2000 to 2003, joined the Reserve Bank as deputy governor in 2003, and ran the New Zealand Superannuation Fund from 2007 until his appointment. It part-owns the Bank for International Settlements, and Note Printing Australia prints its banknotes. Orr resigned on 5 March 2025 with three years of his second term left, which the board chair put down to a personal decision. Documents released that June under the Official Information Act showed the cause was a deadlock over the bank's next five-year funding agreement: Orr argued that what the finance minister and the Treasury proposed was well below what the bank needed, and the board was willing to settle for less than he was. He had sought $1.031 billion and the settled package was close to $776 million. In August the Ombudsman forced the bank to disclose that Orr had stepped down temporarily on 27 February and agreed to resign on the basis that a letter of concerns from the board was withdrawn. The board chair resigned at the end of that month.

2025-03-05 · resignation under pressure. Adrian Orr resigned as governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand on 5 March 2025, with three years left to run of his second five-year term. Board chair Neil Quigley said at the time that it was a personal decision and would not elaborate. Documents released in June 2025 under the Official Information Act showed the cause was an impasse over the bank's next five-year funding agreement: Orr argued that what Finance Minister Nicola Willis and the Treasury proposed was considerably below what the bank needed, and the board was willing to accept less than he was. The bank said the disagreement was distressing to Orr and risked damaging the working relationship. Orr had sought $1.031 billion; in mid-April Willis confirmed a package of nearly $776 million, about 8 percent more than the previous five years. In August 2025 the Ombudsman compelled the bank to disclose that Orr had temporarily stepped down on 27 February, as tensions with the board, the Treasury and the minister came to a head, and that he agreed to resign on the basis that a letter of concerns from the board was withdrawn. CENTRAL RESERVE BANK OF PERU
Peru
The Central Reserve Bank of Peru issues the sol, managed within a band of about 5 per cent against the US dollar, and Peru scores 28 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Congress passed law 31143 against usury by insistence on 11 March 2021, overriding the executive's objection. It requires the bank to set maximum and minimum interest rates every six months for consumer loans up to two tax units, about 8,800 soles, and for loans to small and micro enterprises. The bank had opposed rate ceilings in public and said so again in the announcement setting the first ceiling at 83.4 percent a year: ceilings are not the most appropriate mechanism, because they ration credit away from borrowers whose credit risk sits above the cap. Its own study of the period from May 2021 to March 2024 estimated more than 542,000 people affected, 40 percent of them borrowers who left the financial system. In November 2021 the justice minister, Anibal Torres, criticised Governor Julio Velarde for having come out against the law. Congress reached into the design of the money as well. Law 32251, published on 19 January 2025 and following a Constitutional Court ruling, requires the bank's coins and banknotes to carry the full national coat of arms, the words Republica del Peru and the motto Firme y feliz por la union. A bank official, Abraham de la Melena, said the bank was not consulted in drafting the law or in approving it, and the bank set out what the change costs in practical terms: the full coat of arms shrinks the central part of a coin's obverse, which makes it harder to strike and makes the coin's security features harder for the public to recognise; fitting the motto in means cutting the bank's own name from the design; and on banknotes the coat of arms cannot go on the front without disturbing the security elements, watermarks and fluorescent zones among them. On the Ministry of Defence's draft regulation of July 2025 the bank added that coin-handling machines nationwide would need recalibrating, that two versions of one denomination in circulation would confuse users and open a door to counterfeiters, and that redesigning, tendering, printing and distributing new notes would take 14 to 15 months at high cost. Velarde said the bank would comply but that the change introduces costs, and that the arms the bank uses predate the bank's own 102 years. Congress then moved to undo it: bills 10738 and 10769 cleared the constitution committee, and in March 2026 Congress approved an amendment making the use of the coat of arms and the motto conditional on the bank's own board approving it, which the committee framed as preserving the bank's technical and operational autonomy. One matter, from 1986 to 1991, is alleged and unproven. A New York grand-jury indictment of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International in 1991 alleged three million US dollars in bribes in return for depositing part of Peru's 1986-87 reserves in that bank's Panama branch, after the Peruvian board approved moving 100 million dollars and later doubling it. The indictment named no officials of the Peruvian bank; the Christian Science Monitor identified Figueroa and Neyra, and both strenuously denied the charges, Neyra calling the decision purely technical. All Peruvian deposits were withdrawn by the end of 1987, and a Peruvian parliamentary commission also looked into the bank. Separately, Eduardo Torres-Llosa spent 21 years at BBVA in Peru, left in June 2019 as its managing director, sat on the boards of Financiera Confianza and BBVA in Uruguay and chaired the engineering firm Cosapi, and became the central bank's general manager in March 2022; no ethics finding is recorded. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Perum Peruri won the tender to print the 10, 20 and 50 nuevo sol notes, reported as still unsigned in January 2020 and as secured by December 2022, with no value given, and a member firm of PricewaterhouseCoopers audits the accounts.

2025-01-19 · law change. Law 32251, published on 19 January 2025, unified the rules on national symbols and required that the coins and banknotes issued by the Banco Central de Reserva del Peru carry the full national coat of arms, the words Republica del Peru and the national motto Firme y feliz por la union, giving state bodies a year from the regulation's entry into force to bring their own rules into line. It followed a Constitutional Court ruling requiring the bank to use those emblems. A bank official, Abraham de la Melena, said the BCRP was not consulted either in drafting the law or in approving it. The bank set out what it would cost in technical terms: putting the full coat of arms on a coin means shrinking the central part of the obverse, which makes the arms harder to strike and the coin's security features harder for the public to recognise; fitting the motto in means removing the issuing bank's own name from the design or cutting it down; and on banknotes, putting the coat of arms on the front is not feasible without disturbing the security elements, including watermarks and fluorescent zones. When the Ministry of Defence published its draft regulation in July 2025, the bank added that coin-handling machines across the country would have to be recalibrated, that two versions of the same denomination in circulation would confuse users and open a door to counterfeiters, and that redesigning, tendering, printing and distributing new notes would take 14 to 15 months at a high cost. Governor Julio Velarde said in March 2025 that the bank would comply but that the change introduces costs, and that the coat of arms the bank uses predates the bank's own 102 years. Congress then moved to undo it: bills 10738 and 10769 were approved in the constitution committee, and in March 2026 Congress approved an amendment making the use of the national coat of arms and the motto on money conditional on approval by the BCRP's own board, which the committee framed as preserving the bank's technical and operational autonomy. 2021-03-11 · law change. Congress passed law 31143, protecting consumers of financial services from usury, by insistence on 11 March 2021 with 85 votes for, eight against and 12 abstentions, overriding the executive's objection; it was published on 18 March 2021. The law requires the Banco Central de Reserva del Peru to set maximum and minimum interest rates every six months for consumer loans up to two tax units, about 8,800 soles, and for loans to small and micro enterprises - taking a price-setting duty the bank did not want and had opposed in public. Governor Julio Velarde had stated the bank's position against limiting interest rates before the vote. When the bank published the methodology on 29 April 2021, setting the first ceiling at 83.4 percent a year from 10 May, it said in the same announcement that, notwithstanding the law, it considers rate ceilings not to be the most appropriate mechanism for improving credit conditions or deepening financial inclusion, because ceilings ration credit away from borrowers whose credit risk sits above the cap. In November 2021 the justice minister, Anibal Torres, publicly criticised Velarde for having come out against the law. The bank kept saying so with its own measurements: its central manager for economic studies, Adrian Armas, said the ceilings pushed informal and lower-income borrowers out of the formal system and into informal lending, and a bank study of the period from May 2021 to March 2024 estimated more than 542,000 people affected, 40 percent of them borrowers who left the financial system. Velarde later called the law almost useless and said it had fed loan rackets that had moved into criminal territory. The ceiling reached 112.98 percent a year for the period from November 2024. The Constitutional Court upheld the law as constitutional in case 00010-2021-AI; Congress approved repeal in a second vote in March 2025, and in July 2026 the government asked Congress for delegated powers to repeal it, citing the bank's technical opinion. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas issues the Philippine peso, and the Philippines scores 36 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Six cases are recorded. BANK OF PAPUA NEW GUINEA
Papua New Guinea
The Bank of Papua New Guinea issues the kina, whose rate against the US dollar is shifted in small steps rather than left to the market, and the country scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One case is on record. Court documents obtained by the journalism group OCCRP show that the National Fraud and Anti-Corruption Directorate searched the bank's offices in August and September 2023 in a money-laundering investigation into Genia, then acting governor; she won a temporary halt that was later dismissed, she has not been charged, and it remains under investigation and unproven. She had earlier been under fraud-squad investigation over a firearms deal for the bank's security team, and became governor in early 2024. In April 2024 the Prime Minister announced new board members, among them Sir Robin Fleming, former chief executive of the commercial bank Bank South Pacific, and Mark Baker, former country head of the commercial bank Australia and New Zealand Banking. The 2024 annual report names Pictet Asset Management as the weakest of the outside firms running part of the reserves that year, with DWS and BlackRock the strongest. p:POL:
NATIONAL BANK OF POLAND
Poland
Poland's money is the zloty, issued by the National Bank of Poland. Six matters are recorded. In the ArtB cheque-float affair of 1991, those arrested after the company's owners fled included the bank's president, Grzegorz Wojtowicz, who was charged with unintentionally causing bank losses of about 72 billion old zloty; the court acquitted him. In February 2009 the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau detained eight people in a case against the head of a division in the bank's IT and telecommunications department, accused of taking at least 350,000 zloty in bribes to rig tenders between 2001 and 2008; he was charged and nothing is proven. Warsaw's district prosecutors are investigating the disclosure of material classified as secret from the closed part of a Monetary Policy Council meeting on 8 September 2023, and on 12 June 2025 secured documents at the bank's head office after it had twice refused to hand them over. In March 2024 ruling-coalition members of parliament filed a motion to bring the bank's president, Adam Glapinski, before the State Tribunal, the court that hears cases against senior officials, on eight charges, among them bond purchases in 2020 and 2021 said to have indirectly financed the budget deficit by at least 144 billion zloty, and breaching the bank's political neutrality. On 20 August 2024 the Constitutional Tribunal dismissed that attempt, ruling the enabling law unconstitutional; it had earlier held, on 12 January 2024, that a three-fifths majority was needed, where the coalition held 241 of 460 seats against a threshold of 276. A Sejm committee then upheld all eight charges on 9 October 2026, with the full vote still to come in the second half of November 2026; Glapinski and the bank call the accusations groundless, and nothing is proven. Dariusz Filar went from chief economist of Bank Pekao to the Monetary Policy Council, with no ethics finding recorded. Leszek Balcerowicz, governor from 2001 to 2007, is a member of the Group of Thirty, sitting alongside private-sector members including Jane Fraser of Citi, Philipp Hildebrand of BlackRock, Gail Kelly of the UBS Group board, Maria Ramos of Standard Chartered and Guillermo Ortiz of BTG Pactual. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, whose capital is held by central banks alone since private shares were bought back in 2001, and KPMG Audyt Spółka z ograniczoną odpowiedzialnością sp.k. audited its 2025 accounts. The notes are made to the bank's order by Polska Wytwornia Papierow Wartosciowych, and of the 448 tonnes of gold held at the end of December 2024 about three quarters sits abroad, in roughly similar portions in the vaults of the Bank of England and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which store the bars rather than manage the holding. A bank publication says it moved 100 tons of gold in 2019 from the Bank of England to the domestic vaults, finishing in November that year, and that almost 124 tons were left in the Bank of England after the move; the bank's own text names only domestic vaults, while a research report, In Gold We Trust, says they are in Warsaw and Poznan, which is that report's claim and the bank has not confirmed it. It scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

p:PRT:
BANK OF PORTUGAL
Portugal
Portugal uses the euro, so interest rates are set by the European Central Bank for all 21 European Union countries on the currency rather than by the Banco de Portugal, which has its notes printed by Valora S.A., a printer it owns. It scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Governor Carlos Costa says prime minister Antonio Costa telephoned him on 12 April 2016, while the bank was stripping Isabel dos Santos of her fitness to sit on the board of EuroBic, and said the daughter of the president of a country friendly to Portugal could not be treated badly. The two sides agree the call happened and disagree what it was: Observador reported a written message in which the prime minister confirmed the call and said he had considered the removal inopportune, while the prime minister told parliament he had never made any approach in her favour, called the account false and filed a civil action, which the former governor answered with one of his own; both were dropped by agreement in May 2025. The bank did not change the decision and Isabel dos Santos was removed from the board. A 600-page report by a committee the bank itself appointed, with technical support from Boston Consulting Group, pointed to failures in its supervision of Banco Espirito Santo going back to the start of the previous decade, and said information on the Espirito Santo group and on the bank's operations in Angola was reportedly not used; the Banco de Portugal twice refused parliament's request for the report. On 20 July 2021 Fernando Anastacio, rapporteur of parliament's inquiry into losses at Novo Banco, presented a draft report saying supervision had failed across the board, which remained a draft that the PSD said its deputies would vote against. The committee approved its final report on 27 July 2021, concluding that the rescue of Banco Espirito Santo and the first capitalisation of Novo Banco, of 4,900 million euros, were a political fraud, with criticism of the Banco de Portugal and the European Commission and no officials named. In April 2019, after an EY audit of the management of Caixa Geral de Depositos, the bank's ethics committee examined governor Carlos Costa's request to be excused from matters concerning that bank, where he had been a board member from 2004 to 2006; no conclusion was published. Two findings concern the European Central Bank itself: the European Ombudsman found maladministration over President Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum that includes private financiers, and recommended in January 2018 that he suspend it, which the bank declined; and a speech by Coeure to a private London event on 18 May 2015, saying asset purchases would be front-loaded, was published only the next morning, which the ECB put down to an internal procedure error. Vitor Constancio was governor from 1985 to 1986, an executive director of Banco Portugues de Investimento from 1995 to 2000, governor again until May 2010 and then ECB Vice-President, with no ethics finding recorded. PricewaterhouseCoopers & Associados audits the accounts for 2022 to 2026. Of 382.7 tonnes of gold, about 45 per cent was kept in the bank's own vaults in 2023, 49 per cent at the Bank of England, 5 per cent at the Bank for International Settlements and 1 per cent at the Banque de France; those institutions store the metal, they do not manage it.

Costa had been a CGD board member from 2004 to 2006 and may have sat on extended credit council meetings that approved operations which caused losses, while now heading the supervisor assessing former CGD directors. Vice-governor Elisa Ferreira did not recuse herself but told the committee of a possible conflict of interest relating to her husband's past role at La Seda. The committee's conclusions were not made public. No conclusion was published. Comissao de etica do Banco de Portugal analisou escusa do governador na Caixa (Observador)

2016-04-12 · pressure. In April 2016 the Banco de Portugal was withdrawing the fitness-and-propriety approval of Isabel dos Santos, daughter of the then president of Angola, as a director of the bank EuroBic. Governor Carlos Costa says the prime minister, Antonio Costa, telephoned him on the afternoon of 12 April 2016, after a meeting the governor had held with Isabel dos Santos, her business partner Fernando Telles and the bank's head of supervision Carlos Albuquerque, and told him that "the daughter of the president of a country friendly to Portugal" could not be treated badly. The governor published the account in the book "O Governador", a set of interviews with the journalist Luis Rosa, in November 2022, and called it an attempt at political interference with the banking supervisor. The two sides agree the call happened and disagree about what it was: Observador reported that about ninety minutes after a chapter of the book was published the prime minister sent Carlos Costa a written message confirming the call and saying that in 2016 he had considered the removal of Isabel dos Santos inopportune. Antonio Costa said in parliament he had never made any approach to the governor or anyone else in her favour, called the governor's statements false, and filed a civil defamation action in the Lisbon civil court in April 2023 asking for a public retraction rather than damages; Carlos Costa answered in May 2023 with an action of his own. President Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa publicly defended the prime minister. The Banco de Portugal did not change its decision and Isabel dos Santos was removed from the board. Both lawsuits were dropped by agreement in May 2025. Antonio Costa e Carlos Costa desistem de processo sobre Isabel dos Santos no BIC (Publico)

CENTRAL BANK OF PARAGUAY
Paraguay
The Central Bank of Paraguay issues the country's money, the guaraní, and scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Impeachment proceedings opened in January 2003 against President Luis González Macchi over an alleged 26 million US dollar embezzlement from the bank, and the Senate vote fell short that February. On 6 June 2006 a court in Asunción sentenced him to six years for breach of trust over 16 million US dollars diverted from Unión and Orienta, two private banks the central bank had taken over, and former banking superintendent José Pecci to eight years; an appeals court later cleared González Macchi for insufficient evidence. In February 2007 President Nicanor Duarte Frutos dismissed bank president Mónica Pérez over her disagreements with the economic team. Police searched the bank on 13 July 2021 over embezzlement and money laundering, an open investigation. On 3 November 2026 governor Carlos Carvallo resigned at President Santiago Peña's request, after a prosecutor sought an investigation around ueno, a digital lender Carvallo had headed until August 2023. An earlier head of the bank went the other way: Carlos Fernandez Valdovinos led it for five years, from 2013 to 2018, after being appointed by Horacio Manuel Cartes, and in October 2018 he joined the board of directors of the commercial bank Banco Basa.

NATIONAL BANK OF ROMANIA
Romania
The National Bank of Romania issues the Romanian leu, which in practice tracks the euro. It scores 23 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. On 28 December 2018 the government imposed a tax of 0.3 percent on banks' financial assets and set the rate of that tax by reference to ROBOR, the interbank money market rate, so the tax rose as the bank raised rates. Appearing with the whole board before Senate committees in February 2019, Governor Mugur Isarescu called it a tax on monetary policy that ties the central bank's hands and said that linking the asset tax to ROBOR is an attack on the independence of the National Bank. The European Central Bank wrote to the finance minister on 5 February 2019 saying it had not been consulted, contrary to its obligation under EU rules, and that the measure came with no impact assessment. The government published amendments removing the link to ROBOR on 26 March 2019. One case is recorded. In 2014 the High Court of Cassation and Justice placed the sitting deputy governor, Olteanu, under 30-day house arrest in a National Anticorruption Directorate case alleging that in 2008, while parliament speaker, he asked for and received a 1 million euro bribe from the businessman Sorin Ovidiu Vantu. He was convicted of influence peddling and given a final five-year sentence in October 2020, but on 31 March 2023 the Bucharest Court of Appeal confirmed the case closed as time-barred and annulled the conviction, while ordering the money confiscated. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Nicolae Danila ran Banca Comerciala Romana from 1999 to 2008, then sat on the bank's board until September 2014 and later chaired First Bank SA; no ethics finding is recorded. The bank said on 10 September 2024 that it is the holder of an account at the Bank of England where about 60 of its 103.6 tonnes of gold sit, that the custodian cannot use that gold in any form, and that transactions happen only on the bank's instruction; 42.4 tonnes are held in Romania. That account comes from a newspaper quoting the statement rather than from a document on the bank's own site.

2019-02-12 · law change. The Romanian government adopted emergency ordinance 114/2018 on 28 December 2018, imposing a 0.3 percent tax on banks' financial assets from 1 January 2019 and setting the rate of that tax by reference to ROBOR, the interbank money market rate. Because ROBOR moves with monetary policy, the tax rose as the National Bank of Romania raised rates. Governor Mugur Isarescu, appearing with the whole BNR board before Senate committees in February 2019, called it a tax on monetary policy that ties the central bank's hands and said that linking the asset tax to ROBOR is an attack on the independence of the National Bank. He had declined two earlier invitations from the committees; the MP who pressed for the hearings, Daniel Zamfir, had accused the bank of manipulating ROBOR, which Isarescu rejected, telling the committees that lower interest rates required low inflation and low budget and external deficits. Separately, a government adviser close to the ruling party leader, Darius Valcov, told Bloomberg that the central bank could cancel the tax by changing how ROBOR is calculated or scrapping the rate altogether, and that a decision would be taken with the central bank, which could change its internal market rules without parliamentary approval; the BNR's spokesman called the statement extremely confusing and said he did not know whom Valcov was speaking for. The European Central Bank wrote to the finance minister on 5 February 2019 saying it had not been consulted on the ordinance or on an earlier draft, contrary to its obligation under EU rules, and that the measure came with no impact assessment. On 26 March 2019 the government published amendments that removed the link to ROBOR, and the finance minister said the amendments had the BNR's approval. BANK OF RUSSIA
Russia
The Bank of Russia issues the ruble, and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the central banks' own bank. It scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it. Government pressure was reported in 5 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, every time to cut rates or loosen policy. In October 1994 President Boris Yeltsin fired chairman Viktor Gerashchenko over his part in the Black Tuesday ruble crash and named Tatyana Paramonova in his place; the State Duma rejected her by secret ballot, 107 to 127, opponents saying the constitution barred hiring or firing the bank's chief without the Duma's approval. On 19 October 2005 the Moscow prosecutor's office indicted Alexei Mishin, chief legal expert at the bank's Moscow directorate, and a deputy department head of the tax service, for taking a bribe of 1 million US dollars; at the Moscow City Court on 17 April 2007 prosecutors asked for 15 years for Mishin and 12 years for the tax official Oleg Alekseev, but the verdict is not known, so nothing is proven. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Western countries immobilised the bank's assets held in their jurisdictions, put at around 300 billion euros worldwide, and on 12 December 2025 the European Union agreed to freeze 210 billion euros of them indefinitely, replacing six-monthly renewals that Hungary or Slovakia could veto. It holds 2,283 tonnes of gold and has swap lines, standing arrangements to lend each other currency, with China and with Kazakhstan, the latter signed on 28 May 2026 for up to three years. Oleg Vyugin, a First Deputy Chairman of the bank, also held private finance posts at Troika Dialog, Morgan Stanley Bank, MDM Bank, Binbank and Safmar Financial Investments; the CV listing them gives no dates, so the order of the moves is not established, and no ethics finding is recorded. Its accounts are audited by B1 - Audit LLC and by the Accounts Chamber of the Russian Federation. Goznak, owned entirely by the federal government under the Ministry of Finance, prints Russian money, though the page describing it does not name the bank as its customer.

p:RWA:
NATIONAL BANK OF RWANDA
Rwanda
The National Bank of Rwanda issues the Rwandan franc, which in practice follows a crawling peg against the US dollar, meaning the rate is allowed to drift slowly in a managed way. It scores 27 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded: the bank lost 63 million Rwandan francs from deposit accounts in early 2014 in a fraud reported to involve its own staff. Its director for information technology said the suspects had manipulated the bank's internal security system before taking the cash. One person was arrested and the file went to the Prosecutor General, while police said the main suspect was believed to have fled to Uganda; the matter is under investigation, so nothing in it is proven. De La Rue printed the 2,000-franc note introduced on 3 September 2024. John Rwangombwa was Governor from 2013 until February 2025, and came to the post from the government: he was Minister of Finance and Economic Planning from 2009, and earlier in the same ministry he directed the National Treasury Department, set up the Accountant General's Office in 2005 and became Rwanda's first Accountant General, then Permanent Secretary and Secretary to the Treasury; he had joined the Rwanda Revenue Authority in 1998 and was Deputy Commissioner of Customs for Operations by 2002.

SAUDI CENTRAL BANK
Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia's money is the riyal, issued by the Saudi Central Bank and held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. It scores 28 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. The independence the law gives it is thinner: 0.501 of 1 on an index of 42 rules, rank 138 of 155, where 1 would mean the bank rather than the government holds the power, and 0 on the part covering control of its own money and budget. It tells the public little, 5.5 of 15 on a transparency measure, and no case at the bank is documented, which is not proof that none happened. The bank part-owns the Bank for International Settlements, the bank for central banks in Basel; its officials also sit on the Financial Stability Board, and it holds 323.1 tonnes of gold. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, signed with China on 20 November 2023 for three years and worth 50 billion yuan or 26 billion riyals. Governor Fahad Al-Mubarak came from private finance: general manager of Rana Investment Company from 1992 to 1999, then chairman and managing director of Morgan Stanley Saudi Arabia. He was governor from 2011 to 2016, and King Salman named him governor again by royal decree on 24 January 2021; no ethics finding is recorded against him. Banknotes are reported to be printed at home by the Saudi Central Bank Printing Works. CENTRAL BANK OF WEST AFRICAN STATES (BCEAO)
Senegal
Senegal uses the West African CFA franc, issued for eight countries by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which is based in Senegal. The franc is fixed at 655.957 to the euro, and the French Treasury promises to advance euros if the bank's reserves run out; an agreement signed on 21 December 2019 ended the rule that at least half those reserves sit at the Treasury. One case is recorded. In January 2011 a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution; the report says the BCEAO paid out 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime afterwards. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo; that is unproven, and no audit result is given. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of its reserves sits in two funds run by other institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it bought units in a fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and grouped with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The same accounts say the bank joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program, managed by the World Bank, whose units were worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025.
