2011-01-22 · forced resignation. The Central Bank of West African States is the central bank of eight countries, and in January 2011 its own member heads of state removed its governor. After the disputed Ivorian presidential election of November 2010, the bank recognised Alassane Ouattara as head of state and revoked Laurent Gbagbo's access to Ivorian state accounts in December, and the union's finance ministers decided on 23 December that only representatives of Ouattara's government would have signing authority. The Ouattara camp complained in mid-January that the bank was still channelling cash to Gbagbo, and the governor, Philippe-Henry Dacoury-Tabley, an Ivorian and a close confidant of Gbagbo, was accused of not cooperating. At an emergency summit of the heads of state of the West African Economic and Monetary Union in Bamako on 22 January 2011 he handed in his resignation. The bank's own statement, issued in Dakar that evening, said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders. He told reporters afterwards: "I agreed to hand in my resignation as that is what was asked of me", and defended his conduct by pointing to practical and technical reasons for not transferring control of the accounts. The union accepted the resignation and called on Ouattara to propose a successor; a deputy governor, Jean-Baptiste Compaore, took over in the interim. Gbagbo's administration, on state television it still controlled, rejected what it called the forced resignation of the governor and rejected the leaders' decision to let Ouattara name a replacement. The European Union listed Dacoury-Tabley, giving as its ground that as governor of the BCEAO he refused to recognise the authority of the democratically elected President and was helping to fund the illegitimate administration of Mr Laurent Gbagbo. This record is the removal of the governor by the member states; what he is alleged to have done with the bank's money is recorded separately as a corruption case. Keyed to the union, so it counts for all eight member countries. Pro-Gbagbo bank head quits (Al Jazeera)
OWNERSHIP AND OUTSIDE CONTROL

West African CFA franc (WAEMU/UMOA) – France cooperation (external guarantee)

The currency (XOF) is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs.
France gives an unconditional and unlimited convertibility guarantee through advances to the central bank if its foreign exchange reserves run out.
A new cooperation agreement was signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019, replacing the 1973 agreement; France stated the reform would enter into force in 2020.
The 2019 agreement ended the centralisation of BCEAO reserves at the French Treasury, ending the requirement that the BCEAO hold at least 50% of its reserves there.
The BCEAO's operations account at the French Treasury was closed in April 2021 (French Senate report); the Treasury page states it has had no operations account since January 2020.
France approved the agreement by Law no. 2021-108 of 3 February 2021.
France withdrew its representatives from the BCEAO board, the Monetary Policy Committee and the UMOA Banking Commission; one independent member of the Monetary Policy Committee is appointed in consultation with the French government.
The agreement provides that the currency will be renamed 'ECO'; the Banque de France page says the name 'is set to change' at member states' will, i.e. the CFA franc name remains in use.
ECOWAS Convergence Council (7 September 2026) kept 2027 as the target launch year for an ECOWAS single currency named the ECO.

CENTRAL BANK OF SOLOMON ISLANDS
Solomon Islands
The Solomon Islands dollar is issued by the Central Bank of Solomon Islands, created in 1976 and holding the currency at a crawling peg to the US dollar as of December 2025, meaning the rate is moved in small steps announced in advance. The country scores 31 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and the weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank. The bank is near the bottom of 112 places for what it tells the public, at 3 of 15. One case is recorded: a former employee, Bobongi, was convicted on 39 counts of money laundering and two counts of larceny and embezzlement for stealing more than 1.7 million dollars in old banknotes in 2007 to 2009, while the bank was destroying them, and was sentenced to nine years. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, with no date or value given. Crown Agents Investment Management manages about 95 percent of the bank's allocation of special drawing rights, a reserve asset issued by the International Monetary Fund, and the Auditor General's Office audits the accounts.

p:SLE:
BANK OF SIERRA LEONE
Sierra Leone
The Bank of Sierra Leone issues the leone and scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption and secrecy, at 66. Under the 2019 Bank of Sierra Leone Act, sacking the governor needs a two-thirds majority in parliament. In August 2018 the recently elected president dismissed the governor, and Kelfala Kallon was appointed on 15 August as the bank's third governor in 17 months; neither the dismissed governor nor either side's reason is named. On 22 November 2021 Kallon told parliament that he had bribed people hoarding the leone to bring it back into the banking system. The Anti-Corruption Commission investigated and said in May 2022 that he had meant cash swap operations in which the bank sold about 68.6 million United States dollars of foreign currency in 2021, that the word was used in error, and that it had closed the investigation after advising him to choose his words more carefully. On 13 March 2023 President Julius Maada Bio sent Kallon on indefinite leave and named his deputy, Ibrahim Stevens, interim head; no official reason was given, Kallon did not respond, and the president was reported to be bypassing the 2019 Act. De La Rue printed the 10-leone note of the redenominated series introduced on 1 July 2022, and the West African Monetary Institute manages the Stabilization and Cooperation Fund, in which the bank holds 63.59 million new leone.

p:SMR:
CENTRAL BANK OF THE REPUBLIC OF SAN MARINO
San Marino
San Marino uses the euro, and its central bank is the Central Bank of the Republic of San Marino. It scores 45 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, mainly because its money is issued or backed from abroad. The bank is owned mostly by the state: the Eccellentissima Camera della Repubblica di San Marino holds 72%, four banks hold the rest: Cassa di Risparmio della Repubblica di San Marino 16%, Banca di San Marino 6%, Banca Agricola Commerciale Istituto Bancario Sammarinese 5% and Banca Sammarinese di Investimento 1%, as of 31 December 2025. One case is recorded, from 2019 to 2020, over a 220,000 euro payment from the bank to Sandro Gozi for a consultancy that investigators suspected was fictitious. The case, against Gozi and bank president Catia Tomasetti, became public in April 2019. The Tribunal of San Marino dismissed it in 2020, finding no relevant conduct by either suspect; the article reports the consultancy was real. The bank's accounts are audited by Solution S.r.l. of Borgo Maggiore, a San Marino firm belonging to no international network, which signed its report on the 2025 accounts on 5 May 2026 and reports to the shareholders rather than to the board.

p:SOM:
CENTRAL BANK OF SOMALIA
Somalia
Somalia's money is the Somali shilling, and the Central Bank of Somalia issues it, though the notes are printed abroad: the circulating 2,000-shilling note comes from Sudan's state currency printing works. Two cases are recorded. In 2013 governor Abrar resigned after seven weeks, writing to the president that from her appointment she had continuously been asked to sanction deals and violate her fiduciary responsibility; she had refused to sanction a contract over frozen government assets with the United States law firm Shulman Rogers, which denied wrongdoing. A July 2013 report by the United Nations Monitoring Group for Somalia and Eritrea, an official finding, said 80 per cent of withdrawals from the bank were made for private purposes, that the governor was key to the irregularities, and that 12 million of 16.9 million US dollars transferred by the accounting firm PricewaterhouseCoopers could not be traced; the bank rejected the allegations. The bank later joined the World Bank's Reserves Advisory and Management Program, described in its own newsletter as technical support and advice rather than management of its assets. Somalia scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

p:SRB:
NATIONAL BANK OF SERBIA
Serbia
The National Bank of Serbia issues the Serbian dinar, and makes its own notes and coins at its Institute for Manufacturing Banknotes and Coins at Topčider, which has been operating since December 1929 and also produces for foreign countries. A bill, expected to pass on 15 July, would have placed the bank under government control and allowed the dismissal of governor Mladjan Dinkic: Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic wanted a devaluation Dinkic resisted, and members of the DOS coalition said a party official cannot be governor. Dinkic said the law would make the bank dependent on government and parliament; the authorities said his claims had no foundation. On 18 July 2003 he resigned, with two of the bank's three deputy governors, after parliament passed a law letting members of parliament nominate and appoint the bank's top officials; Energy Minister Kori Udovicki was nominated to succeed him. On 11 January 2006 police arrested vice-governor Dejan Simić, along with Vladimir Zagrađanin, on suspicion of taking bribes; an investigation was ordered and the bank's Council removed him on 16 January 2006, but no indictment, verdict or acquittal followed, so the suspicion is unproven. On 10 May 2011 Erste Bank Hungary named a former governor, Radovan Jelašić, its chairman and chief executive, to start that June. Serbia holds 54.6 tonnes of gold, is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

p:SSD:
BANK OF SOUTH SUDAN
South Sudan
South Sudan's money is the South Sudanese pound, issued by the Bank of South Sudan, and its notes are printed by De La Rue, which won a contract for 2.8 billion banknotes in 2011. The country scores 39 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, almost all of it from corruption in the country. A United Nations Human Rights Council commission report said De La Rue transferred about 1.4 million US dollars between 2016 and September 2017 into an Equity Bank account in Nairobi held by a consultant to the bank, against a banknote contract worth about 144 million dollars, and noted suspected corruption. That report stands as an official finding, but the United Kingdom's Serious Fraud Office, which opened its own investigation in July 2019, closed it in June 2020, saying the case did not meet the test for prosecution. On 9 June 2025 President Salva Kiir Mayardit removed Johnny Ohisa Domian as governor by decree, with no reason given; the first deputy governor, Addis Ababa Othow, replaced him. In February and March 2026 security forces detained former governor Manguak, placed under house arrest, with former finance ministers and other officials, and the information minister said a committee was investigating financial malpractices; no charges had been announced as of March 2026, so nothing is proven, and Manguak denies the allegations. The Auditor General audits the accounts.

CENTRAL BANK OF SURINAME
Suriname
The Central Bank of Suriname issues the Suriname dollar, which it lets move within a managed range against the US dollar. It scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side, at 63, is corruption and secrecy around it. Two cases ended in convictions. On 31 January 2022 a court convicted former governor van Trikt of breaking the Anti-Corruption Act and of forgery, embezzlement, money laundering and taking part in a criminal enterprise, in a matter involving more than 800,000 US dollars taken at the bank's expense, and sentenced him to eight years in prison and a 500,000 Suriname dollar fine; the bank's legal director and others were convicted too, and on appeal in January 2026 his sentence was cut to six years. On 17 December 2021 a court sentenced Hoefdraad, who was not present, to 12 years and a fine of the same size for conspiring to defraud the bank while he was finance minister; on appeal on 19 January 2026 the court imposed 10 years for breaking the anti-corruption law and for embezzlement, and dropped the criminal-organisation count. Hoefdraad, who left Suriname in 2020, calls the case a political show trial. One career move is documented, and it is his: Gillmore Hoefdraad began working for the International Monetary Fund in Washington DC in 1999, with no job title given, was Governor of the Central Bank of Suriname from 2010 to 2015, and then served as Suriname's Minister of Finance from 2015 to 2020 under President Desi Bouterse. The government also took money out of the bank. In February 2020 it admitted taking 197 million US dollars from the central bank for imports, debt payments and other purposes it did not specify. The money came from term deposits and from the foreign currency cash reserves that commercial banks held at the bank, and was reportedly used without their permission or knowledge; the commercial banks had been told in 2019 to deposit half the foreign currency they held for customers there. On 3 February 2020 the Surinamese Bankers' Association said the bank had misled them for months with incorrect and incomplete information about the state of that reserve, and named the then governor as mainly responsible for the disappearance of more than 100 million dollars out of a 426 million dollar reserve. Opposition parties demanded that President Desi Bouterse explain himself in Parliament and said the government should resign if he could not, accusing it of using the money to service foreign debts; the Vice President said the government had made agreements with the commercial banks about the use of their cash reserves and that the bank had not kept its end. Van Trikt was removed in January 2020 and resigned on 4 February. On 22 March 2020 the government passed a law temporarily blocking foreign exchange transactions as the currency fell. The bank holds 1.2 tonnes of gold and has three agreements with China to exchange currencies, signed on 18 March 2015, in 2017 and on 11 February 2019, though whether any of them is still in force is not known; one source records drawings of 988,182,600 renminbi in 2020. BDO Assurance NV audited its 2020 accounts, and notes have been printed by Giesecke+Devrient, an expansion of the initials the source gives rather than its own wording.

2020-02 · reserves taken. In February 2020 the government of Suriname admitted that it had taken 197 million US dollars from the Central Bank of Suriname for imports, debt payments and other purposes it did not specify. The money came from term deposits and from the foreign currency cash reserves that commercial banks held at the central bank, and was reportedly used without their permission or knowledge. The commercial banks had been instructed in 2019 to deposit half the foreign currency they held for their customers at the central bank. The Surinamese Bankers' Association said publicly on 3 February 2020 that the central bank had misled them for months with incorrect and incomplete information about the state of the foreign currency cash reserve, and named the then governor as mainly responsible for the disappearance of more than 100 million dollars out of a 426 million dollar reserve. Opposition parties demanded that President Desi Bouterse appear in Parliament to explain why the bank had misled the commercial banks and how depositors would get their savings back, and said the government should resign if he could not; they accused the government of using the money to service foreign debts. The Vice President said the government had made certain agreements with the commercial banks about the use of their cash reserves and that the central bank had not kept its end of the deal. The governor, Robert van Trikt, was removed in January 2020 and resigned on 4 February; he was later arrested, and his prosecution and conviction are recorded separately as a corruption case. On 22 March 2020 the government passed a law temporarily blocking foreign exchange transactions as the Surinamese dollar fell. 2020 Investment Climate Statement: Suriname (US Department of State)

NATIONAL BANK OF SLOVAKIA
Slovakia
Slovakia uses the euro, so the National Bank of Slovakia does not set interest rates; the European Central Bank does that for the 21 euro countries. The Slovak bank is also one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, whose capital is held by central banks alone. Slovakia's own case ended in a conviction: on 29 May 2025 the Specialised Criminal Court found the sitting governor, Kazimir, guilty of paying a 48,000 euro bribe in 2017 and 2018, while he was finance minister, to the head of the tax office in connection with audits of private companies, and fined him 200,000 euros. He denied wrongdoing and said he would appeal, and the offence predates his central bank post. Two findings concern the European Central Bank. The European Ombudsman found maladministration over president Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and bank executives, and recommended in January 2018 that he suspend it; the ECB declined and he did not. And Coeure's remark to a private London event on 18 May 2015 that the ECB would front-load asset purchases was published only the next morning, which the ECB put down to an internal procedure error. The Slovak bank owns 31.694 tonnes of gold in bars, stored for it by the Bank of England as depositary, which safekeeps rather than manages it. Deloitte Audit s.r.o. audited its accounts and Grant Thornton Audit, s.r.o. is the approved auditor for 2024 to 2027. Governor Jozef Makuch told the bank's Banking Council on 27 November 2018 that he would leave in March 2019, two years before his term ended, so that his successor would be chosen before the 2020 general election rather than by the parliament that followed it; he argued that appointing a governor early would strengthen the bank's independence, and no source reports anyone pressing him to go. He stayed until Kazimir was appointed on 1 June 2019. Slovakia scores 25 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

2018-11-27 · pressure. Governor Jozef Makuch told a meeting of the National Bank of Slovakia's Banking Council on 27 November 2018 that he would leave his post in March 2019, although his term ran to 2021, and would stay until a successor was appointed. His stated reason was the political fight he expected over the succession. He had said in September 2018 that the parliament elected in the 2020 general election might have a problem electing anyone, and that it would be better for the bank to have a governor appointed before that vote, who would not be exposed to that political pressure; appointing one early, he argued, would strengthen the bank's independence, and otherwise the governor election would be held in 2021 in a very hectic environment. Parliament approved finance minister Peter Kazimir as the government's nominee in December 2018 and President Andrej Kiska appointed him on 1 June 2019; Makuch stayed on until then. This is a governor cutting his own term short to move the choice of his successor out of a contested parliament - the pressure is on the appointment, not on a policy decision, and no source reports anyone pressing Makuch to go. BANK OF SLOVENIA
Slovenia
Slovenia uses the euro, so the Bank of Slovenia does not set interest rates itself; the European Central Bank sets them for the 21 countries using the euro. Both are among the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. The main local matter is the 2013 bank bailout, in which a 960 million euro bail-in, meaning losses forced on investors, hit about 100,000 junior bondholders and shareholders. Police have filed a second criminal complaint alleging abuse of office over it, after a 2016 attempt hit a dead end over procedural errors; the specialised prosecutor has asked the court to investigate, so nothing is proven. That inquiry included a search of the bank's premises on 6 July 2016, over which the European Central Bank's President wrote to Slovenia's prosecutor general and to the European Commission about information seized. The police took all communications from the governor's email account, every electronic document in his workspace and on his laptop dated between 2012 and 2014 whatever its content, part of the paper files in his office from those years and documents from the bank's central IT server, and went ahead without involving the European Central Bank after the bank objected. On 17 December 2020 the Court of Justice of the European Union held, in Commission v Slovenia, that the material seized must have included documents forming part of the European Central Bank's archives and that Slovenia had infringed their inviolability; it also held that Slovenia then failed to cooperate, by not letting the bank identify which seized documents related to central bank tasks and by not returning even those the authorities themselves regarded as irrelevant to the investigation. Two findings concern the European Central Bank itself: on 18 May 2015 Benoit Coeure told a private London event it would front-load asset purchases before the speech was published; and in January 2018 the European Ombudsman found maladministration and asked Mario Draghi to suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and financiers, which the bank declined. Six career moves are recorded between that board and private finance, among them Otmar Issing advising Goldman Sachs and Lorenzo Bini Smaghi leaving to chair Societe Generale, with no ethics finding on them. 2016-07-06 · seizure. On 6 July 2016, acting on two orders of the Ljubljana Regional Court dated 30 June and 6 July, Slovenian police searched the premises of Banka Slovenije as part of a criminal investigation into the 2013 rescue of Slovenian banks, in which staff of the central bank including the governor were suspects. They seized all communications sent through the governor's email account, all electronic documents in his workspace and on his laptop dated between 2012 and 2014 regardless of content, part of the paper documents in his office from the same years, and documents held on the bank's central IT server. Banka Slovenije argued at the time that the measures breached the inviolability of the European Central Bank's archives, and the authorities went ahead without involving the ECB. On 17 December 2020 the Grand Chamber of the Court of Justice of the European Union held in Commission v Slovenia (C-316/19) that, given the number of documents seized and the duties a national central bank governor carries out on the ECB's Governing Council, the seized material must have included documents forming part of the ECB's archives, and that Slovenia had infringed their inviolability. The Court further held that Slovenia breached its duty of sincere cooperation by not letting the ECB identify which seized documents related to the tasks of the European System of Central Banks, by not returning them, and by not returning documents the authorities themselves regarded as irrelevant to the investigation - which Slovenia admitted at the hearing. The ECB said the ruling confirmed its original concern. ECJ judgment in Case C-316/19 Commission v Slovenia (AEA-EAL)

SVERIGES RIKSBANK
Sweden
Sveriges Riksbank is Sweden's central bank and issues the krona. It scores 15 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 99 per cent of the 194 places with a figure. The Riksdag adopted a new Sveriges Riksbank Act on 23 November 2022, in force from 1 January 2023. The inquiry that preceded it proposed limits on what the Riksbank may do in monetary policy, which its Executive Board objected to in its consultation response and some of which were dropped from the final Act. What stayed includes a requirement of exceptional grounds before the bank may buy or sell financial instruments other than Swedish government securities for monetary policy purposes, on the reasoning that such trading carries much greater financial risk for the bank and for state finances; limits on its equity and a cap on borrowing for the foreign exchange reserve; and an obligation to ask the Riksdag to restore its equity when that falls below the floor, which it had to do after the bond purchases it made earlier lost money as rates rose. The Riksdag also now approves the specification of the inflation target. The bank's own account is two-sided: it says the Act leaves it a strong and clear mandate and carries the ban on taking instructions over unchanged, while governor Erik Thedeen said after a year of it that the governance is too strong on strengthening the foreign exchange reserve and on buying securities for financial stability purposes. Two linked cases run from 2020 to 2021. On 18 June 2021 the Riksbank said a routine check of staff securities dealings had found a few employees making transactions that did not fit its ethics rules, including share trades close to monetary policy decisions and trades in companies whose corporate bonds it was buying; it called this inappropriate, held talks with those involved and began revising the rules. After media reports that Stefan Ingves and Skingsley had conflicts of interest from shares they held while deciding on corporate bond purchases, the bank's General Council reviewed the matter and on 17 December 2021 concluded the link was too weak to amount to a conflict of interest, finding no shortcoming in their conduct. Ingves was appointed governor in October 2005, having headed a department at the International Monetary Fund since 1999; that move is not an accusation. Its 125.7 tonnes of gold sit partly at the Riksbank and partly abroad, 61.4 tonnes at the Bank of England, 33.2 at the Bank of Canada, 13.2 at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and 2.8 at the Swiss National Bank, which is storage of the gold and not management of its money. Crane AB printed the notes at Tumba until the Riksbank gave notice to end the contract on 19 June 2018 because Crane was moving printing to Malta; De La Rue replaced it under an agreement announced on 19 September 2018.

2022-11-23 · law change. The Riksdag adopted a new Sveriges Riksbank Act (2022:1568) on 23 November 2022, replacing the 1999 Act, and it entered into force on 1 January 2023. The Riksbank Inquiry's proposal that preceded it contained limitations on the monetary policy toolbox that the Riksbank's Executive Board objected to in its consultation response; some of those limitations were dropped from the final Act. What remained includes a requirement of exceptional grounds before the Riksbank may buy or sell financial instruments other than Swedish government securities for monetary policy purposes, on the Government's reasoning that such trading carries much greater financial risk for the Riksbank and for state finances than changing the policy rate or buying government securities. The Act also sets upper and lower limits for the Riksbank's equity, caps borrowing for the foreign exchange reserve, and obliges the Riksbank to ask the Riksdag to restore its equity when reported equity falls below the floor - which it had to do after the bond purchases made before 2022 lost money as rates rose. The Riksdag now approves the specification of the inflation target, and its scrutiny bodies were given more funding. The Riksbank's own account is two-sided and should be read as such: it says the Act gives it a strong and clear mandate, that the ban on taking instructions carries over unchanged, and that in several respects the Act does not change the substance of the monetary policy framework. Governor Erik Thedeen said after a year under it that the governance is too strong on strengthening the foreign exchange reserves and on buying securities for financial stability purposes, and that having to ask for capital injections repeatedly would run against the principle of financial independence. CENTRAL BANK OF ESWATINI
Eswatini
The Central Bank of Eswatini, set up in 1974, issues the country's currency, fixed at par to the South African rand under the Common Monetary Area. One licensing fight runs through two findings. In 2017 the bank's evaluations team recommended rejecting Farmers Bank's application for a commercial banking licence, warning it would tarnish the integrity of the bank's licensing policy, and it was turned down late that year. Governor Majozi Sithole said a royal command required him to attend a meeting about the venture on 14 July 2017, and in May 2018 finance minister Martin Dlamini told the bank that King Mswati III had ordered an investigation into its reluctance to license it. A conditional licence followed in September 2018 after a royal command. The bank revoked it on 5 October 2020 because the source of the seed capital was unexplained; an appeal chaired by commerce minister Manqoba Khumalo ruled in December 2020 that the licence should stand, and the bank reinstated it in January 2021 while objecting to procedural improprieties. A 2022 forensic report by Kroll, commissioned by the bank, said parties outside the bank had likely intervened and instructed it to proceed, and that 89 million rand of seed capital had gone from 2019 into silver bullion the bank could not verify existed. That finance minister had run the bank himself: Martin Dlamini was its Governor from July 1997 to November 2013, having worked there for 30 years in all, and was Minister of Finance from November 2013 to November 2018, which is the one career move documented here and names no commercial employer. In October 2023 the bank moved its portfolio of special drawing rights to Crown Agents Investment Management, which manages it and trains bank staff; Giesecke+Devrient of Germany printed the new 20 lilangeni note. Eswatini scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its written independence is 0.373 of 1 on the Cukierman method, where 1 means the bank holds the power. The bank's accounts are audited by SNG Grant Thornton Chartered Accountants (Eswatini) of Mbabane, which signed its report on the statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 on 26 August 2026.

Common Monetary Area (common monetary area)

The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho; it was replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and by the Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined.
Member currencies have been pegged to the rand at par since their introduction; they are legal tender only in the issuing country.
Lesotho and Namibia must fully back their currency issues with rand assets; Eswatini does not face this requirement.
The rand has not been de jure legal tender in Eswatini since 1986.
South Africa makes compensatory payments representing an imputed return on rand circulating as legal tender in Lesotho and Namibia; Eswatini has received none since 1986.

Seychelles
The Central Bank of Seychelles, set up in 1983, issues the Seychelles rupee and, as of December 2025, holds it within a band of plus or minus 2 percent against the US dollar. It scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, below three-quarters of the places measured; its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 49, from laws that hide who owns money and money-laundering risk in its banks. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. Part of its foreign currency savings is handled by outsiders. The World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership runs a portfolio of its reserves, first funded with 100 million US dollars in 2019 and still held at the end of 2025, and during 2025 it also ran workshops and executive forums and paid for staff qualifications. Crown Agents Investment Management runs a bond portfolio split evenly between US dollars and Chinese renminbi, begun in 2014 with 25.0 million US dollars and topped up by another 25.0 million in April 2022. UBS Asset Management runs a money market fund holding part of the reserves, first funded with 10.0 million US dollars in 2017 and still held at the end of 2025, and has invited bank staff to its annual reserves seminar. A trade report says the bank's new family of banknotes was printed by the British printers De La Rue, giving no contract value, volume or term. BANK OF CENTRAL AFRICAN STATES (BEAC)
Chad
Chad uses the XAF, issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The XAF is pegged, meaning held at a fixed rate, at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees to supply euros if the region cannot pay for imports. On a scale where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Chad scores 47, more exposed than 93% of places with a figure, mainly from corruption in the country and money-laundering risk. One BEAC case is documented: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from its Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008, and on 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs. The bank also lost a governor over money missing in Paris: Philibert Andzembe, a Gabonese national, had been governor since July 2007, and in October 2009 Gabon's president Ali Bongo fired him in response to a scandal in which 28.3 million US dollars went missing from the bank's Paris branch; Gabon held the right to appoint the governor at the time, and Lucas Abaga Nchama took the post in 2010. A leaked US diplomatic cable made public in December 2010 alleged that Gabonese officials working at the bank had taken about 36 million US dollars from the pooled reserves over roughly five years. Part of its reserves is still held in Paris: the French Treasury's own page on how the Franc Zone works says the BEAC must deposit part of its foreign exchange reserves with the French Treasury, in an operations account (compte d'operations) opened in the BEAC's name, and that the required share is at least 50 per cent of the reserves for the CEMAC zone, cut from 65 per cent in 2007. That required share earns interest at the European Central Bank's marginal lending facility rate, 0.25 per cent since 16 March 2016, and anything the BEAC chooses to deposit above the share earns the ECB's minimum rate on main refinancing operations, 0 per cent since 16 March 2016. KPMG Afrique Centrale and Mazars Cameroun audited the accounts jointly for 2018. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The BEAC's own site cannot be read by automated requests, so this does not rest on a BEAC document.

Central African CFA franc (CEMAC/UMAC) – France cooperation (external guarantee)

The currency (XAF) is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs; the euro replaced the French franc as anchor on 1 January 1999 with no change in parity.
France provides an unlimited convertibility guarantee, committing euro funds if the sub-region cannot pay for imports in foreign currency.
The BEAC must deposit at least 50% of its foreign exchange reserves in its operations account at the French Treasury (lowered from 65% in 2007).
Mandatory deposits earn the ECB marginal lending facility rate (stated as 0.25% since 16 March 2016); amounts above earn the ECB main refinancing rate; holdings are protected against euro depreciation against the SDR.
France designates two BEAC administrators and two Monetary Policy Committee members, the same number as each of the six CEMAC states.
A France–CEMAC ministers and governors meeting on 17 March 2026 discussed reserves, public finances and integration; the French Treasury's account records no decision changing the operations account, reserve deposit, French representation or currency name. The next meeting in this format is planned for 2027.
The CFA franc was devalued 50% on 11 January 1994.

p:TGO:
CENTRAL BANK OF WEST AFRICAN STATES (BCEAO)
Togo
Togo uses the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The currency is fixed at one euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees it by lending to the BCEAO if its foreign exchange reserves run out; an agreement signed on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one and ended the rule that at least half those reserves sit at the French Treasury. One case is recorded: a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution, and the article says the BCEAO paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime afterwards. The bank's own statement said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders, and Dacoury-Tabley said afterwards that he agreed to hand it in because that is what was asked of him. Togo scores 42 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Its money is printed in France. The French foreign ministry's own page on the Franc Zone says the African central banks place the orders for notes and coins under a contract with a manufacturer, in this case the Banque de France, and that CFA franc notes and coins have been made at its works at Chamalieres since 1945; the heads of state and government of the Franc Zone may decide together to change where they are printed. The Banque de France's own director general of banknote manufacturing has called the BCEAO its largest export customer. The BCEAO's published accounts do not name the maker. Its gold is mostly not in Africa. Note 6 of the BCEAO's own financial statements for 2024 lists three places: the bank's head office, the Banque de France and the Bank for International Settlements. On deposit at the Banque de France are 1,054,479.65 ounces, valued at 1,756,111 million CFA francs, out of a stock of about 1.52 million ounces worth 2,531,800 million, which is about 70 per cent; press reporting places it in the Banque de France's underground vault in the first arrondissement of Paris. The Bank for International Settlements holds close to 106,000 ounces, and only about 120,000 ounces, under 8 per cent, sit physically at the head office in Dakar. In the 2018 statements the Paris deposit was 85 per cent of holdings; the share has fallen because the rest of the stock grew, not because gold left Paris. Answering Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, the French economy ministry said the rules for the deposit are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. The concentration is contested: pan-Africanist currents and some economists read it as a continuing post-colonial dependence and ask whether the gold will be repatriated as the member states' operating account deposits at the French Treasury were. Part of its reserves sits in two funds run by other institutions. The BCEAO's own audited accounts for 2025 say it bought units in a fund called BISIP K, managed by the Bank for International Settlements, worth 205,811 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 222,297 million FCFA a year earlier, and grouped with the holdings kept for immediate liquidity. The same accounts say the bank joined the RAMP fund, the Reserve Advisory Management Program, managed by the World Bank, whose units were worth 138,800 million FCFA on 31 December 2025, down from 149,873 million FCFA a year earlier. Together the two came to 344,611 million FCFA at the end of 2025.

2011-01-22 · forced resignation. The Central Bank of West African States is the central bank of eight countries, and in January 2011 its own member heads of state removed its governor. After the disputed Ivorian presidential election of November 2010, the bank recognised Alassane Ouattara as head of state and revoked Laurent Gbagbo's access to Ivorian state accounts in December, and the union's finance ministers decided on 23 December that only representatives of Ouattara's government would have signing authority. The Ouattara camp complained in mid-January that the bank was still channelling cash to Gbagbo, and the governor, Philippe-Henry Dacoury-Tabley, an Ivorian and a close confidant of Gbagbo, was accused of not cooperating. At an emergency summit of the heads of state of the West African Economic and Monetary Union in Bamako on 22 January 2011 he handed in his resignation. The bank's own statement, issued in Dakar that evening, said the resignation resulted from pressure from the region's leaders. He told reporters afterwards: "I agreed to hand in my resignation as that is what was asked of me", and defended his conduct by pointing to practical and technical reasons for not transferring control of the accounts. The union accepted the resignation and called on Ouattara to propose a successor; a deputy governor, Jean-Baptiste Compaore, took over in the interim. Gbagbo's administration, on state television it still controlled, rejected what it called the forced resignation of the governor and rejected the leaders' decision to let Ouattara name a replacement. The European Union listed Dacoury-Tabley, giving as its ground that as governor of the BCEAO he refused to recognise the authority of the democratically elected President and was helping to fund the illegitimate administration of Mr Laurent Gbagbo. This record is the removal of the governor by the member states; what he is alleged to have done with the bank's money is recorded separately as a corruption case. Keyed to the union, so it counts for all eight member countries. Pro-Gbagbo bank head quits (Al Jazeera)

A new cooperation agreement was signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019, replacing the 1973 agreement; France stated the reform would enter into force in 2020.
The 2019 agreement ended the centralisation of BCEAO reserves at the French Treasury, ending the requirement that the BCEAO hold at least 50% of its reserves there.
The BCEAO's operations account at the French Treasury was closed in April 2021 (French Senate report); the Treasury page states it has had no operations account since January 2020.
France approved the agreement by Law no. 2021-108 of 3 February 2021.
France withdrew its representatives from the BCEAO board, the Monetary Policy Committee and the UMOA Banking Commission; one independent member of the Monetary Policy Committee is appointed in consultation with the French government.
The agreement provides that the currency will be renamed 'ECO'; the Banque de France page says the name 'is set to change' at member states' will, i.e. the CFA franc name remains in use.
ECOWAS Convergence Council (7 September 2026) kept 2027 as the target launch year for an ECOWAS single currency named the ECO.

That is about 70 per cent of the stock; the same deposit was 1,054,521.73 ounces, or 85 per cent of holdings, in the 2018 statements, the share having fallen as the rest of the stock grew rather than as gold left Paris. The French economy ministry, answering a question from Senator Pierre Laurent on 20 October 2022, said the rules for depositing the BCEAO's monetary gold with the Banque de France are set by a specific convention covering the services the Banque de France provides to the BCEAO, including financially, and that the gold, like the union's foreign exchange reserves, is pooled at the BCEAO rather than apportioned by country. Press reporting puts the Paris holding in the Banque de France's underground vault, La Souterraine, in the first arrondissement. BANK OF THAILAND
Thailand
The Bank of Thailand issues the baht and prints its own notes: its history records that the Cabinet authorised it to set up the Note Printing Works in 1961, built for Thai banknote production. It is also one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and Thailand scores 39 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. On 29 May 2001 the government fired governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul after Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said he was not satisfied with the bank's low interest rates, and Finance Minister Kittiratt Na-Ranong later pressed for governor Prasarn Trairatvorakul to be replaced over the 2.75 percent rate. More recently Pheu Thai leader Paetongtarn Shinawatra said the law keeping the bank independent gets in the way of solving economic problems, and Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin said he had no plan to remove Governor Sethaput Suthiwartnarueput. A case brought in 2001 against former governor Rerngchai Marakanond, over using the reserves to defend the baht during the Asian financial crisis, ended on 5 October 2016 when the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that he had not acted improperly, so he was acquitted. Former finance minister Surapong Suebwonglee was convicted of malfeasance for putting three representatives of banks the Bank of Thailand supervises on the committee that selects its board in 2008; he was given a one-year jail term suspended for a year and fined 20,000 baht.

Thai PBS World reported on 10 November 2024 that the selection committee for the chair of the Bank of Thailand's board was choosing between three candidates, and that the government's nominee was Kittiratt Na-Ranong, a former finance minister and deputy prime minister under Yingluck Shinawatra. The report describes Kittiratt as a Pheu Thai Party loyalist and a staunch critic of the central bank governor, Sethaput Suthiwartnarueput. More than 800 academics and economists, four former central bank governors and former bank officials signed a statement opposing the appointment, saying: "We are deeply concerned about the implications of political intervention on monetary policy." The report notes that the board chair appoints four of the seven members of the Monetary Policy Committee and takes part in choosing the next governor, whose term was due to end in September 2025, and that the decision on the chair had already been deferred twice. NATIONAL BANK OF TAJIKISTAN
Tajikistan
The National Bank of Tajikistan issues the somoni, which it keeps within a band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar. One case is recorded, as an official finding: in March 2008 the International Monetary Fund's Executive Board found the bank had supplied inaccurate information on the cotton sector, international reserves, net domestic assets and credit policy, reporting reserves of about 450 million US dollars when they were roughly a third of that and concealing that reserves were pledged as collateral for cotton loans; Tajikistan was required to repay 47.4 million US dollars. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency: 3 billion yuan with China, signed on 3 September 2015 to run three years and extendable by agreement, drawn on for 1 million yuan in January 2016; whether it is in force is not known. Its commemorative 100-somoni note, circulated on 30 October 2025, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient of Germany, that note alone and not the regular series.

p:TTO:
CENTRAL BANK OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
Trinidad & Tobago
The Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago issues the Trinidad and Tobago dollar and in practice holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar. Both of its records come out of the collapse of the conglomerate CL Financial and of the Hindu Credit Union. The commission of enquiry into that collapse, set up in November 2010 under a single commissioner, Sir Anthony Colman, found the bank's powers to regulate insurers 'fundamentally deficient', tracing that to how narrowly the Insurance Act was drawn; it said the Inspector of financial institutions tried to use the limited tools then available but that Clico and CL Financial management largely ignored them, and that the collapse might have been avoided had powers in an unpassed Insurance Bill been in force by 2008. It blamed no named bank official. The enquiry sat from March 2011 to May 2013 at an estimated cost of 36.2 million dollars, including a 7 million dollar fee for Colman. At the same enquiry, on 6 December 2012, Queen's Counsel Peter Carter put it to former governor Ewart Williams that intervening in 2006 would have kept more than 10 billion Trinidad and Tobago dollars out of danger; Williams said the bank had seen early warning signs at CLICO that year but held off to avoid a run on the insurer, and intervened in 2009. That was the questioning of a witness rather than a finding, and the claim is unconfirmed. The bank is listed as a member of the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which offers members advice, training and the management of assets without the listing saying which applies here. BDO T&T audited its accounts for 2024, De La Rue printed its 100-dollar plastic note of December 2019, and it holds 2 tonnes of gold. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and it scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. A governor was removed, though, for what he said in public. At the bank's Monetary Policy Forum on 4 December 2015, Governor Jwala Rambarran named the five largest users of the foreign exchange market by sector and the amounts they had used over three years, and said the country had entered a recession. The companies named complained to the finance minister and threatened to sue. On 22 December he was summoned to a meeting with the finance minister, Colm Imbert, and handed a bank press release recording the private and financial sectors' reaction; on 24 December 2015 the Acting President, on the advice of the Cabinet, revoked his appointment under the Central Bank Act, two and a half years before his five-year term was due to end. Imbert said he had broken several laws, and both Imbert and Prime Minister Keith Rowley said he had not backed the recession claim with government data. Rambarran said the law gave him the authority to release the names and that the public had a right to know how much foreign exchange was going to import and distribution. A deputy governor, Alvin Hilaire, replaced him. Hilaire, who was Governor from 2015 to 2025, had spent 11 years at the International Monetary Fund before that, as a senior economist and as IMF resident representative to Guinea and Sierra Leone, and worked on IMF programmes in Croatia, Colombia, Cameroon, Ecuador and Nicaragua. In June 2022 Justice Devindra Rampersad held the termination unlawful and in breach of his constitutional rights; the State appealed, and the case went on to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The governor who replaced him was then removed for the opposite conduct. Alvin Hilaire was reappointed for three years in December 2020 and again in December 2023, with his final term due to end in December 2026; his appointment was revoked on 24 June 2025, about 18 months early, with no formal grounds stated. In the weeks before it, Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar publicly accused him of refusing to provide information about the country's largest users of foreign exchange, the same information Rambarran had been dismissed for disclosing. She said at a post-Cabinet news conference in June 2025 that getting information out of the bank was like a bed of thorns or pulling teeth, that Hilaire had failed to provide information to the Auditor General in 2024 and again in 2025, and that this was a blocker to the government's efforts to investigate the foreign exchange market. He challenged the revocation in court and a settlement out of court was reported in early November 2026, with the terms not described. Six of the bank's eleven governors since December 1964 have served fewer than five years, and these two are the ones who went to court over it.

Imbert said he had violated several laws, and both Imbert and Prime Minister Keith Rowley said he had not backed his recession claim with government data. Rambarran said local law gave him the authority to release the names and that the public had a right to know how much of the foreign exchange was going to import and distribution. A deputy governor, Alvin Hilaire, replaced him in December 2015. Rambarran sued under the Constitution: in June 2022 Justice Devindra Rampersad held the termination unlawful and in breach of his constitutional rights, and ordered the bank to calculate what he was owed from dismissal to July 2017, when his term would have ended. The State appealed, and the case went on to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. CENTRAL BANK OF TUNISIA
Tunisia
The Central Bank of Tunisia issues the dinar, which follows a slowly adjusted fixed rate against the euro. On 27 June 2012 President Moncef Marzouki fired the governor, Mustapha Kamel Nabli, saying he had refused to bring monetary policy in line with the country's economic needs; the elected assembly approved the removal in July 2012. In February 2018 Tunisian prosecutors said five of the bank's agents had been arrested, two of them jailed, in a currency-trafficking investigation. They were accused of money laundering, corruption and abuse of power for exchanging small euro notes for 200- and 500-euro notes without recording the exchanges, and the bank said it had referred the operations to the courts itself. They stand charged and the accusations are unproven. One career move is documented: Marouane Abassi, a former World Bank economist who had been the World Bank's representative in Libya since 2010, became governor after parliament approved him, as reported on 16 February 2018. The bank's 2025 accounts were audited jointly by FMBZ - KPMG Tunisie and Cabinet C.M.C, it holds 6.8 tonnes of gold, and Tunisia scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Oberthur Fiduciaire, printed in the source under its former name Oberthur Technologies, printed the 20-dinar note.

CENTRAL BANK OF THE REPUBLIC OF TÜRKIYE
Türkiye
Turkiye's money is the Turkish lira, issued by the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkiye, which has shareholders: at the end of 2025 the Ministry of Treasury and Finance held 55.12 per cent, a share the law bars from falling below 51, the state-owned Ziraat Bankasi 19.22 per cent and Mervak Ic ve Dis Ticaret 5.12 per cent. Four governors have been removed by presidential decree: Murat Cetinkaya in July 2019, after the bank held its rate at 24 per cent; Murat Uysal on 7 November 2020, after the lira lost 30 per cent of its value that year; Naci Agbal on 20 March 2021, four months in and after a rate rise; and Sahap Kavcioglu on 8 June 2023, having cut rates from 19 to 8.5 per cent. His replacement, Hafize Gaye Erkan, joined Goldman Sachs in 2005, was a managing director by 2011 and went to First Republic Bank in 2014, becoming co-chief executive in 2021. Government pressure was reported in 23 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, all of it for lower rates and 21 of those quarters in election periods. In October 2025 Istanbul prosecutors took former deputy governor Sener and six others into custody and arrested him, in an investigation into corruption and tender-rigging in two 2023 tenders at the Interbank Card Center, the national payment network the bank majority-owns; that investigation is open and nothing is proven. The notes are printed at the Banknote Printing Plant, which operates under the bank itself. About 34 tonnes of its gold sit in its own vaults, about 382.9 tonnes are stored at the Turkish exchange company Borsa Istanbul and about 119.2 tonnes at the Bank of England, all safekeeping rather than management. It scores 46 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

1 documented case at the central bank:

2019 · questioned procurement at a central bank subsidiary · alleged. A September 2019 Mirror Media investigation questioned how the Central Engraving and Printing Plant, which the article describes as being under Taiwan's central bank, came to hold the contract to produce the country's new digital national identity cards. The plan was announced by Premier Su Tseng-chang on 22 August with the plant in charge and about NT$4 billion budgeted, and an open tender had been planned for October 2019. On 14 June 2019 the tender was switched to a restricted tender, which the article says was not publicly justified, and the budget reportedly rose to about NT$4.8 billion. A subcontract tender issued by Bank of Taiwan on 26 August for chip cards and printing equipment required bidders to show more than NT$1.2 billion in sales experience, which the article says no domestic firm could meet. Two anonymous domestic card makers argued the plant had no chip-card experience and that the rules favoured foreign suppliers. The article notes the plant had previously printed about 550,000 passports with a wrong airport photograph inside, at a cost to the treasury of about NT$220 million; the plant said it was only the contractor and did not lead that project. The article alleges no bribery and reports no criminal investigation, charges or court outcome. Mirror Media investigation into the Central Engraving and Printing Plant's digital ID card contract (2 September 2019)

BANK OF TANZANIA
Tanzania
The Bank of Tanzania issues the Tanzanian shilling. It scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and government pressure on it was reported in 2 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018. An audit by Ernst & Young of the bank's External Payment Arrears account found about 133 billion shillings paid out wrongly in 2005 and 2006 to 22 local companies, many phoney or using fake documents. President Jakaya Kikwete dismissed governor Ballali in January 2008, the companies were ordered to refund the money, and some lower-level defendants were jailed. In the first court cases to follow, reported on 27 May 2011, the Kisutu Resident Magistrate's Court in Dar es Salaam convicted the businessmen Farijala Hussein and Rajabu Maranda of offences related to financial impropriety, forgery and obtaining credit under false pretences, jailed them for five years and ordered them to return what they had taken. The bank is also audited by the Controller and Auditor General, and in 2024 the printing firms De La Rue and Crane Currency won its tender to reprint its banknotes. Emmanuel Tutuba was appointed governor on 7 January 2023, succeeding Florens Luoga; he came from the finance ministry, where he had been made permanent secretary to the treasury in April 2021, its most senior civil servant, a role in which he already sat on the bank's board, and he had earlier been the ministry's budget commissioner.

2008-01-09 · dismissal. President Jakaya Kikwete revoked the appointment of the governor of the Bank of Tanzania, Daudi Ballali, in January 2008, after an audit by Ernst & Young of the bank's External Payment Arrears account found that more than 133 billion shillings, about 116 million US dollars, had been paid improperly to 22 companies in the country, many of them said to be fictitious. The finance minister had brought in the auditors after allegations about payments out of the bank's commercial external debt account, which Ballali had denied, calling them rumour. A State House release said the president had been deeply angered and disappointed by what had happened at the bank. Of the 22 companies, 13 were paid about 99 billion shillings on forged documents and a further 46 billion was paid with no supporting documents at all. Ballali had been governor since 1998 and was in his second five-year term. The deputy governor, Benno Ndulu, took over. Africa Confidential reported that Ballali had resigned several weeks before he was sacked and was allowed to leave for medical treatment in the United States, and that Kikwete had been told of fraud at the bank by Deloitte & Touche and Ernst & Young, and two years earlier by Tanzania's own Controller and Auditor General, without acting. Kikwete then appointed a three-man team of the Attorney General, the Inspector General of Police and the head of the anti-corruption bureau to investigate further. This record is the removal of the governor by the head of state; the audit findings and the prosecutions that followed are recorded separately as corruption cases. Tanzania's Ballali fired over central bank fraud (Central Banking)

BANK OF UGANDA
Uganda
The Bank of Uganda issues the Ugandan shilling, and the Auditor General audits its accounts. It scores 34 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption in the country. On paper it is among the less independent central banks, scoring 0.467 of 1 on a 42-rule measure of independence written into law. One case is recorded. A confidential 2018 Auditor General report to parliament said bank managers, including governor Mutebile, acted without guidelines, regulations or policies and may have intentionally neglected aspects of the closure and sale of at least seven commercial banks, including Crane Bank in 2016 and 2017. These are the findings of a report, not court verdicts. Sudhir Ruparelia, dfcu Bank and Nile River Acquisition Company are named in the case, the last two as having received money, favours or contracts from the central bank. Parliament then put the bank through a public inquiry over the same closures. The Auditor General, John Muwanga, presented his special audit to the Speaker of Parliament on 27 August 2018; it had been requested by the chairman of Parliament's Committee on Commissions, Statutory Authorities and State Enterprises the previous November, and the bank had tried to stop it. The committee, chaired by Abdu Katuntu, took evidence from the governor, Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, his deputy Louis Kasekende and other officials from late 2018 into 2019. On 1 November 2018 Katuntu sent the governor and deputy governor away for arriving without the documents on the closures. Mutebile told the committee on 12 November that the seven banks were put under resolution largely because they were insolvent, said he had never delegated his powers to agree the sale of Global Trust Bank to DFCU Bank, and said liquidation reports had been kept from him by junior staff, which raised the question in public of whether he was in charge of his own institution; he also acknowledged that the inquiry had exposed problems at the bank. The committee's report, finalised in February 2019, recommended individual accountability for the officials implicated. Demands in Parliament for action against them later stalled. Northern Trust supplies the bank with compliance, performance and risk analysis, and a dashboard for watching the outside firms that invest its money; that is analysis and advice, not management of the money.

NATIONAL BANK OF UKRAINE
Ukraine
The National Bank of Ukraine issues the hryvnia and prints the notes itself, at the Banknote Printing and Minting Works that is part of the bank. Its independence written into law is high, 0.893 of 1, but its governors have been pushed. In January 2009 parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, voted no confidence in governor Volodymyr Stelmakh, 227 of 450 seats in favour, as the hryvnia lost nearly half its value; President Viktor Yushchenko's office called the vote illegal and kept backing him, and he was not removed. In July 2020 governor Yakiv Smolii resigned, telling President Volodymyr Zelensky that systematic political pressure had been exerted on the bank. One case is open: on 11 November 2019 the National Anti-Corruption Bureau detained seven people, including former first deputy governor Pysaruk, on suspicion of embezzling 1.2 billion hryvnia, about 49 million US dollars, from a 2014 loan the bank made to prop up VAB Bank, which was declared insolvent that November; it is unproven. Valeria Gontareva, governor from 2014 to 2017, had worked at Societe Generale, ING Bank and the Ukrainian financial services group Investment Capital Ukraine. Ukraine scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

Uruguay
Uruguay's money is the peso, issued by the Central Bank of Uruguay and held within a moving band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar as of December 2025. It scores 17 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 43, although the country scores 73 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index. One case is recorded, from 2017, and it was dismissed: prosecutor Rodrigo Morosoli, investigating the Cambio Nelson fraud at a currency exchange house, sought the formal indictment of Humberto Capote, a former president of the bank, for taking part in a continuing crime of misappropriation. Judge Marcelo Souto freed Capote at first instance, finding the evidence insufficient to prosecute him, and the prosecutor appealed in April 2017. No government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018. The accounts are audited by the Tribunal de Cuentas under the 1995 charter law. The bank is also named among the central bank clients of a fixed-income fund built around environmental and social standards, developed jointly by Amundi and the Latin American Reserve Fund; it invests in that fund rather than handing them its reserves to manage. Two people have moved between the bank and outside jobs. Guillermo Tolosa confirmed in December 2024 that he would preside over the bank once Yamandu Orsi took office as president of Uruguay; he had worked as an economist at the International Monetary Fund and as a consultant at Oxford Economics, and was academic director of the research centre Ceres from 2018 to 2020. Washington Ribeiro spent 15 years on the bank's board, as director from June 2010 to March 2020, vice president from March 2020 to July 2024 and president from July 2024 to March 2025, and on 7 April 2026 he started as head of Uruguayan macro and sovereign strategy at the Uruguayan brokerage Latin Securities.

FEDERAL RESERVE SYSTEM
United States
The US dollar is issued through the Federal Reserve System. Banks that join hold stock in their district's Reserve Bank, and at the end of 2018 Citibank held 42.8 per cent of the New York Fed and JPMorgan Chase 29.5 per cent; member banks elect six of each Reserve Bank's nine directors, though the Board says the System is not owned by anyone. It scores 54 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, more than 98 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, and its weakest side is influence from inside. Many moves between the Fed and private finance are recorded, and none is an accusation: Alfred Hayes came to the New York Fed presidency from the New York Trust Company in 1956 and became chairman of Morgan Stanley International in November 1975; Allan Sproul left that presidency in 1956 for a Wells Fargo Bank directorship; Timothy Geithner was made president of the private equity firm Warburg Pincus in November 2013; Brian Sack ran the New York Fed's Markets Group until 2012 and joined the hedge fund manager the D. E. Shaw group; Loretta Mester joined the board of the reinsurer RenaissanceRe Holdings in November 2024; and Alberto Musalem became St. Louis Fed president in April 2024, having worked at Tudor Investment Corporation, the New York Fed and Evince Asset Management. Janet Yellen's disclosures show more than 7 million dollars of speaking income, including 952,200 dollars from Citigroup. On trading by officials, the Fed's Inspector General found in September 2024 that trades made for Raphael Bostic from 2017 broke ethics rules but no insider trading law; in January 2024 that Robert Kaplan's 2020 trades looked like acting on confidential policy information, with Eric Rosengren having failed to report his; and on 15 November 2025 that Adriana Kugler's 2024 trades broke Fed rules. Jerome Powell's and Richard Clarida's trades were cleared, and Jeffrey Lacker resigned in April 2017 over a 2012 leak, without charges. President Donald Trump has said Powell should resign, the Justice Department subpoenaed the Fed in January 2026, and after he moved to fire Governor Lisa Cook the Supreme Court ruled on 29 June 2026 that she stays.
