5 documented cases at the central bank:

2024-2025 · officials trading · official finding. A report released on 15 November 2025 by the US Office of Government Ethics, after a Fed referral to its inspector general, showed that Kugler's 2024 financial disclosure listed more than a dozen individual stock trades, several during FOMC blackout periods, which violated Fed rules barring officials from holding individual stocks; the largest was an April 2024 Apple purchase of $100,000-$250,000. Former Fed governor's stock trades violated the central bank's ethics rules (AP via ClickOnDetroit)
2020-2021 · officials trading · official finding. The Fed Inspector General's January 2024 report found that Kaplan's 2020 trading created an 'appearance of acting on confidential FOMC information' and an 'appearance of a conflict of interest', and that Rosengren failed to report multiple trades and that his 2020 REIT trades created an 'appearance of a conflict of interest'. Report of Investigation on the Closing of 22-0030-I Reserve Bank Trading Activity (Federal Reserve OIG)
2019-2020 · officials trading · acquitted. The Fed Inspector General investigated Powell's December 2019 and Clarida's 2020 trades and did not find evidence that either violated laws, rules or policies then in effect, while stating that those rules 'did not sufficiently support public confidence'. No referral for law enforcement was made. Report of Investigation on the Closing of 22-0028-I Board Trading Activity (Federal Reserve OIG)
2017-2024 · officials trading · official finding. A Fed Inspector General report issued 11 September 2024 found that trades made on Bostic's behalf over about five years from 2017, including several during FOMC blackout periods, violated Fed ethics policies and 'created the appearance' of acting on confidential information and of a conflict of interest, but found no violation of federal insider trading or conflict of interest laws. Atlanta Fed official broke ethics rules but didn't violate insider trading laws, probe finds (AP via WABE)
2012-2017 · leaked decisions · resigned. In April 2017 Lacker resigned with immediate effect, stating that in October 2012 he spoke with a Medley Global Advisors analyst who held confidential information on options discussed at the September 2012 FOMC meeting and that he may have confirmed it, and that he had not disclosed this in a 2012 internal inquiry. His lawyer said the investigation was complete and no charges would be brought. Richmond Fed Head Resigns, Admits Leaking (AP via Courthouse News)

78 documented career moves between the bank and private finance, the IMF or the World Bank:

Adriana D. Kugler (Governor, Board of Governors, 13 September 2023 to 8 August 2025): from U.S. Executive Director at the World Bank Group to Federal Reserve governor. The Federal Reserve History biography says Kugler took office as a member of the Board of Governors on 13 September 2023 and resigned on 8 August 2025, and that prior to her appointment at the Board she served as the U.S. Executive Director at the World Bank Group. The page gives no dates for the World Bank role and names no private finance employer. Adriana D. Kugler (Federal Reserve History)
Alan Greenspan (former Fed chairman): from Fed chairman to advisory board of hedge fund Paulson & Co. Central Banking reported on 15 January 2008 that Greenspan, a former chairman of the Federal Reserve, would sit on the advisory board of Paulson & Co, a hedge fund it says made billions the previous year betting against the US housing market. No ethics finding is recorded. Greenspan joins Paulson & Co (Central Banking)
Alan Greenspan (former Fed chairman): from Fed chairman to senior adviser at Deutsche Bank. CNN Money reported that Deutsche Bank hired Greenspan as a senior adviser, after his tenure as Fed chairman ended on January 31 of the previous year. No ethics finding is recorded. Greenspan hired as Deutsche Bank senior adviser, August 2007 (CNN Money)
Alberto G. Musalem (President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis): from Tudor Investment Corporation to the New York Fed, then to Evince Asset Management, then to President of the St. Louis Fed. The St. Louis Fed states Alberto Musalem was managing director, partner and global head of research at Tudor Investment Corporation, then executive vice president and senior advisor to the president at the New York Fed, and then CEO, co-chief investment officer and co-founder of Evince Asset Management. He was to begin as president on April 2, 2024. St. Louis Fed Names Alberto G. Musalem as Its Next President and CEO (St. Louis Fed)
Alfred Hayes (President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 1956-1975): New York Trust Company to New York Fed presidency, then New York Fed to Morgan Stanley International as chairman. Federal Reserve History states that Alfred Hayes began his banking career in 1933 as an analyst in the investment department of the City Bank Farmers Trust Company, transferred seven years later to the bond department of the National City Bank, and joined the New York Trust Company in 1942 as an assistant secretary in the investment department. The page states he came to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from the New York Trust Company, where he had been vice president in charge of the foreign division between 1949 and 1956. He was named president of the New York Fed and vice chairman of the Federal Open Market Committee on August 1, 1956. The page states that Hayes retired from the New York Fed on August 1, 1975, and joined Morgan Stanley International Inc. as chairman in November 1975, and was named chairman emeritus in 1981. No ethics finding is recorded. Alfred Hayes (Federal Reserve History)
Allan Sproul (President, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 1941-1956): New York Fed presidency to a directorship at Wells Fargo Bank. Federal Reserve History states that Allan Sproul served as president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from January 1941 to June 1956, and was named vice chairman of the Federal Open Market Committee in 1942. The page states that in 1956 he resigned from the New York Fed and returned to California to serve as a director of Wells Fargo Bank. The page also records that he served as a director of Kaiser Aluminum and Chemical Corporation. Sproul died in 1978. No ethics finding is recorded. Allan Sproul (Federal Reserve History)
Angel Ubide (former staff economist at the International Monetary Fund): from staff economist at the International Monetary Fund to Senior Vice President and Co-Director of Global Economics at the D. E. Shaw group. The same D. E. Shaw group release says Angel Ubide joined alongside Brian Sack as a Senior Vice President and Co-Director of Global Economics in the firm's discretionary macro investing unit, and that his prior public-sector role was as a staff economist at the International Monetary Fund. The D. E. Shaw Group Further Strengthens its Macro Investing Unit with Two Senior Economist Hires (PR Newswire)
Ben Bernanke (former Fed chair): from Federal Reserve chair to senior adviser at hedge fund Citadel. In April 2015 Citadel announced that former Fed chair Bernanke, would become a senior adviser. No ethics finding is recorded. Former Fed Chair Bernanke Joins Citadel As Senior Adviser (Law360)
Beth M. Hammack (President, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland): from cohead of global financing at Goldman Sachs to President of the Cleveland Fed. The Cleveland Fed states Beth Hammack joined Goldman Sachs in 1993, was named managing director in 2003 and partner in 2010, and most recently was cohead of global financing and a member of the management committee. She was to take office as president on August 21, 2024. Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Names Beth M. Hammack as Next President and CEO (Cleveland Fed)
Brian Sack (head of the New York Fed's Markets Group from mid-2009 to 2012, executive vice president and special adviser to the bank's president; earlier six years at the Board of Governors, ending as head of the Monetary and Financial Market Analysis section): from head of the New York Fed's Markets Group to Senior Vice President and Co-Director of Global Economics in the discretionary macro investing unit of hedge fund manager the D. E. Shaw group. The D. E. Shaw group release says Brian Sack joined as a Senior Vice President and Co-Director of Global Economics in its discretionary macro investing unit, and that from mid-2009 to 2012 he served as head of the New York Fed's Markets Group, managing the Federal Reserve's System Open Market Account portfolio. It says he earlier spent six years at the Board of Governors, ending as head of the Monetary and Financial Market Analysis section. The D. E. Shaw Group Further Strengthens its Macro Investing Unit with Two Senior Economist Hires (PR Newswire)
Darryl R. Francis (President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, 1966-1976): Boatmen's National Bank and Memphis commercial banking to the St. Louis Fed presidency; chairman of Merchants Bank, Fort Smith. Federal Reserve History states that Darryl R. Francis began his career at the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis in 1944 as an agricultural economist, and that from 1949 until 1953 he was employed as a commercial banker in Memphis and later served as a vice president at Boatmen's National Bank in St. Louis. He rejoined the St. Louis Fed as a vice president in 1953, became first vice president in 1959, and became president on January 17, 1966, retiring February 29, 1976. The page states that before his retirement he also served as chairman of Merchants Bank in Fort Smith, Arkansas. He died in 2002. No ethics finding is recorded. Darryl R. Francis (Federal Reserve History)
David W. Mullins Jr. (Governor from May 21, 1990; Vice Chair from July 24, 1991; resigned effective February 14, 1994): from the Treasury to the Fed vice chairmanship, and from there to the investment firm Long-Term Capital Management. Federal Reserve History states that David W. Mullins Jr. was on the finance faculty of Harvard Business School from 1974 to 1988 and then assistant secretary for domestic finance at the US Department of the Treasury from 1988. He became a Governor on May 21, 1990 and Vice Chair on July 24, 1991, and his resignation took effect February 14, 1994. The page states that he left the Board in 1994 to join Long-Term Capital Management, which it describes as an investment firm, and names no other post-Fed employer. No ethics finding is recorded. David W. Mullins Jr. (Federal Reserve History)
Dennis P. Lockhart (President and CEO, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, 1 March 2007 to 28 February 2017): from Citibank (1971-1988), Heller Financial (1988-2001) and private equity firm Zephyr Management LP (2001-2003) to President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta. The Federal Reserve History biography says Lockhart spent 1971 to 1988 at Citicorp/Citibank, including international posts and heading a Latin American debt-to-equity swap investment programme, then 1988 to 2001 at Heller Financial as president of Heller International Group, then 2001 to 2003 as managing partner of Zephyr Management LP, which it calls a private equity firm based in New York. He became Atlanta Fed president on 1 March 2007. The page names no private finance employer after his 2017 retirement. Dennis P. Lockhart (Federal Reserve History)
Donald Kohn (Fed vice chairman 2006-2010): from Federal Reserve vice chairman to director at AlliancePartners, a firm advising banks and backed by BlackRock and BlueMountain. Fortune reported in 2013 that after leaving the Fed in 2010, Kohn became a director at AlliancePartners, which advises small and mid-sized banks on their lending portfolios and whose main investors are BlackRock and hedge fund BlueMountain. It also says he received speaking fees from events sponsored by Wall Street firms, and that he has never worked directly for a big Wall Street firm. The article records no ethics finding. Fed candidate Don Kohn's Wall Street ties (Fortune)
E. Gerald Corrigan (President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis 1980-1984 and of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from 1 January 1985 to 19 July 1993): from President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to partner at Goldman Sachs. The Federal Reserve History profile states he led the Minneapolis Fed from 1 August 1980 to 31 December 1984 and the New York Fed from 1 January 1985 to 19 July 1993, and that he joined Goldman Sachs as a partner in 1994, the year after he left. It gives no end date for the Goldman Sachs role. No ethics finding is recorded. E. Gerald Corrigan (Federal Reserve History)
Edward W. Kelley Jr. (Governor, Board of Governors, sworn in May 26, 1987; reappointed April 20, 1990; retired December 31, 2001): from the chairmanship of Investment Advisors, Inc. to a Fed governorship, with founding directorships at Southern National Bank, Westwood Commerce Bank and West Belt National Bank and a directorship at Promontory Interfinancial Network. Federal Reserve History states that Edward W. Kelley Jr. returned to Houston after earning his MBA in 1959 to become president of Kelley Manufacturing Company, the firm his father established in 1937, and expanded it into a holding company. The page states that he sold his company in 1981 and became chairman of Investment Advisors, Inc. that same year. He was sworn in as a Governor on May 26, 1987, reappointed and sworn in for a second term on April 20, 1990, and retired December 31, 2001. The page lists him as a founding director of Southern National Bank, Westwood Commerce Bank and West Belt National Bank, a director of Promontory Interfinancial Network, LLC, and a trustee of the Financial Accounting Foundation Inc., without stating whether these roles came before or after his Fed service. It names no employer after 2001. No ethics finding is recorded. Edward W. Kelley Jr. (Federal Reserve History)
Elizabeth Duke (former Fed governor): from Fed governor to Wells Fargo director, then chair of its board. American Banker reported on 15 August 2017 that Duke, a community bank executive and Fed governor before joining the Wells Fargo board nearly three years earlier, would take over as chair of the board the next year. No ethics finding is recorded. It's official: Elizabeth Duke is Wells Fargo's next chairman (American Banker)
Emmett J. Rice (Governor, Board of Governors, June 20, 1979 to December 31, 1986): from senior vice president at The National Bank of Washington to a Fed governorship. Federal Reserve History states that Emmett J. Rice taught economics at the University of California, Berkeley and at Cornell University, was a research associate at India's central bank in the early 1950s on a Fulbright fellowship, was an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York during a 1960 sabbatical, helped establish the Central Bank of Nigeria from 1962, was deputy and then acting director of the Treasury Department's Office of the Developing Nations from 1964, and was appointed alternate US director at the World Bank in 1966. The page states that he joined The National Bank of Washington in 1972 and rose to senior vice president. He was appointed to the Board by President Jimmy Carter in April 1979 and served from June 20, 1979 to December 31, 1986. The page names no private employer after his Fed service, listing only civic board seats. No ethics finding is recorded. Emmett J. Rice (Federal Reserve History)
Eric S. Rosengren (President and CEO, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, 2007 until his retirement in 2021): from Federal Reserve Bank of Boston president to the board of directors of Berkshire Hills Bancorp and Berkshire Bank, effective 5 April 2023. The Berkshire Hills Bancorp release says Rosengren was elected to the boards of Berkshire Hills Bancorp and its subsidiary Berkshire Bank effective 5 April 2023 as an independent director and financial expert, and appointed to the Risk Management, Capital and Compliance, and Audit committees. It says he previously served as president and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston from 2007 until his retirement in 2021. Berkshire Hills Bancorp news release dated April 10, 2023 (SEC Form 8-K exhibit)
Frank E. Morris (President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, August 1968 to December 1988): from vice president of Loomis Sayles and Co. to President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston. Federal Reserve History states that Morris was research director of the Investment Bankers Association in Washington from 1955 to 1961, worked at the Treasury as assistant to the secretary for debt management, and was a vice president of Loomis Sayles and Co. in Boston from 1963, before becoming president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston in August 1968, a post he held until December 1988. The page gives no end date for the Loomis Sayles role, and lists an earlier spell as a consultant at Leigh Fisher and Associates from 1948 to 1951. No ethics finding is recorded. Frank E. Morris (Federal Reserve History)
Frederic S. Mishkin (Governor, Board of Governors, September 2006 to August 2008; executive vice president and director of research, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 1994-1997): between Federal Reserve governor and consulting for the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (source gives no dates or order). The Federal Reserve History biography says Mishkin was appointed to the Board of Governors on 5 September 2006 and resigned on 31 August 2008, and that he has been a consultant to the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank and the International Monetary Fund. The page gives no dates for the consultancies and names no private finance employer. Frederic S. Mishkin (Federal Reserve History)
Frederick H. Schultz (Vice Chair, Board of Governors, took office July 27, 1979; resigned February 11, 1982): from the chairmanship of Barnett Investment Services and his own Schultz Investments to the Fed vice chairmanship. Federal Reserve History states that Frederick H. Schultz served as an artillery officer in Korea from 1952 to 1954, joined Barnett National Bank of Jacksonville in 1956, opened his own firm Schultz Investments in 1957, and was chairman of the board of Barnett Investment Services, Inc. at the time of his Fed appointment, as well as a director of Barnett Banks of Florida and several other major companies the page does not name. He was Vice Chair of the Board of Governors from July 27, 1979 until his resignation on February 11, 1982. The page states that he returned to Florida and continued public service, founding The Schultz Center for Teaching and Leadership in Jacksonville in 1997, and names no post-Fed private employer. He died in 2009. No ethics finding is recorded. Frederick H. Schultz (Federal Reserve History)
H. Robert Heller (Governor, Board of Governors, August 19, 1986 to July 31, 1989): from Bank of America to a Fed governorship, and from there to Visa U.S.A. as chief executive and then Fair Isaac Corporation. Federal Reserve History states that H. Robert Heller taught economics at UCLA from 1965 to 1971 and later at the University of Hawaii, was chief of the financial studies division at the International Monetary Fund from 1974, and from 1978 was senior vice president and director of international economic research at Bank of America in San Francisco. He was a Governor from August 19, 1986 to July 31, 1989. The page states that after leaving the Board he joined Visa, was president and chief executive officer of Visa U.S.A. from 1991 for two years, and was executive vice president of Fair Isaac Corporation from 1994 to 2001. It also lists current board seats at Bank of Marin and Bank of Marin Bancorp and at Sonic Automotive, Inc., and a past seat at BMW of North America. No ethics finding is recorded. H. Robert Heller (Federal Reserve History)
Henry C. Wallich (Governor, Board of Governors, March 8, 1974 to December 15, 1986): from securities analysis in New York City (firm not named) to the New York Fed staff and later a Fed governorship. Federal Reserve History states that Henry C. Wallich worked in the export business in Argentina and Chile and was a securities analyst in New York City from 1933 to 1940; the page does not name the firm. It states that he joined the staff of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in 1941 and was chief of its Foreign Research Division from 1946 to 1951, was a professor of economics at Yale University from 1951 to 1970 and the Seymour H. Knox Professor of Economics from 1970 to 1974, was assistant to Treasury Secretary Robert B. Anderson from 1958 to 1959, served on the President's Council of Economic Advisers from 1959 to 1961, and was a senior consultant to the Treasury from 1969 until his Board appointment. He was a Governor from March 8, 1974 until his resignation on December 15, 1986, and died in 1988. The page says he was a former director of a number of business firms but names none and gives no dates. No ethics finding is recorded. Henry C. Wallich (Federal Reserve History)
J. Charles Partee (Governor, Board of Governors, January 5, 1976 to February 7, 1986): from Northern Trust Company of Chicago to the Fed staff and a governorship, and from there to the board of State Farm Insurance and a mutual fund trusteeship. Federal Reserve History states that J. Charles Partee joined the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago as an economist in 1949, joined Northern Trust Company of Chicago in 1956 as associate economist and was its second vice president from 1958 to 1961, then joined the Board of Governors staff in 1962, holding several roles including managing director for research and economic policy from November 1973. He was a Governor from January 5, 1976 to February 7, 1986. The page states that afterwards he was a board member of State Farm Insurance and a trustee of a family of mutual funds, giving no dates and not naming the funds. No ethics finding is recorded. J. Charles Partee (Federal Reserve History)
J. Dewey Daane (Governor, Board of Governors, November 29, 1963 to March 8, 1974): from the Treasury to a Fed governorship, and from there to the vice chairmanship of Commerce Union Bank and its successor Sovran Bank. Federal Reserve History states that J. Dewey Daane rose from statistician to monetary economist, assistant vice president and vice president in charge of research at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, was a consultant to an International Monetary Fund fiscal mission to Paraguay from 1950 to 1951, became vice president and economic adviser at the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis in May 1960, and from July 1960 was assistant to the Treasury Secretary for debt management and then deputy undersecretary for monetary affairs. He was appointed to the Board by President Kennedy and served from November 29, 1963 to March 8, 1974. The page states that afterwards he was the Frank K. Houston Professor of Banking at Vanderbilt University, and a senior official including vice chairman of the board at Commerce Union Bank and its successor Sovran Bank in Nashville, with no dates given. It also lists him as a public director of the Chicago Board of Trade from 1979 to 1982, a public director of the National Futures Association from 1987 to 2002, and a director of Whittaker Corporation in Los Angeles from 1974 to 1989. No ethics finding is recorded. J. Dewey Daane (Federal Reserve History)
Janet Yellen (Fed chair until early 2018): from Federal Reserve to paid speeches for financial firms named in her disclosures. CNN reports that Yellen's financial disclosures, filed ahead of her Treasury confirmation, show she made more than $7 million from speeches in recent years, including $952,200 from Citigroup. Other firms listed include PIMCO, Barclays, Citadel, BNP Paribas, UBS, Credit Suisse, ING, Standard Chartered and City National Bank; CNN also names Google, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America and Salesforce. She pledged to seek written authorization before taking part in matters related to Barclays, Citi, Citadel, Credit Suisse and Goldman Sachs. Yellen's disclosed speaking income, January 2021 (CNN)
Jeffrey M. Bucher (Governor, Board of Governors, 1972-1976): 1st Interstate Bank of California to the Board of Governors, then on to bank boards and chairmanships including First Interstate Bank of Washington. Federal Reserve History states that from 1957 to 1972 Jeffrey Bucher worked for the 1st Interstate Bank of California, serving as its senior vice president from 1969 until his appointment to the Board of Governors on June 5, 1972. He served as a governor until his resignation on January 2, 1976. The page states that after leaving the Board he served on the board of directors of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank of California, as a trustee of Mortgage and Realty Trust in Philadelphia, as a director of Manufacturers Bank in Los Angeles from 1978 to 1980, as chairman of First Interstate Bank of Washington from 1983 to 1987, and as a member of the board of directors of Mizuho Corporate Bank of California. From 2001 to 2009 he was a member of the board of directors of MCG Capital Corporation, serving as chairman from 2007 to 2009. The page also records law-firm roles at Pepper, Hamilton & Scheetz, Bryan Cave LLP, Lillick & Charles LLP and Kozusko Lahey Harris LLP, and teaching roles. No ethics finding is recorded. Jeffrey M. Bucher (Federal Reserve History)
Jeffrey R. Schmid (President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City): from president of American National Bank and Mutual of Omaha's banking entry to Kansas City Fed president. Schmid's Federal Reserve History biography states he was president of American National Bank in Omaha from 1989 to 2007, and in 2007 was selected by Mutual of Omaha to lead its entry into banking. He took office as Kansas City Fed president on August 21, 2023. No ethics finding is recorded. Jeffrey R. Schmid (Federal Reserve History)
Jeremy C. Stein (Fed governor May 2012 to May 2014): from Fed governor to consultant for private investment firm BlueMountain Capital Management. A BlueMountain press release dated March 24, 2015 states the firm entered a consulting agreement with Stein, a Fed governor from May 2012 to May 2014. It says he will advise on monetary and macroprudential policy, financial regulation, market evolution, and risk and capital management. No ethics finding is recorded. BlueMountain Capital Management Enters Consulting Agreement with Former Fed Governor Jeremy Stein (PR Newswire)
Jerome Powell (Fed governor; chair from February 2018 to May 2026 per Fed biography): from partner at The Carlyle Group (1997-2005) to Federal Reserve governor. The Federal Reserve Board's biography states Powell was a partner at The Carlyle Group from 1997 through 2005 before joining the Board. No ethics finding on the move is recorded. Jerome H. Powell (Federal Reserve Board)
Jerry L. Jordan (President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, March 1992 to January 2003): from chief economist of Interstate Bancorp to President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. Federal Reserve History states that Jordan was at the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis from 1967 to 1975, ending as senior vice president and director of research, then senior vice president and economist at Pittsburgh National Bank from 1975 to 1980, a university dean from 1980 to 1985 with a period on the Council of Economic Advisers, and senior vice president and chief economist at Interstate Bancorp in Los Angeles from 1985 to 1992, before becoming president of the Cleveland Fed in March 1992. No ethics finding is recorded. Jerry L. Jordan (Federal Reserve History)
John J. Balles (President of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, September 1972 to February 1986): from senior vice president of Mellon National Bank to President of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. Federal Reserve History states that Balles joined the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland in 1954 as a senior financial economist, rose to vice president in charge of its credit department and special adviser on monetary policy to its president, and left in 1959 for Mellon National Bank in Pittsburgh as senior vice president over its economic and corporate planning office. He rejoined the system as the ninth president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco from 25 September 1972 to 1 February 1986. The page gives no end date for the Mellon role. No ethics finding is recorded. John J. Balles (Federal Reserve History)
John P. LaWare (Governor, Board of Governors, August 15, 1988 to April 30, 1995): from Chemical Bank & Trust and Shawmut Bank to a Fed governorship, and from there to Stewart Information Services Corp.. Federal Reserve History states that John P. LaWare began a career in finance in 1953, rose through the ranks at Chemical Bank & Trust Co. in New York, and later worked at Shawmut Bank in Boston, where he served as a Federal Advisory Council member from 1986 to 1988 and as a director of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston in 1988. He was a Governor from August 15, 1988 until his resignation on April 30, 1995. The page states that after retiring from the Board in 1995 he became an advisory director of Stewart Information Services Corp., and that he was a director of Liberty Mutual Insurance Company and a trustee of Travelers Real Estate Investors Trust, with no dates given. No ethics finding is recorded. John P. LaWare (Federal Reserve History)
Joseph A. Erickson (President, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, 1948-1961): National Shawmut Bank executive vice presidency to the Boston Fed presidency. Federal Reserve History states that in 1920 Joseph A. OWNERSHIP AND OUTSIDE CONTROL

Commercial banks that are members of the Federal Reserve System hold stock in their District's Reserve Bank; holding a set amount of stock is by law a condition of membership. The Board's FAQ states the System 'is not owned by anyone'. The stock may not be sold or pledged as collateral and does not carry the control and financial interest of common stock; member banks elect six of the nine directors on each Reserve Bank board. Federal Reserve Act section 7 (12 U.S.C. 289): stockholders with total consolidated assets over $10 billion (inflation-adjusted) receive the smaller of 6% or the high yield of the 10-year Treasury note at the last auction; stockholders at or below that receive 6%; dividends are cumulative. Aggregate surplus is capped at $6,785,000,000 and earnings beyond that go to the Treasury general fund. Federal Reserve Board FAQ 'Who owns the Federal Reserve?'; Federal Reserve Act section 7; St. Louis Fed 'Who Owns the Federal Reserve Banks?' · statute as published 2026

CENTRAL BANK OF UZBEKISTAN
Uzbekistan
The Central Bank of Uzbekistan, created in 1991, issues the country's money, held at a de facto crawling peg to the US dollar as of December 2025, meaning the rate is moved in small steps. It scores 23 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; outside influence scores 8 and corruption and secrecy around the bank 60. Written independence from government scores 0.862 of 1 on one index and 0.604 on another. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. The head of state has moved against a chairman: on 11 December 2024 presidential press secretary Sherzod Asadov announced that President Shavkat Mirziyoyev had submitted a proposal to the Senate of the Oliy Majlis for Mamarizo Nurmuratov to leave his post as chairman of the bank, which he had held since June 2017, and the announcement gave no reason; under Uzbek law the Senate acts on the president's nomination. The man who took over that day has moved between the bank and the finance ministry: Timur Ishmetov started at the bank as an economist in 2000, worked through its foreign exchange and reserves departments, was First Deputy Chairman of the State Committee for Investments in April 2017, was the bank's First Deputy Chairman from June 2017 to 2019, left to be First Deputy Minister of Finance in May 2019, was Minister of Finance from February 2020 until the end of 2022, was First Deputy Adviser to the President on economic development, investment and foreign trade policy from December 2022, and became chairman of the bank with effect from 11 December 2024. Gold holdings are 431.7 tonnes, 87.5% of reserves. A swap line, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, with China was set at 0.7 billion renminbi in April 2011; whether it is in force is not known. The notes are made by Davlat Belgisi, a state production association that the bank lists among its own subordinate organisations, taking in the Tashkent Printing Factory, the Tashkent Paper Factory and the Tashkent Mint.

EASTERN CARIBBEAN CENTRAL BANK
St. Vincent & Grenadines
St Vincent and the Grenadines shares the East Caribbean dollar with seven other places, all served by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, set up under an agreement signed on 5 July 1983. The rate has been fixed at 2.70 East Caribbean dollars to one US dollar since July 1976, and the law requires reserves worth at least 60 per cent of the currency in circulation. The bank's legal independence is 0.549 of 1 on an index of 42 rules, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power, and government pressure was reported in none of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded. After the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors; on 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, and did not decide whether the allegations were true. The country's own prime minister has since pressed the bank's governor. In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions. He wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable and that the spending invites disciplinary action, proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis, and said he had supported Antoine's appointment but wanted suitable and comfortable accommodation for him instead. On 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. The score for St Vincent and the Grenadines is 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence; the weakest part is corruption and secrecy around it, mainly laws that hide who owns money and money-laundering risk in its banks. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are made of and, by one report, printed the updated 2027 banknote family; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. The bank's 2020/2021 annual report says it continued its engagement with the World Bank's Reserves Advisory Management Partnership (RAMP), and that a second engagement was judged appropriate to go on building up its newly formed Risk and Analytics Unit, the unit that reports on the reserves portfolio; the same report says the investment guidelines for its external managers were reviewed and updated and that the foreign reserve portfolio had grown to about EC$4.6 billion. The annual report for 2024/2025 and the audited accounts to 31 March 2025 do not repeat the RAMP engagement, so it stands as a 2020/2021 fact.

In a letter dated 17 February 2025 to Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who chairs the ECCU Monetary Council, St Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves objected to the EC$22 million spent on an official residence for Eastern Caribbean Central Bank Governor Timothy Antoine, calling the spending outrageous and the roughly 10,000 square foot house a mansion of veritable palace proportions. Gonsalves wrote that the governor may wish to consider whether his continued occupancy of the office is tenable, and that the spending invites disciplinary action. He proposed that the Monetary Council sell the residence to the government of St Kitts and Nevis, and said he had supported Antoine's appointment but wanted suitable and comfortable accommodation for him instead. On 5 March 2025 Gonsalves told NBC Radio he would neither confirm nor deny sending the letter. The Monetary Council is made up of the member states' finance ministers, so this is pressure from heads of government on the union's own central bank. PM Gonsalves wants ECCB governor to consider resigning amid controversy over his official residence (Caribbean Times)

Eastern Caribbean Currency Union (monetary union)

The ECCB is the monetary authority for Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.
The ECCB agreement was signed on 5 July 1983 and the Bank was commissioned on 1 October 1983.
The EC dollar has been fixed at EC$2.70 = US$1.00 since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling to the US dollar.
Section 24(2) of the ECCB Agreement Act requires an external reserve of not less than 60% of currency in circulation and other demand liabilities.
The IMF AREAER 2023 classification lists the ECCU members as a currency board.

p:VEN:
CENTRAL BANK OF VENEZUELA
Venezuela
The bolivar is issued by the Central Bank of Venezuela. On paper the bank is protected, scoring 0.816 of 1 on an index of 42 legal rules where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power, but government pressure was reported in 18 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, including 13 demands to print money. In January 2017 President Nicolas Maduro announced the firing of bank chief Nelson Merentes, who the report says handed in his resignation, and named Ricardo Sanguino to succeed him; no reason was given. Merentes had moved the other way before that: he had been president of the central bank since 2009 when Maduro named him finance minister on 22 April 2013, two days after being sworn in as Hugo Chavez's successor, replacing Jorge Giordani, and the report calls it his third stint as finance minister without saying when the first two were. In January 2020 the prosecutor Tarek William Saab said a payments head at the bank and others had forged purchase files so the bank paid about 1.7 million US dollars to three companies it had never contracted, for goods never delivered. Eight arrest warrants were sought, the case began with a complaint by the bank's president, Calixto Ortega, and no trial or conviction is reported, so the accusations are unproven. On 29 July 2022 London's High Court ruled that Venezuelan supreme court judgments backing the Maduro-appointed board should be disregarded, keeping more than 1 billion US dollars of Venezuelan gold held at the Bank of England out of Maduro's control. Russia's state printer Goznak signed a contract to print the bank's notes in November 2019. Venezuela scores 37 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

p:VNM:
STATE BANK OF VIETNAM
Vietnam
The State Bank of Vietnam issues the dong and moves its rate against the dollar in small steps rather than leaving it to the market. On paper its law gives it almost no independence, 0.301 of 1 and 154th of 155 places, and government pressure was reported in 6 of 37 quarters up to 2018. In April 2024 the Ho Chi Minh City People's Court sentenced Truong My Lan, chair of Van Thinh Phat, to death for fraud at Saigon Commercial Bank, finding that she had ordered subordinates to bribe State Bank inspectors; state media reported that head banking inspector Do Thi Nhan took 5.2 million US dollars and deputy chief inspector Nguyen Van Hung 300,000. In October 2011 Securency, a subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign public officials to win banknote business with Vietnam's note-issuing authority between 2001 and 2004; the officials are not named. The bank's notes are printed by the state-owned National Banknote Printing Factory, whose chairman the Governor appoints. Cao Si Kiem, governor from 1989 to 1997, joined the board of the joint-stock commercial DongA Bank in March 2012 and became its chairman on 26 April 2014. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and Vietnam scores 33 of 100 on exposure to outside influence.

RESERVE BANK OF VANUATU
Vanuatu
Vanuatu's money, the vatu, is issued by the Reserve Bank of Vanuatu, created in 1980 and held within a band of 2 percent or less against the Australian dollar. The country scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank; independence written into its law scores 0.498 of 1. One case is on record. An Ombudsman report of 3 July 1996 found that governor Samson Ngwele improperly signed ten bank guarantees worth 100 million US dollars in total, without the board's approval and under pressure from Finance Minister Barak Sope, breaching the Reserve Bank Act and the Leadership Code. The guarantees went to Peter Harold Swanson for a trading programme the Ombudsman called a scam, and were still in circulation when the report was written. The report commended Ngwele's later attempts to put things right; he disagreed with its adverse comments about him. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, without a date or contract value, and the 2019 accounts were audited by KPMG, a Fiji partnership.

CENTRAL BANK OF THE REPUBLIC OF KOSOVO
Kosovo
Kosovo has no currency of its own and uses the euro; its central bank is the Central Bank of the Republic of Kosovo. It used the Deutsche Mark from September 1999 and changed to the euro in 2002, the changeover finishing on 28 February 2002 in cooperation with the ECB. No exposure score is given, because too little data exists. In July 2010 European Union law enforcement officials arrested governor Hashim Rexhepi on suspicion of abuse of position, bribery, tax evasion, trading in influence and money laundering. A judge of the EU mission Eulex threw out all the charges on December 12, and in January 2012 Eulex said its prosecutor would take no further action after losing an appeal; he was acquitted. The bank has also joined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, or RAMP. It describes that membership as building its own capacity in asset management, risk management and financial reporting rather than a handover of reserves; the World Bank, announcing an agreement signed on 16 April 2026 by Jorge Familiar and Governor Ahmet Ismaili, says a portion of the reserves will be managed from 2026.

p:ZAF:
SOUTH AFRICAN RESERVE BANK
South Africa
South Africa's money, the rand, is issued by the South African Reserve Bank, which is unusual in having private shareholders: 2,000,000 shares held by just over 800 holders, no holder allowed more than 10,000 shares alone or with associates, voting confined to South African residents at one vote per 200 shares, and no shareholder role in monetary policy, financial stability or regulation. A shareholder list as at 30 June 2022, reported secondhand, names the South African Mutual Life Assurance Society at 20,000 shares and the SA Police Widows' and Orphans' Fund at 10,520, both above that cap, with Absa Bank, Discovery, FirstRand, First National Nominees, Beluga Trust and several other companies, trusts and funds at 10,000 each. An Economic Freedom Fighters bill to have the state buy the shareholders out reached parliament's Standing Committee on Finance, where at public hearings on 2 July 2025 the National Treasury called it a forced takeover; no vote or enactment has followed. The one case against the bank ended with the finding thrown out: in June 2017 the Public Protector ordered the bank Absa to repay 1.125 billion rand over an apartheid-era rescue loan the Reserve Bank had made to Bankorp, and on 16 February 2018 the Pretoria High Court set aside that report and its remedy and ordered the Public Protector to pay part of the Reserve Bank's costs herself. The same report carried a second instruction that went further: it directed Parliament to amend section 224 of the Constitution so as to change the bank's mandate, away from protecting the value of the currency and towards economic growth. Such an instruction binds unless a court sets it aside, so the bank went to court urgently, and the governor called it a gross overreach; the High Court struck the instruction down on 15 August 2017. The Constitutional Court upheld the personal costs order on 22 July 2019 while refusing to declare that she had abused her office. Gill Marcus went from chairing Absa Group to governor from 9 November 2009, having been a deputy governor from 1999 to 2004, and former governor Tito Mboweni joined Goldman Sachs as an international adviser in 2010 and again, as a regional adviser, in February 2022; no ethics finding attaches to either move. Its banknotes are printed by the South African Bank Note Company, which the bank says is its own subsidiary, and a parliamentary reply reported in June 2016 said a large share of the country's gold is stored in the vaults of the Bank of England and other offshore bullion centres, then four million ounces, which is storage rather than management. It scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.

2017-06-19 · attempted law change. On 19 June 2017 the Public Protector, Busisiwe Mkhwebane, published a report on a 1.125 billion rand loan the South African Reserve Bank had made to Bankorp, and included remedial action directing Parliament's justice committee to amend section 224 of the Constitution so as to change the Reserve Bank's mandate, moving it away from protecting the value of the currency and towards economic growth and citizens' socio-economic rights. Under South African law such remedial action is binding unless a court sets it aside, so the Reserve Bank brought an urgent review. Governor Lesetja Kganyago called the instruction a gross overreach. The North Gauteng High Court set the mandate instruction aside on 15 August 2017 and declared it unconstitutional, and in February 2018 a second judgment set aside the rest of the report, finding the remedial action unlawful and that there was a reasonable apprehension of bias. The High Court ordered Mkhwebane to pay 15 percent of the bank's costs personally on a punitive scale, with her office paying the remainder; the Constitutional Court upheld that order on 22 July 2019, while dismissing the bank's separate application for a declaration that she had abused her office. Parliament and the finance minister also went to court against the instruction. Public Protector's remedial action on Reserve Bank's mandate is set aside by High Court (TimesLIVE)

Common Monetary Area (common monetary area)

The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho; it was replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and by the Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined.
Member currencies have been pegged to the rand at par since their introduction; they are legal tender only in the issuing country.
Lesotho and Namibia must fully back their currency issues with rand assets; Eswatini does not face this requirement.
The rand has not been de jure legal tender in Eswatini since 1986.
South Africa makes compensatory payments representing an imputed return on rand circulating as legal tender in Lesotho and Namibia; Eswatini has received none since 1986.

RESERVE BANK OF ZIMBABWE
Zimbabwe
The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe issues the ZiG, which circulates alongside foreign currency. From 2003 to 2013, under governor Gideon Gono, it ran quasi-fiscal activities, handing out cash and farm equipment at events presided over by President Mugabe and raiding private foreign-currency accounts to fund state operations, leaving debts of close to 1.3 billion dollars that a 2014 government bill moved onto taxpayers. In 2009 the Movement for Democratic Change demanded Gono be replaced, saying Western donors would not fund reconstruction until he went; Mugabe said he would stay, and he was not removed. Gono stepped down in December 2013, and in March 2014 finance minister Patrick Chinamasa, citing President Robert Mugabe, announced the appointment of John Mangudya, then chief executive of the Harare-based commercial bank CBZ, to head the bank from 1 May 2014. At a parliamentary Public Accounts Committee hearing in September 2019, deputy governor Mlambo confirmed the bank had issued 663.8 million US dollars in Treasury Bills in 2017 and 2018 to Sakunda Holdings, owned by presidential ally Kudakwashe Tagwirei, on Finance Ministry instruction; the committee also cited a 1.37 billion dollar overdraft issued without parliamentary approval. Both matters stand as official findings. Government pressure was reported in 8 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, always to ease policy. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is an international lender based in Washington, United States, tied to 16 central banks and one other party. Its former staff have gone on to lead central banks. Kamau Thugge went from IMF staff to governor of the Central Bank of Kenya, and Reza Baqir from IMF staff to governor of the State Bank of Pakistan. Agustín Carstens went from IMF deputy managing director to governor of the Bank of Mexico, and Raghuram Rajan from IMF chief economist to governor of the Reserve Bank of India. Ahsan H Mansur went from IMF staff to governor of Bangladesh Bank. These are career moves, not accusations. The IMF also appears in cases. In May 2023 Argentina's central bank used 99.2% of a transfer limit it had agreed with the IMF. In December 2021 Malawi police arrested Kabambe and Mwanamvekha, saying they falsified figures to make the IMF believe Malawi met loan conditions. In March 2008 the IMF Executive Board found that the National Bank of Tajikistan had supplied inaccurate information, including reporting reserves of about $450 million when they were roughly one-third of that, and Tajikistan was required to repay $47.4 million. The IMF also sits on the Financial Stability Board.

n:Securency:
COMPANY · PART OF RESERVE BANK OF AUSTRALIA
Securency

Melbourne, Australia

Securency is a banknote-material company in Melbourne, Australia, tied to six central banks. It was a 50-50 joint venture of the Reserve Bank of Australia and Innovia, and it is now called CCL Secure. It supplies the polymer plastic used for the Bank of Canada's banknotes that began circulating in 2011. In October 2011 Securency and Note Printing Australia pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign officials to win banknote business with the note-issuing authorities of Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Nepal. Securency paid a penalty of A$19,809,772. Its former chief financial officer received a suspended six-month sentence for false accounting in 2012, and its agent Radius Christanto a suspended two-year sentence in 2013. The officials who received the benefits are not named. In Nigeria, the anti-corruption agency EFCC questioned former governor Soludo around 2013 in a probe into whether Securency bribed Central Bank of Nigeria officials to win a contract to print polymer notes between 2006 and 2008. No outcome is given.

n:Note Printing Australia:
COMPANY · PART OF RESERVE BANK OF AUSTRALIA
Note Printing Australia

Craigieburn, Victoria, Australia (marker placed at the country, not the exact office)

Note Printing Australia (NPA) is a banknote printer in Melbourne, Australia, wholly owned by the Reserve Bank of Australia and tied to nine central banks. In 2006/07 it produced 245 million notes for the Reserve Bank of Australia and filled export orders for the central banks of Chile, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Brunei, Singapore and New Zealand. In October 2011 NPA and Securency pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign officials to win banknote business in Indonesia, Malaysia and Nepal. NPA paid a penalty of A$1,856,710. The officials are not named. Separately, a former Bank Negara Malaysia official, Mohamad Daud, was charged in July 2011 with taking two bribes of RM50,000 each in 2004-2005, linked to a RM95 million polymer note contract won by NPA. The Shah Alam Sessions Court acquitted him on 6 December 2015 without calling his defence, and the Attorney-General withdrew the appeal in February 2016.

n:De La Rue:
COMPANY
De La Rue

Basingstoke, United Kingdom

De La Rue is a banknote printer based in Basingstoke, United Kingdom, tied to eight central banks. It prints notes for the Bank of England (a 500 million pound contract decided 29 September 2014, extended to 2028), Kenya, Sweden, Libya, South Sudan, Tanzania and, per a trial witness, historically for Nigeria. In South Sudan, a UN report said it sent about 1.4 million dollars between 2016 and September 2017 to a Nairobi account held by a Bank of South Sudan consultant, against a contract worth about 144 million dollars, and noted 'suspected corruption'. The UK Serious Fraud Office opened an investigation in July 2019 and closed it in June 2020 without charges. In September 2010 De La Rue said some employees had falsified banknote paper test certificates, followed by a supply suspension to the Reserve Bank of India.

n:Surinamese court:
COURT
Surinamese court

Paramaribo, Suriname

The Surinamese court is a criminal court in Paramaribo, Suriname, that heard two cases tied to the Central Bank of Suriname. On 17 December 2021 it sentenced Hoefdraad, a former finance minister, in his absence to 12 years and a fine of 500,000 Surinamese dollars for a conspiracy to defraud the central bank. On 31 January 2022 it convicted former governor van Trikt of corruption, forgery, embezzlement, money laundering and taking part in a criminal enterprise, in a case involving over 800,000 dollars. It gave him eight years and the same fine, and the bank's legal director and others were also convicted. On appeal in January 2026 Hoefdraad's term became 10 years and van Trikt's became six. Hoefdraad, who left Suriname in 2020, calls his case a political show trial.

Credit Suisse is a bank based in Zurich, Switzerland, tied to four central banks. Stema Cambios is an exchange house in Argentina. La Nación reported on 17 April 2026 that the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic (BCRA) is examining a circuit that moved at least 900 million US dollars between January 2022 and October 2023. In it, dollars bought at the official rate allegedly ended up in the parallel market through exchange houses. The BCRA opened procedures against officials over its ethics rules, after raids at the bank that followed reports from the UIF and Procelac. The companies deny wrongdoing. The matter is unproven.

n:Bank for International Settlements:
INTERNATIONAL BODY
Bank for International Settlements

Basel, Switzerland

The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) is based in Basel, Switzerland, and is tied to 63 central banks. Those 63 own it; its capital is held by central banks only, and private shares were bought back in 2001. Examples are the Bank of Algeria, the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic and the Reserve Bank of Australia. It also appears in the revolving-door record of the Deutsche Bundesbank: Joachim Nagel, Bundesbank Executive Board member 2010-2016 and President since January 2022, moved to the KfW Executive Board and later to the BIS.

Source says: Bank of Japan (Japan). The Bank for International Settlements holds gold reserves belonging to the Bank of Japan (Japan). A Bank of Japan statistics notice explains that the Bank's gold claims on the Bank for International Settlements were moved out of a "Gold Sight Account" and into a "Gold Ear-marked Account" with the BIS, an ear-marked account being gold held for the depositor. The notice says "The Bank of Japan opened its sight account by paying US dollar cash and the BIS purchased gold using the cash", that "Sight account holders can withdraw the equivalent amount of gold anytime", and that "the claims are now booked as 'gold' together with the existing gold holdings by the Bank." It calls the change technical, with no new gold bought. The notice dates from 2000 and covers only this portion of the holding; the Bank of Japan does not say where its other gold sits. n:Financial Stability Board:
FORUM
Financial Stability Board

Basel, Switzerland

The Financial Stability Board is a forum based in Basel, Switzerland, where central banks and other financial authorities take part. It is chaired by Andrew Bailey, who is Governor of the Bank of England, and its member list was last updated on 1 October 2026. Twenty-six central banks and seven other parties are tied to it. The central banks named include those of Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, Hong Kong, India and Indonesia. For each country the board lists the institutions that sit on it, usually the finance ministry and the central bank, and sometimes a market or banking regulator such as the Securities and Exchange Board of India or Germany's BaFin. Officials of these central banks take part in the board. The same central banks also belong to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).

n:Crane Currency:

Crane Currency

Dalton, United States

Crane Currency is a banknote printer based in Dalton, United States. A release from Curaçao says it is headquartered in Massachusetts, has plants in Malta and Sweden, and supplies more than 50 central banks. Seven central banks are tied to it. It prints for Curaçao and Sint Maarten (the new Caribbean guilder), Liberia, and Tanzania, where Crane Currency of Malta was one of two winners of a tender reported on 28 May 2024 to reprint the 10,000, 5,000, 2,000 and 1,000 shilling notes. It has supplied banknotes or related materials to Mexico, Guyana and Aruba. It has supplied banknote paper and security features to the US Treasury since 1879, though the customer there is the Treasury, not the Federal Reserve. In Liberia, Crane printed under two contracts totalling 15 billion Liberian dollars at a cost of US$15,331,689.20. A presidential investigation team alleged that Crane conspired with Central Bank of Liberia officials to print 18,151,000,000 Liberian dollars, more than contracted, and its report also named former governor Charles Sirleaf. Crane denied wrongdoing and kickbacks and said it had not been charged. This is an allegation and no court has found it proven.

n:World Bank Treasury Reserve Advisory a:
INTERNATIONAL BODY
World Bank Treasury Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership (RAMP)

Washington, DC, United States

The Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, RAMP, is run by the World Bank's treasury department in Washington, DC, and offers member central banks three things: advice, training for senior staff, and the actual handling of money. Fourteen central banks are tied to it, and what each gets differs. Guatemala, Trinidad and Tobago, Cambodia and Bulgaria are listed only as members, Bulgaria also co-hosting a RAMP forum. Ecuador, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Cape Verde, Liberia, Libya and Zimbabwe signed up for advice, technical assistance or capacity building. Armenia rejoined for advice and training, after membership from 2006 to 2014. Paraguay joined in 2017 and used RAMP advice to rewrite its own investment policy, still running its reserves itself. Only in Seychelles does RAMP run money: a portfolio of international reserves first funded with 100 million US dollars in 2019 and still held at the end of 2025.

18 central banks tied to it.

n:French Treasury:
GOVERNMENT
French Treasury

Paris, France

The French Treasury is a government body based in Paris, France. It is tied to 15 central banks, and ten of them are: the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) as it operates in Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo, and the Bank of Central African States (BEAC) in Cameroon and the Central African Republic. In each case the tie is a guarantee. France backs the currency the bank issues under a cooperation agreement. The West African CFA franc is fixed at 1 euro for 655.957 CFA francs, and France promises unconditional and unlimited convertibility, meaning it advances money to the central bank if its foreign exchange reserves run out. The Central African CFA franc has the same rate. The euro replaced the French franc as its anchor on 1 January 1999 with no change in the rate, and France commits euro funds if the region cannot pay for imports in foreign currency. These are cooperation arrangements, and the text reports no wrongdoing.

Lisbon, Portugal

The Government of Portugal is based in Lisbon, Portugal. It is tied to one central bank, the Bank of Cape Verde. Portugal guarantees the currency that bank issues, the Cabo Verde escudo, under a cooperation agreement on exchange rates. The agreement, called the Acordo de Cooperação Cambial, was signed on 13 March 1998. The rate was set at 0.55 Cape Verde escudos per Portuguese escudo, and it became 110.265 Cape Verde escudos per euro. This is a currency arrangement between the two countries, and no wrongdoing is reported.
